| Symbol | Name | What it stands for in a data centre |
|---|---|---|
| E | energy / excitation | how hard the system is being driven: queues, overload, power, heat |
| U | order parameter | how healthy and settled the system is: +1 healthy basin, -1 failed basin |
| I[U] | integrated need | unmet need accumulated over time: memory of pressure that has not been relieved |
| S | stress | slow structural stress from heat, power, network, security, staleness |
| B, Ḃ | bath and its rate | a damped oscillator driven by stress: the slow "tide" of physical load |

### 21.2 The equations (omnicompass/core.py, lines 5-12)

```
(1) dE/dt     = −α[E] E + β[int] + β[ext] + v[eff]
(2) dU/dt     = μ U (1 − U²) − (dE/dt)/E[max] − λ[U] U + u,          |u| ≤ 25
(3) dI[U]/dt  = (1 − U) − σ₁ E − δ S − λ[I] I[U]
(4) v[eff]    = cos(ω[B] t / 2) · c · tanh(λ₀ + λ₁ (U − 0.5) + λ₂ S)
(5) Φ(S)      = αₛ S² / 2 + βₛ S³ / 4 − δ S
(6) dS/dt     = −dΦ/dS = δ − αₛ S − (3/4) βₛ S²
(7) dB/dt     = Ḃ ;   dḂ/dt = γ[c] δ S − (ω[B] / Q[B]) Ḃ − ω[B]² B
(8) R[B]      = finite-difference audit of (7) at every step, never fed back
```

Each term does one job:

- **(1) Energy.** Energy decays at rate α[E] = 3.487. It is driven by two forcings: internal pressure `β[int]` (queue and
  overload) and external pressure `β[ext]` (power, heat, network, staleness, security). The drive term `v[eff]` (4) is
  bounded by `c` through the hyperbolic tangent, so no input can drive E without limit. This is the saturation (the tanh
  "speed limit"): however extreme the observation, the engine's response rate is capped at c = 1.
- **(2) Order.** `μ U (1 − U²)` is a double-well (bistable) drift with two stable basins, U = +1 (healthy) and
  U = -1 (failed), and an unstable ridge at U = 0. A rise in energy (`dE/dt`) pushes U out of the healthy basin. `u` is
  the bounded control input.
- **(3) Integrated need.** I[U] grows while U is below 1 (the system is not settled). It is reduced by energy and stress
  already being dealt with, and it leaks at λ[I] = 0.719. It is the engine's memory of unrelieved pressure.
- **(5)-(6) Stress.** A cubic potential (the "well in the basin"). S rolls downhill to its stable root. This is the
  slowest restoring force.
- **(7) Bath.** A damped harmonic oscillator (natural frequency ω[B] = 1, quality Q[B] = 2.5) driven by stress. It turns
  stress into a smooth, lagged "tide". It is the only second-order element.
- **(8) Audit.** The bath equation is re-checked numerically every step. The check is never fed back.

Integration: classical 4th-order Runge-Kutta, 10 micro-steps of 0.01 per macro step (`rk4_step`, `macro_step`). The C++
twin matches the Python to 3.6e-15 on 500 reference trajectories.

### 21.3 From telemetry to state (omnicompass/adapter.py, `observe_vector`, `assimilate`)

Each decision the telemetry is normalised to nine observations: q (queue), load, power, thermal, network, drift, stale,
security, conflict. An observed state is computed from them:

```
E[obs]   = 0.25 q + 0.18 max(0, load − 0.85) + 0.16 power + 0.13 thermal + 0.10 network + 0.08 drift + 0.06 conflict + 0.04 stale
U[obs]   = 1 − (0.27 q + 0.18 power + 0.16 thermal + 0.12 network + 0.12 drift + 0.10 conflict + 0.05 stale)
S[obs]   = 0.36 thermal + 0.28 power + 0.18 network + 0.10 security + 0.08 stale − 0.20 q
B[obs]   = 0.52 power + 0.26 thermal + 0.22 drift
I[obs]   = q + drift + conflict
β[int] = 0.58 q + 0.42 max(0, load − 0.75)        β[ext] = 0.33 power + 0.27 thermal + 0.20 network + 0.12 stale + 0.08 security
```

The state is blended toward the observed state with weight a = 0.339: `x ← (1 − a) x + a x[obs]`. It is then evolved
by one macro step (0.1 engine time units) of equations (1)-(7).

### 21.4 From state to action (the allocation law, `Governor.step`)

```
push     = u(x) / 25,  u(x) = clip(−f[U](x) + 12 (1 − U), −25, 25)        equation (2)'s controller, evaluated, not applied
ρ*     = clamp(ρ₀ − k[I] I[U] − k[E] E, ρ[min], ρ₀)                      target utilisation (the HPA target)
n[req]    = ceil(n load / ρ*) + ceil(k[q] q n)                               machines wanted
release  only while push ≤ push_release (the engine reports convergence), after band and dwell
cap      = clamp(cap_now load (1 + margin), cap_min, 1) when calm, U ≥ U[gate] and the line clean for the governor's
           own clear time (omni-v15: the request cannot switch back and forth at one threshold); 1 under backlog or a breach;
           always ≤ 1 − cap_gain max(0, B − B[cap])                         the bath limits the power cap
change   permitted only while U ≥ U[gate] and no security block
rollback authorised if S ≥ S[rollback], U is falling, or a security block is seen
```

### 21.5 Which equation drives which muscle

| Muscle | Engine quantity used | Where |
|---|---|---|
| HPA target (pods) | rho* from I[U] and E, equations (1) and (3) | adapter `Governor.step`; live `omni_controller/controller.py` |
| Node pool (machines) | n[req] from load, queue and rho*; release gated by push from equation (2) | same |
| Power cap (pod CPU limits, CPU frequency, GPU limit) | cap from U gate and bath B, equation (7) | same; `omni_controller/muscles.py` |
| Rollout guard | change_permitted (U), rollback (S, dU) | `muscles.py` |
| Security hold | security observation raises S and blocks expansion | adapter, shield |
| Speed-first law | rho* for pods; push gates machine release | `omnicompass/speed.py` |
| Right-sizing | rho* sizes CPU; E widens the memory margin; push gates scale-in | `omnilab/rightsize.py` |
| Cold start | rho* sizes instances; I[U] sets how long to keep warm | `omnilab/coldstart.py` |
| GPU packing | I[U] pre-warms nodes; push gates power-off | `omnilab/gpupack.py` |
| Training power | E tightens the applied ramp limit under sustained grid stress | `omnilab/powersmooth.py` |
| GPU health | S and E shorten the checkpoint interval | `omnilab/health.py` |
| Cooling | E widens the inlet-temperature margin | `omnilab/cooling.py` |
| Inference | the full allocation law (node_delta) sizes replicas | `omnilab/inference.py` |
| Agent containment | I[U] throttles; the security observation contains | `omnilab/containment.py` |
| VM energy | I[U] and E raise the learning rate when attribution goes stale | `omnilab/vmenergy.py` |

### 21.6 Measured: what the equations actually do inside the governor

Measured on a real observation stream (fleet plant, web services, fleet mode, 360 decisions):

| Mode (eigenvalue of the Jacobian at the operating point) | Time constant | In decisions |
|---|---|---|
| -7.90 | 0.13 | 1.3 |
| -3.10 | 0.32 | 3.2 |
| -0.72 | 1.39 | 13.9 |
| -0.20 +/- 0.98i (the bath) | 5.0, period 6.4 | 50, rings every 64 decisions |
| -0.17 | 6.0 | 60 |

- **Every mode is stable** (all real parts negative). The operating point is a stable equilibrium inside the healthy basin:
  E = 0.095, U = 0.976, S = 0.315, B = 0.10. This is the basin keeping everything in, stated as mathematics.
- **Per decision, the equations and the observation move the state about equally.** Across all six variables the
  equations contribute 45-50% of each step's movement and the observation blend the rest.
- **Equation (2)'s control input u is not applied during governance.** The engine evolves open-loop (u = 0). The control
  law is evaluated only to produce `push`, which decides when capacity may be released.
- **Compute:** about 95 microseconds per decision in Python, and about 2.9 microseconds in the C++ twin.

### 21.7 What this explains, and what it points to

- **Why "engine off" scores close to "engine on" in the muscle benchmarks.** With the equations frozen, the observation
  blend still moves the state. Both versions are then low-pass filters of the same telemetry. The engine's fast modes
  (1-3 decisions) behave almost like the blend itself. Its distinct contribution is its slow memory: I[U] (14 decisions),
  S (60) and the bath (period 64 decisions). The muscle mappings mostly read E and rho*, which live on the fast modes.
- **The engine clock is not matched to the workload's rhythm.** One decision advances engine time by 0.1. At 60-second
  decisions the bath rings every 64 minutes, but web demand has a 24-hour rhythm and training power a 2-second one. This
  is a wiring choice in the adapter (engine time per decision), not a property of the equations.
- **The controller in equation (2) is unused as an actuator.** Wiring its output u (or U's trajectory under u) directly
  to the actuators is the unexplored way to "let the math do the work".

Three wiring experiments follow directly. None changes a single equation:

1. **Clock matching.** Set engine time per decision so that the bath's natural period equals the workload's rhythm.
   The oscillator in (7) then carries the cycle and can anticipate it.
2. **Slow-mode actuation.** Drive machines from I[U], S and B (the memory modes) rather than E (a fast mode).
3. **Closed-loop actuation.** Apply equation (2)'s u and use its magnitude, not only its sign, as the actuator command.

Each is testable in the existing harness against every platform in the league (tuning/league.py), and will be tested
there.


### 21.8 One pedal: push, lift off, idle, reset, and the kill switch

Omni-Compass drives a system the way a self-driving car drives itself: it feels, gauges and adjusts, with nobody in
the seat. The words below are used the same way everywhere in this repository.

**Two names only.** **native** is the system as it runs on its own (Kubernetes and its autoscalers, the card's
firmware, CityLearn's controller). **omni** is Omni-Compass on top of native: the same native system, with Omni-Compass
governing it. Omni-Compass never runs instead of native, only on top of it, so every comparison is native against omni.

**The modes.** Off (manual): Omni-Compass not driving, native runs alone. Watching: Omni-Compass reads every gauge and
logs what it would do, and writes nothing. Autopilot: the one pedal below. Cruise and idle at once: for work that comes
as a pile.

| Term | Meaning | In the code |
|---|---|---|
| **Push** | Traffic climbs and capacity is added at once, never held back; the whole cluster can take work the instant it is needed | (8.3); a lower HPA target is never limited |
| **Lift off** | Traffic falls and capacity is eased off a step at a time, handed back toward native, never below idle | (8.4)-(8.5); coasting, rule 6 |
| **Idle** | The pedal lifted all the way: calm traffic, the engine running at its floor (two machines in service, ready) | `MIN_NODES`, the floor of the staging law (8.8) |
| **Reset** | Every setting the governor ever wrote is handed back to where native had it, read back, and the record removed; the next run starts fresh. Every benchmark arm ends with one and checks it | the reset file (`--kill-file`, a name kept for compatibility), `Controller.restore` |
| **Cruise** | A pile of work waiting for a place: machines in service up to the pool's own top, read live (a fixed pool's every machine at once, a growing pool a step a decision), held there without second-guessing, until the line has been empty for two decisions | rule 7, `--cruise-after` |
| **Idle at once** | The work is done and demand is at zero (the service at its least pods, wanting no more, at half its target or less): the pedal lifted all the way in one move, straight to idle (the floor), every safety check still holding | rule 8, `--idle-demand`, amendment 9 |
| **Kill switch** | Security only: one switch in a human hand that turns Omni-Compass's governing off across the whole system at once, for anything rogue or anyone trying to drive a system through Omni-Compass's brain | `omnicompass/master.py`, `tools/omni_switch.py off` |

The floor is a number the operator sets; lifting off never takes the system below it, however far the pedal is
lifted. Earlier dated records, and the sealed original engine files, call the reset a "kill switch"; they
are kept word for word.

### 21.9 The staging law: machines on and off in order, with demand that moves

Demand climbs, spikes, eases part way, climbs again and settles to idle. The staging law decides how many machines are
in service at every decision, and which ones, so that capacity follows demand up at once and comes back down only as
far as it safely can. It is the compass law (`omnicompass/compass_law.py`) applied to the machine pool
(`omni_controller/controller.py`), the release gate (`omnicompass/nervous_system.py node_release_gate`), the verdict
(`omnicompass/verdict.py`) and the actuator (`scripts/kind_nodepool.sh`). Every symbol below is a line of that code.

**Position and force.** The service reading r (the 95th-percentile response time, or the pressure that stands for it)
is placed in its band [lo, hi], where hi is the response line:

    p = (r - lo) / (hi - lo),      v = s v + (1 - s) (p - p_prev) / dt                       (8.1)
    F = A                                       if p >= 1 - c        (fail up, past the wall)
    F = A tanh( (kp (p - p0) + kd v) / A )      otherwise; F = 0 if F < 0 while v > 0 and p > p0   (8.2)

with the band's center p0 = 0.5, cushion c = 0.05, authority A = 1, kp = 1 and kd = max(0, 2 sqrt(kp tau / dt) - 1) dt
(critical damping for a muscle that answers in tau seconds). F > 0 asks for capacity, F < 0 offers it back.

**How many machines.** With n machines in service now, n[nat] the count native ran, m the floor (two by default, `MIN_NODES`) and M the
machines that exist (every machine usable; an operator may hold whole machines back with `NODE_CUSHION`, off by
default), every count stays in m <= n' <= M. The protection is not a machine sitting out: it is the band inside every
machine. Capacity is added at 95% of the response line, before the line is reached (8.2-8.3), and a machine goes back
only if the ones left still run at or under the engine's utilisation target rho (8.5): a margin spread over all of
them.

    up      n' = min(M, max(m, n + 1))                              if p >= 1 - c                     (8.3)
    down    n' = max(m, n - 1)                                      if F < R and p < p0 and the verdict
                                                                    allows n_nat - (n - 1) and the gate G holds  (8.4)
    hold    n' = n                                                  otherwise

with the release threshold R = -0.2. Up is immediate and is never gated. Down is one machine per decision, never below the floor, and only
when every term of the release gate holds:

    G = [n > 1] and [nothing pending] and [pods not scaling up] and [no breach now] and
        [ used / ((n - 1) x per_node) <= rho ] and [contraction authority] and [every sense live] and
        [the last machine command landed]                                                          (8.5)

rho is the engine's utilisation target: after a machine goes back, what remains runs at or under rho. The verdict
(section 21.7 of the GPU preregistration, `omnicompass/verdict.py`) allows a machine count below native only after a
paired trial showed the service at that count at most a 2% LOSS than at the count before; that 2% is where the trigger
sits, inside the engine.

**This is hysteresis by construction.** The up condition (p >= 0.95) and the down condition (p < 0.5 with F < -0.2)
are far apart, so a demand that hovers never makes machines flap; a spike crosses the wall and adds a machine at once;
a dip has to be deep, calm and sustained before one goes back, and then only one per decision. Between the two, the
count holds.

**Which machines.** The actuator orders the pool:

    idle   the open machine with the fewest serving pods, then the fewest pods, goes first;
           it is marked prefer-not (PreferNoSchedule) and its pods first to go (pod-deletion-cost), so the
           autoscaler's own scale-down empties whole machines; no pod is moved, evicted or restarted   (8.6)
    wake   the idle machine still carrying the most work goes first (it is warm); the mark comes off and it is in
           service at once, with no boot                                                          (8.7)
    floor  two machines always in service (MIN_NODES, the operator may set more), ready for a spike  (8.8)
    margin  every machine usable; the cushion is the band inside each one (the 5% before the line, and rho), not a
            whole machine held out                                                                 (8.9)

An idled machine stays powered and Ready at its floor (park_frac x idle power), never off: a pod that finds the open
machines full lands on it at once, so no request ever waits on a machine Omni-Compass idled. Where a node autoscaler
underneath really removes an empty machine (Azure's cluster autoscaler, Karpenter), that same order hands it the
emptiest machine first, and the bill falls with the machine.

**The same law on every discrete unit.** Machines are one case. In the muscle models (`realms/compass_arm.py
release_safe`), a cooling plant's chillers and a compute pool's machines follow the same law: one unit back only when
the units left cover the recent peak with headroom (RELEASE_MARGIN 0.6 for machines, 0.8 of a unit's capacity for
chillers), one at a time, and back at once when the wall is reached.

**What is proved, measured and open.** The order (8.6)-(8.8) is checked through the real actuator by
`tests/test_staging_order.py` (the emptiest idles first, the warmest wakes first, two always in service, every machine usable, no pod moved).
The gate (8.5) is checked by `tests/test_node_release_gate.py`. On real Kubernetes the law gave the same work 55-65%
faster on 29-36% fewer machines (sets 22-27) and 48% more work on the same machines (the capacity test); its run under
demand that wanders (up, spike, part way down, back up, idle) is in progress. Open: an order across different kinds of
unit (a battery before a generator, a CPU before a GPU) is not wired; each pool is ordered within itself.

### 21.10 The state each muscle carries, and the modes as a state machine

**9.1 The compass on a muscle is a dynamical system, so its state must persist.** On muscle i the compass carries
zᵢ = (pᵢ, vᵢ, xᵢ): the position of the service in its band, its velocity, and the knob's continuous value. At each
decision k, with reading rₖ:

    pₖ = (rₖ - lo) / (hi - lo),   vₖ = s vₖ₋₁ + (1 - s)(pₖ - pₖ₋₁) / dt,   Fₖ = F(pₖ, vₖ) by (8.2)    (9.1)
    xₖ₊₁ = clamp( xₖ + sigma g(Fₖ) Fₖ (x[hi] - x[lo]), x[lo], x[hi] ),   g = UP if Fₖ > 0 else DOWN          (9.2)

with x₀ the native value and sigma = +1 when a higher value is more capacity. Two properties depend on z persisting:
(a) the knob integrates the force, xₖ - x₀ = sum_j sigma g Fⱼ span (until the cover binds), so a calm muscle eases
step by step toward its cover; and (b) the damping term kd vₖ needs pₖ₋₁. If z were made fresh at every decision
(pₖ₋₁ = pₖ, v = 0, xₖ = x₀), (9.2) would collapse to xₖ₊₁ = clamp(x₀ + sigma g F(pₖ, 0) span): a memoryless map
of the present reading, at most one step from native, with no damping. That is a different, weaker law. A renamed
attribute did exactly that on 2026-10-05; `tests/test_compass_arm.py` now fails if the compass is ever made twice on one
muscle.

**9.2 The modes.** The live controller is in exactly one mode at each decision. With qₖ the pods waiting for a place,
uₖ the scaling-up flag, c the cruise count (`--cruise-after`, 2), M the machine ceiling and m the floor:

    cruise on      q_j > 0 for the last c decisions                                                   (9.3)
    cruise off     q_j = 0 and not u_j for the last c decisions                                       (9.4)
    in cruise      n' = min(M, n + s), M the pool's own top read live, s the step; the service's autoscaler target held at the operator's own; the floor step
                   makes no read and no write                                                         (9.5)
    idle at once   (not cruising) q = 0, no breach, not u, every sensed service idle or at demand
                   <= b, the gate G (8.5) holds, every sense live, the last command landed:
                   n' = max(m, smallest n carrying the CPU in use at rho)                             (9.6)
    idle (a service at its floor)   I(h) := current = min = desired, and u_h <= target_h / 2          (9.7)
    push / lift off / idle         (8.3) / (8.4)-(8.5) / (8.8)

**9.3 Why cruise steps back (9.5).** In cruise the machines climb to the pool's own top (a fixed pool's every machine
at once, n = M; a growing pool a step a decision), so the floor step's only action (raise n to the floor the waiting pods
need) adds nothing the climb does not already give: for a fixed pool floor <= M = n. Its reads (every pod, every node, node
metrics, every HPA, each five seconds) carry no value of information, so removing them cannot change any action; they
only cost CPU and API-server time on the machines the queue is using. The service's response time is also confounded
in cruise: with a queue of other work holding the machines, a request waits on contended CPU, R = S / (1 - u[host]), not on
the service's own pods. Reading that R as the service's own queue and adding pods would answer the wrong cause. So in
cruise Omni holds the machines and leaves the service to its own autoscaler. `tests/test_compass_controller.py` checks
that the floor step makes no API read during cruise; the controller before this rule made the full set of reads every
five seconds.

**9.4 Why idle is read from the autoscaler's floor (9.7).** A served service never reads zero: a health probe or a
client's keep-alive keeps one pod at a few percent of its request. In the batch test, one pod at about 10% of its request
read as demand 0.10, above b = 0.05, and idle waited 15 minutes after the queue emptied. The autoscaler's own
floor is the observable of "no demand beyond the minimum": the pods it keeps are its minimum, it wants no more, and they
run under half the target. In the five frozen-engine web tests the service was never at its floor (0 of 5,102 readings),
so (9.7) changes nothing there.

**9.5 Reporting resolution.** A paired change smaller than one part in a million of the value
(|mean difference| <= 1e-6 |native|) is read "same", the number still shown. Below that, a difference is rounding in
floating point and in the models' accumulators, not behaviour; a deterministic run gives a zero-width interval around
it, which would otherwise read as proven.

**9.6 A lever is moved only where moving it can pay.** The compass decides how far and how fast. Whether a lever may
move at all is a property of the muscle's physics. Four cases, each derived from the muscle's own model and each its own
test:

- *Cooling power.* A zone's heat must leave it: over a run, the heat removed equals the heat made plus what the
  room's mass stores. A cap on cooling power q[max] cannot remove less heat. It only lets the temperature drift above
  setpoint while the PI command grows, and the staging rule, units = ceil(command / (0.8 q[unit])), turns that command
  into more units and more fan power, p = q[c] / COP + units x p[unit]. So a lower cap never saves energy, and the lever
  stays native. (The setpoint, which changes the COP, and the units, which change fan power at the same heat, remain
  levers.)
- *A battery's reserve.* Energy D drawn from the cells below the operator's reserve saves D sqrt(eta) of grid import,
  and the deficit is bought back at D / sqrt(eta). The net, D (1 - eta) / sqrt(eta) (10.5% of D at eta = 0.90), is
  always positive. Spending the reserve is never an energy saving; it is the price of keeping the draw under the
  connection's limit. So the reserve is spent only at the wall (p >= 0.95) and only when the battery can cover the
  excess (0 < imp - p[lim] <= p[batt]). Otherwise the operator's reserve holds, and no round trip is paid for nothing.
- *A backup reserve (a UPS).* It is held for an outage, which the model does not contain, so spending it for a peak
  trades away the reason it exists. Never a lever.
- *A compute pool's power cap.* With throughput mu(c) proportional to c^eps and the autoscaler holding utilisation near its
  target u*, the energy per unit of work is e(c) = (p[idle] / u* + p[dyn] c) / mu(c). At c = 1, de/dc > 0 (a lower cap
  saves) if and only if

      eps < p_dyn / (p_idle / u* + p_dyn)                                                                 (9.8)

  At eps = 0.4 the cap saves on CPU hosts (threshold 0.62), GPUs (0.74), databases (0.51) and radio units (0.54). It
  costs energy where idle power dominates: a quantum computer's cryostat (0.19), a network switch (0.32), storage
  (0.26). There, running slower keeps the machines on longer: race to idle. In a deployment p[idle], p[dyn] and the
  speed curve come from the machine's own specification.

- *A motion axis's effort cap.* It lowers the copper loss of a full-acceleration move, (J a[max] / kt)^2 R, and stretches
  the move, which keeps paying the standing draw p[idle] + b v[max]^2. It moves only where the first exceeds the second: a
  reaction wheel (32 W against 5 W), not EV traction, a flight axis or a robot joint.
- *A machine released from a node pool.* A machine boots in minutes, and a burst that arrives in the meantime is served
  late. So a machine goes back only when the machines left cover the recent peak at 0.3 of the pool's own release level,
  the largest margin at which no pool is later than native (`results/realms/RELEASE_MARGIN_SWEEP.md`). This is the
  verdict of the live controller (section 21.9) in model form.

What a lever buys is labelled for what it is. Less work per energy, with no work lost and the time over the line
proven lower, is SERVICE IMPROVEMENT WITH ENERGY TRADEOFF, the mirror of ENERGY IMPROVEMENT WITH SERVICE TRADEOFF.
Without that proof it reads LESS WORK PER ENERGY.

## 22. The Safety Case: Every Hazard, Its Guard, and the Evidence



Omni-Compass writes settings that a native controller would otherwise own. A referee's first question is what happens
when it is wrong, is attacked, or dies. This page answers it hazard by hazard. Each row names the guard in the code that
stands against the hazard and the evidence that the guard holds: a test that runs on every push (`python3 verify.py`), or a
measured run (evidence class L). Where no evidence exists yet, the row says so. The page adds no mechanism; it maps the
mechanisms that are already there. Section 22.3 is the plug's interface, as the code defines it.

### 22.1 The claim this page supports

**Do no harm** (its meaning, `DISCLOSURES.md` section 3): the organism Omni-Compass governs is never left turning out less
than its native controllers make it turn out, nor less healthy (no muscle past its own limit, no service over its own line,
nothing made to fail). On the engine that stands, that means: Omni-Compass never leaves a setting other than native's after
it stops, never acts on a reading it cannot trust, never takes a step that a paired trial on the system itself showed
costs more, never exceeds a bound the system or its operator set, and can be switched off by one human action, everywhere
at once.

### 22.2 Hazards, guards and evidence

| # | Hazard | Guard (where it lives) | Evidence that it holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | The governor dies, hangs or loses its machine, leaving a setting changed | Before its first write, every governor records the exact commands that put every setting back, and renews a lease every decision. A watchdog finds any governor whose process is gone or whose lease is stale and runs those commands for it (`omnicompass/master.py`: `register`, `heartbeat`, `orphans`; `tools/omni_switch.py`: `watchdog`, `reclaim`) | `tests/test_master_switch.py`; the robustness kill test (the governor killed outright mid-run, every setting back within the allowance in every repetition; `docs/ROBUSTNESS_PREREGISTRATION.md`); `tests/test_robust.py`, `tests/test_robust_restart.py` |
| H2 | Someone takes over the governor, or it behaves in a way nobody intended | The kill switch: one file, one command. Every governor sees it at its next decision, writes back every setting it changed, reads each one back and exits. A governor that cannot read the switch treats that as OFF (`omnicompass/master.py`, `tools/omni_switch.py off`) | `tests/test_master_switch.py` |
| H3 | A write is refused or silently fails, so the governor's belief and the system differ | Every write goes through the plug, which reads the value back (`omnicompass/muscle_sdk.py`: `execute`, then `readback`, then a receipt). At the end of every run the reset is read back against the snapshot, and the run fails if any record is left (`scripts/kind_bench.sh`) | `tests/test_muscle_sdk.py`; every three-run table prints "handed back to native's and read back at the end of every omni arm in every run: yes" |
| H4 | It gives back too much, so service breaks when load returns | Floors read live: never below one replica, a pool never below two machines. A machine is given back only after its own trial shows the response time holds, and it wakes at once on a breach (`omni_controller/controller.py`) | `tests/test_node_release_gate.py`; the fault test (`results/live/V7_FAULTS.md`) |
| H5 | On a shared host, one tenant's raise starves the others | No CPU limit is raised while the host is 75% busy or its reading is missing; conveyance stays inside each namespace's CPU quota, and an unreadable quota means no known budget, so Kubernetes admission decides (`omni_controller/capacity.py`, `omni_controller/quota.py`) | `tests/test_capacity.py`, `tests/test_kind_capacity.py`, `tests/test_quota_convey.py`; the noisy-neighbour test (`results/live/V7_FAIRNESS.md`, STEADY) |
| H6 | It acts on a reading it cannot trust | A reading with no machine in service is blind: the decision holds, says why, and writes nothing (omni-v11, `omni_controller/controller.py`). A muscle whose reading is stale reports BLIND, and no command is executed (`omnicompass/muscle_sdk.py`: `MuscleStatus`) | `tests/test_blind_reading.py` (the fault reproduced on omni-v10, gone on omni-v11); `results/model_gate/V11_VS_V10.md`; the extended fault test, the API server frozen and the metrics server gone (queued, A, B and C: `docs/K8S_COMPASS_PREREGISTRATION.md`) |
| H7 | It keeps a step that hurts the system | One trial at a time, on the system itself: a reference phase at the deepest step already allowed, then one notch further. The step is refused if its median cost exceeds the reference's by more than 2%, or the cost first measured at the operator's setting. Refused steps wait 60 s; a trial is abandoned if the service swings (`tools/knob_verdict.py`) | `tests/test_knob_verdict.py`, `tests/test_verdict.py`, `tests/test_verdict_interval.py`; every database table prints each trial's count, allowance and refusal |
| H8 | It writes outside what the operator allows | A capability contract (minimum, maximum, resolution, step and rate limits) and a safety contract (hard bounds, forbidden contexts, fail closed) on every muscle (`omnicompass/muscle_sdk.py`: `CapabilityContract`, `SafetyContract`) | `tests/test_muscle_sdk.py` |
| H9 | It uses more privilege than its job needs | Least-privilege service account (`deploy/kind/rbac-omni.yaml`), and every arm records what it can and cannot do (`kubectl auth can-i`, `rbac_omni.txt` in each run's folder) | The receipts in every run folder on the branch `raw` |
| H10 | It expands while a security hold is on | The shield: no expansion during a security hold (invariant I1), with a C++ twin checked against the Python (`omnicompass/shield.py`, `cpp/`) | `tests/test_shield_properties.py`, `tests/test_cpp_shield_parity.py`, `tests/test_cpp_shield_adversarial.py` |
| H11 | In the cloud, it raises the bill for the same work | The bill is judged, never ruled (the founder's order of 31 October struck the machines-alone rule of 14 October): every cloud set reads the bill beside the work it bought by the one key, the cloud's judged number the work per dollar: a factory tune whose work per dollar falls against native (a bigger bill for the same work) is not admissible (`docs/THE_TUNE.md`) and is a fault of the tune, root-caused in the model first; the machine lever asks the cloud for no machine (`scripts/kind_nodepool.sh`); paid sets capped at 100 repetitions and 1, 10 and 100 copies | Azure: no difference in the bill on the engine of 13 October, at the tune-down on the machines alone (`results/live/AKS_BILL.md`); the sets at the max carry the work meter from 31 October, night, a tuning case first, so each reads the work per dollar. Google and Amazon: **undetermined**, not yet run. |
| H12 | A test machine's limit is reported as the governor's effect | Paired arms on the same runner, rotated order, the refusal rules for an unhealthy window, and the kind rig's image pre-puller (`docs/POD_START_WAIT.md`). `tools/confirm_abc.py` marks any table whose runs differ in engine or rig | `tests/test_confirm_abc.py`, `tests/test_pod_phases.py`, `tests/test_release_campaign.py` |
| H13 | The hand-back itself is turned against the system: a record another local user planted makes the watchdog run a command or stop a process, or a governor's pid given to another process gets that process stopped | The watchdog acts only on records of its own user that no other user can write, read without following a link; a pid counts as the governor's only while its process started before the governor registered (`tools/omni_switch.py`, 18 October). Every threat of misuse is set out in `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` | `tests/test_switch_trust.py` (each fault reproduced on the tool as it stood, gone on the fix) |

### 22.3 The plug, as the code defines it

Every muscle is reached through one interface (`omnicompass/muscle_sdk.py`, `MuscleAdapter`). The sequence is fixed:
observe, bound, request, execute, read back, receipt, restore.

| Call | What it must do |
|---|---|
| `observe()` | Return the muscle's reading with its timestamp; a reading older than its timing contract makes the muscle BLIND |
| `snapshot_native()` | Capture native's setting once, before the first write; this is what every restore returns to |
| `execute(value)` | Write one value, already clamped by the capability contract and permitted by the safety contract |
| `readback()` | Read the value the system actually holds; a mismatch is recorded, never assumed away |
| `restore_native(snapshot)` | Put native's setting back, then read it back |

Each muscle carries three contracts: timing (observation and decision periods, actuation delay, the age after which a
reading is stale, the minimum hold and cool-down between writes), capability (range, resolution, step and rate limits,
reversible, read back) and safety (hard bounds, forbidden contexts, fail closed, a safe default). A muscle built on the SDK
cannot be declared without all three. It starts in recommend mode and writes only when set to automatic or approved from
outside; every command, written or refused, leaves a receipt with the reason, the reading's age, the value asked, the value
bounded, the value the system holds and the difference between the last two (`MuscleRuntime.command`).

### 22.4 What this case does not yet cover

- **No outside security review or penetration test.** H2, H9, H10 and H13 rest on our own tests; the threats still open are listed in `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`, section 3.
- **No formal proof of the whole controller.** The theorems in `docs/TRACKING_THEOREM.md` hold for the compass law's
  channel; global stability of the full six-state system is open (`docs/FORMAL_STATUS.md`).
- **No production deployment.** Every hazard above is exercised on our own rigs (kind on GitHub runners, Azure's managed
  Kubernetes, the database servers in our workflows), not on a customer's system.
- **Physical plants.** The GPU's power and clock guards and every facility muscle are exercised only in our models or a
  stand-in card until the chip runs exist (undetermined).

## 23. The Threat Model: Misuse, Its Guards, and What Is Open



The safety case (`docs/SAFETY_CASE.md`) asks what happens when the governor is wrong or dies. This page asks what happens
when someone wants it to do harm. It names what is worth protecting, where trust changes hands, each threat with the guard
in the code that stands against it and the test that shows the guard holds, and what is still open. It is our own
analysis: **no outside security review or penetration test has been made**, and nothing here stands in for one.

### 23.1 What is worth protecting

| Asset | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| The settings the governor writes (replicas, the autoscaler's target, a node's idle mark, a CPU limit, a power cap, a database pool) | Whoever controls them controls the service's capacity |
| The governor's identity on the system (on Kubernetes its service account and token) | It carries every right the governor has |
| The hand-back: the snapshot of native's settings, the registry of restore commands, the switch file | They put the system back when the governor stops; whoever can write them chooses what "back" means |
| The engine's code (the 65 fingerprinted files of omni-v23, the engine that stands) and the harness that measures it | A changed engine is a different product; a changed harness is a different result |
| The audit lines and the raw receipts | They are the evidence for every result and every decision |
| The cloud and GPU credentials (GitHub secrets) | They spend money and create machines |

### 23.2 Where trust changes hands

1. **The operator and the governor.** The operator starts the governor, grants its rights and sets its bounds. The
   governor is trusted to act only inside them.
2. **The governor's host.** The governor, the switch and the watchdog run as processes of one user on one machine (a pod,
   a runner or a server). Every other local user is outside that boundary.
3. **The governor and the system it governs.** It reads through the system's API (Kubernetes, `nvidia-smi`, a database's
   own commands) and writes through the same API with a least-privilege identity. The readings are inputs it does not
   control.
4. **The repository and the machines that run it.** Code reaches a run through GitHub: a pushed commit, an action, a
   Python package. Secrets reach a run only through GitHub's secret store.

### 23.3 Threats, guards and evidence

| # | Threat | Guard (where it lives) | Evidence | Still open |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Another local user plants a record in the watchdog's registry, so the watchdog runs that user's command, or stops a process, with its own rights | The watchdog acts only on a record that it and the registry directory are owned by its own user (or root, or a uid named with `--trust-uid`), that is no symbolic link and that no other user can write. Each record is opened inside the directory without following a link and checked on the open file, so nothing can be swapped in between. Any other is refused, named, and left in place (`tools/omni_switch.py`: `trusted_records`, 18 October) | `tests/test_switch_trust.py` (a record anyone can write, a registry anyone can write, a record reached through a link, a record of another user: each refused; each fault reproduced on the tool as it stood) | A member of the governors' own group can still write a record the governors' umask leaves group-writable |
| T2 | A governor dies, the system gives its process number to another process, and the watchdog takes that process for the governor, hung, and kills it | A process number is taken for the governor's only while the process holding it started before the governor registered (`governor_alive`, from `/proc`); otherwise the governor is gone, nothing is signalled, and its settings are handed back (18 October) | `tests/test_switch_trust.py` (the watchdog as it stood killed the process holding the number; now it hands back and the process lives); `tests/test_master_switch.py` (a hung governor is still stopped and handed back) | Systems without `/proc` keep the old reading |
| T3 | A link planted at the switch file's path makes `off` overwrite another file | The switch file is opened without following a link; if it cannot be written, every governor is still signalled and the tool says so (`tools/omni_switch.py off`, 18 October) | `tests/test_switch_trust.py` (the file the link points at is left as it was) | — |
| T4 | Anyone who can write the switch's directory, or a governor's own kill file, turns governing off, or keeps it off | Off is the safe direction: every setting goes back to native's (the kill switch's purpose). `status` warns when the switch's or the registry's directory can be written by another user | `tests/test_switch_trust.py` (the warning) | The default directory is `/tmp/omni-compass`, written in `omnicompass/master.py`, an engine file; until the next engine version moves it, set `OMNI_MASTER_OFF` and `OMNI_REGISTRY` to a directory only the governors' user can write. The cloud install keeps it inside the pod, where every container runs as one user (10001) |
| T5 | The governor's identity is stolen | Least privilege: on Kubernetes the service account can read nodes, pods, metrics, autoscalers and workloads cluster-wide; patch nodes and evict pods (the eviction API honours disruption budgets); and, in the service's namespace, patch the one named autoscaler and Deployment, pods (their deletion cost and in-place resize) and Jobs, and read one named ConfigMap. It cannot delete an object directly, create a workload or read a Secret (`deploy/kind/rbac-omni.yaml`). Every arm records what the identity can and cannot do (`kubectl auth can-i`, `rbac_omni.txt`) | The receipts in every run folder on the branch `raw` | The rights it has are enough to cordon and drain nodes; whoever holds the token is limited by the role, not by the governor's floors |
| T6 | Someone feeds the governor false readings (a lying metric, a stalled probe) | A reading with no machine in service holds the decision and writes nothing (omni-v11); a stale reading makes a muscle BLIND (`omnicompass/muscle_sdk.py`); every step is a paired trial on the system itself, refused if its cost rises more than 2% (`tools/knob_verdict.py`, `omnicompass/verdict.py`); every write stays inside the capability and safety contracts | `tests/test_blind_reading.py`, `tests/test_muscle_sdk.py`, `tests/test_knob_verdict.py`; the fault test's blind probe; the extended fault test's frozen API server and missing metrics server (queued) | A false reading that stays consistent and inside the bounds can steer the governor within the room the operator granted |
| T7 | The engine's code is changed | The engine is fingerprinted: `OMNI_V16.json` names the digest of its 55 files, and `python3 tools/omni_version.py` names the engine a checkout carries, or what differs from every fingerprint. `python3 verify.py` holds every place that names the engine to the engine that stands (`tools/land_engine.py --check`) | `tests/` (the release manifest and the version tool); every run's receipt names the engine its commit carries | Releases are not signed artefacts, the repository's bots commit unsigned, and nothing checks the fingerprint when a governor starts |
| T8 | A dependency is replaced (a Python package, a GitHub action) | Every package pip installs is pinned to an exact version with the SHA-256 of every file PyPI publishes for it (`requirements-lock.txt`, hash-checking mode), with a software bill of materials (`sbom/omni-compass.cdx.json`, `sbom/omni-compass.spdx.json`, written by `tools/sbom.py`); every action a workflow uses is named by its commit, its tag beside it (407 uses, 19 October); `security-scan.yml` audits every pin against the public vulnerability databases each week; Dependabot watches both the packages and the actions (`.github/dependabot.yml`) | `tests/test_supply_chain.py` fails a push with an action named by tag or a package without hashes; `tools/sbom.py --check` in `verify.py` | Closed for what Omni-Compass installs; the tools a benchmark machine installs from its own package manager (kind, kubectl, the databases) are pinned by version, not by hash |
| T9 | A secret leaks from a workflow | Secrets reach only workflows started on this repository (a push or a dispatch); no workflow runs on `pull_request_target`, so no fork's code ever runs with them. Secrets are kept in GitHub's store only, and GitHub masks them in every log. A key stored in another form is named by its shape before any cloud's login step reads it, never a character of it printed (`tools/cloud_key_check.py`), because a login step's own refusal can quote the first characters of what it was given, and a piece of a secret is not masked (21 October: Azure's did, on a public run page) | Every workflow names its token's rights; `tests/test_cloud_check.py` fails a push that leaves any Azure login without the shape check before it; the 28 that only build, run and upload get `contents: read` and nothing else (18 October). `tests/test_workflow_permissions.py` fails a push that leaves any workflow on the repository's default, or gives a read-only token to a workflow that pushes, starts a run or reads another run's files | — |
| T10 | A run spends money it should not | In a cloud the whole engine runs at the max (the founder's order of 31 October) on top of the cloud's own autoscaler, which alone adds machines; the governor's lever parks a machine that exists and wakes it, and asks the cloud for none (`scripts/kind_nodepool.sh`); the bill is judged beside the work it bought, a tune whose work per dollar falls against native not admissible (`docs/THE_TUNE.md`), and paid sets stay at 100 repetitions and 1, 10 and 100 copies. A cloud's set starts only after that cloud's $0 check passes (Google, Amazon and, since 22 October, Azure: the key, the login, the plan, the machine type, every quota; `tools/cloud_key_check.py`). Nothing is rented for the grid | `results/live/AKS_BILL.md`; `tests/test_cloud_check.py` | The credentials in the secrets can create clusters; their scope is set in each cloud's console |
| T11 | The evidence is changed after the run | Every archived run is kept byte for byte on the branch `raw` with its SHA-256 sums (`scripts/raw_archive.sh`); every table names its runs and is rebuilt by its own tool from them | `tests/test_raw_archive.py` | Audit lines are not signed when written; the sums protect them from the moment they are archived |
| T12 | The system's control plane is taken away (the API server frozen, the metrics server gone) | The governor holds on a reading it cannot make; a failed decision writes nothing; its lease runs 300 s at a 60-second decision, so a short outage does not hand back what is working | The extended fault test (queued, A, B and C: `docs/K8S_COMPASS_PREREGISTRATION.md`) | Whatever the runs read is reported |

### 23.4 What would close the open rows

- An outside security review and a penetration test of the governor, the switch and the install.
- In the next engine version, the switch and the registry in a private directory by default, created with no access for
  any other user (T1, T4).
- Release artefacts signed, and the fingerprint checked when a governor starts (T7).

## 24. The Static Security Scan, Every Finding Reviewed



Generated by `python3 tools/security_scan.py` (Bandit, the Python security linter of PyCQA) over every Python file that runs (`omni_controller/`, `omnicompass/`, `realms/`, `tools/`, `scripts/`, `fleet/`, `k8s_controlplane/`; 37,470 lines). The workflow `security-scan.yml` runs it on every push to main that touches code, and every week, with `pip-audit` over every pinned dependency; it fails on a finding of high or medium severity that no review below names.

**2 findings of high severity and 35 of medium severity, every one reviewed below; 350 of low severity, counted by kind.** Fixed on 19 October: a world-writable PgBouncer folder (now owned by postgres, 0o755) and the MD5 that PostgreSQL's own password method defines, now marked as not used for security. Fixed in omni-v14 (21 October): the operator's own commands (the site power reading, a muscle's read command, a wall meter's) run without a shell unless they hold a pipe, a redirect or a variable, so the governor's site power reading no longer reaches a shell at all and one high finding is gone.

## 26. The Engine That Stands: Omni v23



Omni v23 (`OMNI_V23.json`, digest `c96ea4105d8747db`, 65 files) is omni-v22 with one guard in the Kubernetes governor's pod muscle of its
own (`omni_controller/controller.py`, `_own_pods` and `_own_refused`), on the founder's order of 31 October, given on reading that
the arm by itself had read like native:

> "Omni direct is directly to muscles, but Omni direct still might need an autoscaler like Kubernetes ... we still might need a
> muscle or two we're using. We're going straight into all the muscles as the brain and orchestrator, scheduler and all that, but
> what Omni-Compass can't do and needs the muscle for has to be achieved even in direct, so that it can work and do everything else
> ... Don't just embed some shit and fail the whole system because we don't have the muscle to do something ... any muscle that we
> don't have, Omni-Compass cannot be it: it has to be there, if that's Kubernetes or whatever."

64 of its 65 files are omni-v22's bytes. No gain, preset, card or law moves; do no harm keeps its strictest form.

**What "direct" can and cannot mean** (the founder's analysis, the same day: "Omni-Compass would have to become the Kubernetes
mechanism to be what's considered direct"). On a Kubernetes stack Omni-Compass is a brain with no organs: Kubernetes' scheduler
places every pod and the kubelet runs every container, in every arm. The arm by itself there is Omni-Compass's own pod rule in place
of the autoscaler's arithmetic and nothing else, so it is never called direct; it is a mechanism test kept in the record, not a
product arm, and the product has two sides, native and Omni-Compass on native (the founder's order of 25 October). The one test
where the word holds is the orchestrator showing without Kubernetes (`docs/OMNI_ORCHESTRATOR.md`), where Omni-Compass's own small
orchestrator is the organs; its three arms read, run by run: Omni-Compass on native the strongest in all three (the most work, the
fastest response in two, fewer machines in all), native the weakest, the arm by itself between them (level with Omni-Compass on
native in run A, behind it in B and C). This guard serves every arm: wherever Omni-Compass's own rule cannot move a knob, the organ
that can gets it back.

### 26.1 What was found

Every arm by itself run on kind from omni-v19 (24 October) to omni-v22 had the governor's pod writes refused by the rig's own
identity: `kubectl scale` patches the scale subresource, `deployments/scale`, a resource of its own under Kubernetes' RBAC, and the
rig's role granted `patch` on `deployments` by name and never the subresource. Fifteen of fifteen decisions a window ended
Forbidden, in every repetition; the workload stayed at the operator's count; the machine and conveyance muscles wrote as always, so
the window's no-write check never fired. omni-v21's three runs of the entry were admitted and are read in no table; omni-v22's two
were marked invalid by a second rig fault. Both rig faults are fixed (`docs/SOLO_PREREGISTRATION.md`, amendment 1). What the engine
lacked is this version: when Omni-Compass cannot be a knob's muscle, the knob must go back to the muscle that can, so the organism
never runs with a knob nobody moves (amendment 2, the founder's order above).

### 26.2 What changes in the engine

- A write of a workload's own scale that the cluster refuses (its permission, its admission, its API) is recorded in the audit
  (`own_replicas`, `refused` n, the cluster's words) and the decision goes on; the cluster keeps the last count that landed. Before
  omni-v23 the exception ended the decision (`decision failed (n in a row)`) and nothing else happened, decision after decision.
- At `OWN_REFUSALS` (3) refusals in a row Omni-Compass cannot be that knob's muscle: it makes native's own pod autoscaler from the
  operator's own target and range recorded on the workload (`kubectl autoscale deployment NAME --cpu-percent=T --min=lo --max=hi`;
  with no range recorded, from one to ten times the operator's count), audits the hand-back (`handed_back`, `after_refusals`,
  `target`, `range`), and leaves the workload to it for the rest of the run: the snapshot's governed set holds it from the next
  decision on, and the reset leaves native's autoscaler standing. A hand-back the cluster refuses too is audited
  (`hand_back_refused`) and tried at the next refusal.
- A write that lands ends the run of refusals.
- Every other arm is untouched: Omni-Compass on native never removes native's controller, so a refused write there leaves native's
  own controller moving the knob as before; the machines, the conveyance, the power cap and the batch muscles are omni-v22's bytes.

### 26.3 What changes in the rig, not the engine

The kind identity (`deploy/kind/rbac-omni.yaml`) gains `create` on `horizontalpodautoscalers` in the default namespace, for the
hand-back alone, and the preflight proves it; a window of the arm by itself in which the knob was handed back is refused as a
result of that arm (the organism was kept whole, but Omni-Compass did not run the arm by itself): `INVALID RUN: by itself, the knob
... was handed back to native's own autoscaler`. `tests/test_kind_rig_rbac.py` fails a rig without either.

### 26.4 The model gate

`results/model_gate/V23_VS_V22.md` (class S, our own models; `tools/model_gate.py`, seeds 1 to 8, the engine that stood, omni-v22,
the candidate omni-v23): every one of the 95 gauge rows of the 11 models reads identical on every seed, the counts identical, no LOSS. No model refuses a write of the cluster, so the guard never fires in the models and the
candidate reads identical to omni-v22 on every gauge; its proof is the tests below and the arm's own files when the entry runs again.

### 26.5 The tests

`tests/test_own_replicas.py`, `HandBack`: a cluster that refuses the scale write three times in a row gets native's own autoscaler
at the operator's 50% target and 1 to 10 range, the muscle writes nothing more to that workload, the count the cluster kept stands
(never a knob nobody moves); a write that lands after two refusals ends the run of refusals and no autoscaler is made; with no range
recorded the autoscaler's ceiling is ten times the operator's count. The unit-test suite, the function tests and the release check
pass on the tree; no C++ twin changes (the Kubernetes governor has none).

### 26.6 What is run again

Every benchmark runs again on omni-v23 from 20:00 UTC on 31 October 2026 (`scripts/reruns.txt`, A of every entry, then B, then C; the conductor's
campaign, `scripts/dispatch_grid.py`). The omni-v22 runs started before that moment run to their end as omni-v22's record; nothing is
cancelled. The entry `kubernetes by itself` runs on the rig as amended, three arms, its table kept in the record and not carried on
the front page (the founder's order of 25 October).

## 27. The Engines and Their Audit

### 27.1 Which engine is which



There is **one** engine. Every other engine-looking file in this repository is either its required C++ twin or a frozen
copy of where it came from. Nothing else runs.

| File | Role | Runs? |
|---|---|---|
| `omnicompass/core.py` | **The engine** (`symmetric_verified`): six states, eight lines, RK4 with microsteps. Everything Omni does goes through it. | yes |
| `cpp/src/core.cpp`, `cpp/include/omnicompass/core.hpp` | The same engine in C++. Required: `verify.py` checks it against the Python on every fixture. | yes (twin) |
| `docs/handoff/mathematics/omni_compass_engine_source_c527df2d.py` | The original source as handed over (sha256 `c527df2d…`). Kept unchanged as proof of origin and as the parameter authority. | no (frozen) |
| `reference/omni_compass_reference_engine.py` | The same original with comments stripped (`tools/strip_reference.py`); same program fingerprint (`reference/PROVENANCE.json`). | no (frozen) |

Fingerprints of the running engine, its parts and its twin: `results/MECHANISM_IDENTITY.json` and `RELEASE_MANIFEST.json`.
`verify.py` fails if any of them changes without a new seal.

#### 27.1.1 Engines from outside packages, not adopted

Copies of this repository passed around as zips (the XPASS packages) carry changes that are **not** in the engine here:

- `batch_claim1.py` (in those zips, not in this tree): a vectorised variant that applies u during the RK4 step (CLAIM1). No C++ twin; not
  verified against the 500 fixtures.
- an adapter that defaults to CLAIM1, takes the target sign from the starting state and adds a disruption budget. Its
  C++ governor was only partly ported, which is where the reported Python/C++ mismatches came from.

None of these enter before the GPU counted run run (the engine is frozen for it, `docs/GPU_PREREGISTRATION.md`). Any of
them can be adopted afterwards only as a full change: Python and C++ together, the parity tests and `verify.py` green,
and a new mechanism id.

#### 27.1.2 The rule from here

One engine, one twin, two frozen originals. A new version **replaces** the old one in place, with a new seal; it is never
added beside it. Older states are in git history and `docs/HISTORY.md`, not in extra files.
### 27.2 My engine, line by line: the source against what runs in your cluster



**The source.** `docs/handoff/mathematics/omni_compass_engine_source_c527df2d.py` (SHA-256 c527df2d…, 31,348 lines).
Every mechanism below is named by its function there, followed by where it runs live and how it is checked on every
`python verify.py`.

| Mechanism | In the source | Where it runs | Checked by | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Six states E, U, I_U, S, B, Ḃ and equations (1)–(7) | `oc_derivatives`, `rk4_step` | `omnicompass/core.py` | `tests/test_core_parity.py`: 20,000 random states, max difference ≤ 1e-12 | exact |
| Spinor closure, 720°: drive × cos(½ ω_B t) | `v_eff`, `spinor_closure_factor` | `core.v_eff` | same parity test | exact |
| Axle rest S* from equation (6) | `stable_S_equilibrium` | `omnicompass/storage.py`, `compass.axle` | parity; `tests/test_compass.py` | exact |
| Double well W(U), basins ±1 | `W_potential`, `W_gradient_flow` | `core.derivatives` | parity | exact |
| Regulation u = −f_U + K_P(σ − U), clipped at the authority | `hybrid_microstep_operator` | `core.control_command`; the governor's push | parity; 500 frozen trajectories (`fixtures/`), 0 mismatches | exact |
| Basin lock, conveyance, certification | `run_monte_carlo`, `macro_step` | `core.simulate` | 500 frozen trajectories, 0 mismatches | exact |
| Composite storage V = V_U + V_W + V_E + V_S + V_I + V_B, the ledger that closes the circle | `composite_practical_lyapunov_value`, `bath_lyapunov_matrix`, weights | `omnicompass/storage.py`, read by the compass every decision | parity on 5,000 states (≤ 1e-13); descends 648 → 8 over 60 regulated steps with no rise | exact |
| Human switch: a file or a variable stops every command | `_oc_runtime_stop_requested` | `--kill-file`, restore of every lever | `tests/test_failsafe.py`, `tests/test_muscles.py`, every live run's switch drill | exact |
| Cap doctrine C1: only a ceiling *above* the reference is admissible; a lower one buys energy by slowing work | `_ci_omni_decision`, certificate C1–C4 | `muscles.convey`: CPU limit never below the operator's, idle CPU conveyed to the work | `tests/test_convey.py` | exact |
| Sleep only in a certified empty interval | `_ci_omni_decision`, sleep channel | `scripts/kind_nodepool.sh`: a machine idles only once its work has left | `tests/test_active_nodes.py`, `tests/test_convey.py` | exact |
| Reference Kubernetes HPA rule | `oc_hpa_desired_replicas` | `cpp/` HPA, pod reflex | `tests/test_cpp_hpa_parity.py` | exact |

#### 27.2.1 Where my live wiring reads the engine differently from the source's own embodiment

**Evolution between decisions.** The source's compute embodiment advances the assimilated state *with* regulation
locked on basin +1. My live governor advances it with u = 0 and reads the regulation command separately, as the push
that gates every machine release.

- Both use the same equations.
- The difference is whether the regulation is applied to the state or only read from it.
- The pre-registered, frozen results were measured with u = 0. I keep that setting, and I report the difference here
  rather than change a frozen law mid-measurement.

## 28. Change Control: How the Engine Changes



The engine is the set of files whose bytes decide what Omni-Compass does: the brain, the compass law, the verdict, the live
governors, the harness the models run in, and the wires that fasten the brain to an outside simulator. Their SHA-256
digests together make the engine's fingerprint (`OMNI_V16.json`: 55 files, digest `5c5502f12b1c0ce4`).
`python3 tools/omni_version.py` reads the tree and names the engine it holds, or says which file differs from every
declared engine.

### 28.1 The rules

1. **Any change to a rule, a gain, a guard, a preset or a muscle makes the next version.** No engine file changes inside a
   version. A fix to a fault found in the engine is the next version, never a patch to the one that stands.
2. **Every change goes through the model gate first** (`tools/model_gate.py`, `results/model_gate/`): the shipped controller on
   the model cluster in the cloud setting, conveyance on one kind host set to a real run's own regime, the verdict on noisy
   work, the same seeds, paired against the engine that stands. A LOSS there is root-caused and fixed in the model; a
   change that reads no LOSS and shows promise goes to its GitHub trials; nothing is dispatched before.
3. **A version lands in one command**, `python3 tools/land_engine.py vN --since <UTC>`: the fingerprint, the version list,
   the conductor's campaign (`scripts/reruns.txt`), the grid's manifest and workflows, the package version (0.N.0), the
   root list and a release group. `tools/land_engine.py --check`, run by `verify.py`, refuses a push in which any of those
   places still names an older engine.
4. **Every benchmark runs again on the new version**, A, B and C, released by the conductor in a fixed order; a run is
   counted on the engine its own commit carries, read from GitHub at its head commit.
5. **No result is read across versions.** A three-run table is one engine's three runs (the table tools refuse to call
   runs on two engines one table); an older table stays its own engine's record, in `results/live/` until each
   benchmark's three runs on the new version land, then the newest table is the one shown.
6. **Every fix lands as the next version, and the founder is told.** A change that reads no LOSS in the model gate lands at once
   as the next version (the founder's order of 19 October, night: "Of course I want you to land version 12 ... every time you
   do that ... it becomes a new version"); he is told what it changes, why and what it read, and is not asked whether to land
   it. A change that reads a LOSS anywhere is root-caused and fixed in the model first and never lands as it stands.

### 28.3 What stability means here

A version is stable for a benchmark when its three runs on that version have landed with no change in between. omni-v12
has stood since 20 October 00:30 UTC, when its campaign opened (it reached main shortly before); its campaign is under way, and its three-run tables go into `results/live/V12_*.md`
as they land. omni-v11 stood from 18 October 16:03 UTC; its 23 three-run tables (`results/live/V11_*.md`) stay its record. The engine's proofs (`docs/ENGINE_PROOFS.md`), its coverage
(`docs/ENGINE_COVERAGE.md`) and its reproducibility check (`tools/reproduce.py`) are run on every push, so a version that
stands is also a version that is re-proved, re-tested and re-built from its receipts each time anything else changes.
