### 66.45 Amendment (2026-10-18): a window with no machine in service is refused in either arm; the add-on's set-up waits for its scaler

Two repetitions of the omni-v10 reruns failed for causes outside Omni-Compass, and each is now caught in words that say so.
Neither change touches the engine, a setting, a gauge or a scored window.

- **No machine in service.** In the CruiseKube test (run 39120444653, repetition 8) every worker of the kind cluster left
  service for two minutes (eight of the capture's readings show no machine in service), while the service answered every probe.
  The omni arm's governor wrote nothing, and two of its fifteen decisions failed on that empty reading. The rig refused the
  window, correctly, but its words said the governor was not running. A reading with no machine in service leaves the
  window's machine count wrong in either arm, so such a window is now refused in both arms (`scripts/kind_bench.sh`). The
  capture records each node's taints and conditions at that moment (`fleet/capture/kube_capture.sh`), and a decision that
  failed is named by its error. The repetition runs again in place.
- **The add-on's scaler not yet answering.** In the KEDA test (run 39108180989, profile both, repetition 2), the native arm's
  set-up stopped before its window. KEDA's first call to the HTTP add-on's scaler met a pod still stopping after its rollout,
  and KEDA built the autoscaler without its HTTP metric within five minutes. The ScaledObject is now applied only once no
  KEDA pod is stopping and the scaler has an address. While the autoscaler lacks its metrics, the ScaledObject is touched
  once a minute with an annotation of the harness (never a setting), so KEDA builds the autoscaler again from the same spec
  (`scripts/kind_addons.sh`). The repetition runs again in place.


### 66.46 Amendment (2026-10-18, omni-v11): the governor holds on a reading with no machine in service

omni-v11 (`docs/OMNI_V11.md`) changes one thing in the governor these tests run. When the cluster's reading shows no machine in
service, the decision is recorded as `held: the cluster's reading shows no machine in service; nothing decided, nothing written`.
Nothing is decided from that reading, nothing is written, and the floor check returns at once. omni-v10 read the same reading
as the highest overload and then divided by the empty capacity, so its decision failed and wrote nothing. The rig counts a held
decision as the governor running (it is a decision record), never among the decisions of a scored window (it is no decision of
the law). A window in which the capture saw no machine in service is refused in either arm (the amendment above), so no scored
window carries a held decision that the capture also saw. Every setting, gauge, load, window and pair is unchanged; every test
runs again on omni-v11.

### 66.47 Amendment (2026-10-18): on kind, the served image pulled onto every worker before each arm

The KEDA add-on test's mean pod start wait read LOSS on omni-v10 under the http setup. The cause is the test machine
(`docs/POD_START_WAIT.md`, the receipt `results/live/POD_START_PHASES.md`, 741 starts in five runs). A serving pod placed on
a node that never served downloaded and unpacked its image (`registry.k8s.io/hpa-example`, untagged, pull policy Always)
inside the window, on the one runner every kind node shares, and the unpacking took longer the busier that runner was. On a
node already serving, a start took 1.3 to 1.7 s in both arms. On an empty node it took 7 to 12 s. Split exactly, the omni
arm's rise in the mean (+1.42 s on omni-v10, +0.65 s on omni-v11) is the shift of its starts into a busier host (+1.57 s,
+1.64 s), the host its conveyed processor keeps busy. At the same host load on the same kind of node its starts were as fast
or faster (−0.14 s, −0.98 s).

From this amendment on, every kind arm runs an image pre-puller (`deploy/kind/prepull.yaml`) before the governor starts or
the window opens. It is one pod on every worker, waited for on every worker and then deleted. A pre-puller that does not
finish fails the arm's checks. Each arm's `preflight.txt` records `images=pre-pulled on every worker before the arm` and the
digest each worker pulled. The rest stays as written: the operator's manifests, every setting, gauge, load, window and pair,
the engine (omni-v11's digest), and the cloud sets, where every node is its own machine. The kind workflows' three runs on
omni-v11 count only when their own commit carries the pre-puller (`RIG_FILE`, `scripts/dispatch_grid.py`). Their runs on the
rig before end as their own record, and `tools/confirm_abc.py` marks any table whose runs differ in rig. In the grid with the real cluster inside this
rig is protocol 4 (`KUBE_PROTOCOL`, carried in each run's name), and only its runs fill a square; no omni-v11 run with the
cluster inside had started on protocol 3. Expected before any run: a pod on an empty node
starts in about the time one beside a serving pod takes, in both arms. Whatever the runs read is reported.

### 66.48 Amendment (2026-10-18): the extended fault test, the two faults that blind a governor (written before its run)

The fault test above meets four faults. None of them takes away what a governor reads or the path it writes through, and a
governor's worst hour is the one in which it cannot see. The extended test (`FAULTS=2`, `scripts/kind_faults.sh`) keeps the
four at their moments and adds two after them, the same in every arm:
5. at 82% of the run, the API server is frozen for 30 s: its process in the control-plane node is stopped, then continued.
   The service's own path (kube-proxy on every node) keeps carrying traffic; no controller, native's or Omni-Compass's, can
   read the cluster or write to it.
6. at 88%, the metrics server is scaled to none for two minutes, then back to one: every autoscaler reads no CPU metric.

Each outage is written to `faults.log` only once it took hold; one that did not take hold is written as failed, and the
report has no row for it. The report (`tools/live_reps.py`, "The fault test") reads the two like the four: the time to
recover from the fault's start until responses stay under the line for 30 s straight, at most 300 s, and the share of
samples over the line or failed in the 300 s after it, paired against native. The run's window is 2,500 s, so the second
outage's 300 s end inside it (12% of 2,500 s is 300 s); the four keep their shares of the window, so they fall later in
seconds than in the 900-second test, and its tables are not read beside this one's. Load (open, fixed rate), arms (native;
native with Omni-Compass on top), the engine (omni-v11's digest), the rig (the pre-puller above), the gauges and the ten
pairs are as written; three runs, A, B and C (`scripts/reruns.txt`, "kubernetes faults extended").

Two readings are named before the run. While the API server is frozen, the capture's readings are not answered and are
skipped (`fleet/capture/kube_capture.sh`), in both arms. While the metrics server is gone, the capture reads no CPU used:
the column records 0 for those two minutes in both arms, so the CPU row's change is diluted by that share of the window and
never reversed by it. Expected before any run: Omni-Compass on top holds every setting while it cannot read (omni-v11 holds
on a blind reading; a decision whose read fails writes nothing, and its lease runs 300 s), so it recovers from both as fast
as native or faster. Whatever the runs read is reported.

### 66.49 Amendment (2026-10-19): a paid cloud set runs to its cap and stops when its bill is read (written before any run of it)

The founder's orders of 19 October: every cloud set gets a three-run reading, A, B and C on one engine, measured as finely as
the cap allows ("the cap we can run it to ... that's all we can run"), at the least cost that still tells what Omni-Compass
can do. Measured from the twelve Azure runs measured to the end (5 paired repetitions each), a run's bill swings about ±9%
of native's (the median half-width of its 95% interval, 1.5% to 36% run to run), so a cut under about 9% read EVEN.

- **Repetitions.** Every Azure set (the steady set, the bursts `1 4 1 6 1 9` and `1 6 1 8 1 6`, the real day on 1 to 9) runs
  up to 100 paired repetitions a run, the founder's cap for paid runs (12 October). At 100 the bill's interval is about ±2%:
  a cut of about 3% reads GAIN eight times in ten.
- **The stopping rule** (`tools/stop_rule.py`, `aks-metered.yml` input `stop_looks`, set to `10,20,40,70`). At each look, on
  repetitions 1 to that look only, the bill's paired change is read with its 99% interval (four looks at 1% each keep the
  rule's error under 5%). The run stops at the first look where the interval clears zero (a cut: GAIN; a rise: power given),
  or holds zero within ±2% of native's bill (EVEN, measured to that precision). It never stops while its 95th percentile or
  its failed requests read a LOSS at that look: a LOSS is measured to the cap. A stopped run's remaining repetitions start,
  read the rule, and spend nothing on Azure. The table is read as every table is (95% intervals, `tools/live_reps.py`); the
  run's summary carries every look (`STOP_RULE.txt`).
- **Unchanged.** The arms (native, then Omni-Compass on top at the tune-down, the machines alone, native's replica cap), the
  sets' loads and windows, the machine family and region, the control plane's tier (standard: amendment 4's way past the
  free tier's capacity refusals; about $0.10 an hour a cluster, not in the bill), and the three-run rule.
- **Both arms at once, on twin clusters,** would remove most of the swing (today the arms run one after the other on fresh
  clusters, each meeting Azure at a different moment). It waits for Azure's processor allowance: one cluster (a system machine
  and four workers of `Standard_D2s_v4`) is the whole 10-vCPU allowance of that machine family in `eastus`, so twins need it
  raised to 20 (asked of Azure, never shrunk to fit). It is written here before any run of it and switched on only by a

- **Counted apart.** A run under the rule carries "to the cap, stopping rule" in its title (`aks-metered.yml` run-name,

### 66.50 Amendment (2026-10-19): a worker held by an add-on's own mark while it serves is in service

Three native repetitions of the omni-v11 CruiseKube test were refused for "no machine in service" while the service answered

(`capture.csv.errors`) records the same cluster:

- every node marked `cruisekube.truefoundry.com/overloaded:NoSchedule`. CruiseKube 0.3.4 puts this mark on a node it judges

machine leaving service. The recorder now counts a node in service when any one of these holds:
- it is open to new work;
- it is closed (cordoned, or marked idle by the governor) and still carries work that is not a DaemonSet's;
- it is Ready and carries such work, and its only marks are NoSchedule marks that are not Kubernetes' own.

Kubernetes' own marks still take a node out of service: `node.kubernetes.io/*` (unreachable, not ready, under pressure) and

## 67. The Pod Start Wait on One Shared Host



One row of the Kubernetes add-on test read LOSS on the engines that stood on 18 October: the mean wait for a serving pod to
start under KEDA's HTTP add-on. This page is that row's root cause, measured from the runs' own files. It sets out the
mechanism and its exact decomposition, says what it predicts on a fleet of separate machines, and records the rig amendment
that takes the test machine's own limit out of both arms. The engine is not changed. The row is never cut: every table that
read it stands as recorded, and every page names it.

### 67.1 The row

The test (`.github/workflows/kind-addons.yml`, `docs/K8S_COMPASS_PREREGISTRATION.md`) runs native as KEDA with its HTTP add-on.
In the http setup the add-on scales php-apache on the requests in flight. The omni arm is Omni-Compass on top of the same. On
omni-v10, the three-run table of the http setup read the mean pod start wait **LOSS in all three of our runs** (+13.0%, +14.1%,
+21.1% a pod). In the same three runs the total start wait read STEADY, pods started fell 24%, the response time fell 57% (mean)
and 72% (95th percentile), and CPU used rose 50 to 54% (power given). On omni-v11, two runs of the same setup have landed. The
third runs to its end on the rig it started on. Under the other setup, both (the CPU target and the requests in flight), the
mean pod start wait, pooled over the repetitions, was lower in the omni arm on both engines (−7.8% on omni-v10, −6.3% on
omni-v11; section 67.3).

### 67.2 What a pod start is made of

From Kubernetes' own timestamps in each repetition's pod watch (`pod_watch.json`), every serving pod created and made Ready
inside the measured window splits into three phases:

- **scheduling**, created → PodScheduled: the scheduler's choice of a node.
- **node side**, PodScheduled → container running: the kubelet, the pod's sandbox and network, and the image.
- **app and probe**, container running → Ready: php-apache's start and its readiness probe (TCP on port 80, every 2 s).

`tools/pod_phases.py` reads them and places each start by two things: the host's busy share over that start (`host_cpu.csv`,
the real machine under kind) and whether its node already carried a Ready serving pod when the pod was created. The receipt
is `results/live/POD_START_PHASES.md`: 741 starts in five runs, three on omni-v10 (39108180989, 39115242861, 39123583570) and
two on omni-v11 (39148024948, 39157778756). Kubernetes stamps these times in whole seconds, so one start is read to ±1 s and
the ranges below are over every stratum holding more than one start:

| Phase | Node already serving | Empty node |
|---|---:|---:|
| scheduling | 0.00 to 0.02 s | 0.00 to 0.20 s |
| node side | 0.72 to 0.94 s | 6.94 to 11.86 s |
| app and probe | 0.49 to 0.86 s | 0.40 to 0.91 s |

The whole difference is the node side on an empty node. php-apache runs `registry.k8s.io/hpa-example`, named without a tag,
so its pull policy is Always. On a node that already serves, the kubelet asks the registry for the image's digest, finds
every layer on the node, and starts the container in under a second. On a node that never served, it downloads the image
and unpacks it, and that takes 7 to 12 s.

### 67.3 Why the omni arm's starts took longer: the exact decomposition

Let s run over strata, each a band b of the host's busy share (0 to 0.5, 0.5 to 0.7, 0.7 to 1) paired with the node's state
(empty or already serving). For arm a, let p[a,s] be the share of its starts in stratum s and W[a,s] their mean wait. Then the
change in the mean wait splits exactly in two:

ΔW̄ = W̄[omni] − W̄[native] = Σₛ (p[omni,s] − p[native,s]) · W[native,s] + Σₛ p[omni,s] · (W[omni,s] − W[native,s])

The first term is the shift of starts into other strata, a busier host or an empty node. The second is the wait at the same
host load on the same kind of node. Where native has no start in a stratum, the first term takes the omni arm's own wait there
(W[native,s] := W[omni,s]), and the two terms still add to ΔW̄ exactly. `tests/test_pod_phases.py` checks the identity on a
constructed run.

| Engine, setup | Native W̄ | Omni W̄ | ΔW̄ | Shift into other strata | Same stratum |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| omni-v10, http | 8.52 s | 9.94 s | +1.42 s (+16.7%) | +1.57 s | −0.14 s |
| omni-v11, http | 8.62 s | 9.27 s | +0.65 s (+7.6%) | +1.64 s | −0.98 s |
| omni-v10, both | 2.64 s | 2.43 s | −0.21 s (−7.8%) | −0.35 s | +0.14 s |
| omni-v11, both | 2.99 s | 2.80 s | −0.19 s (−6.3%) | −0.26 s | +0.07 s |

Under the http setup, every rise in the mean is the shift: 21 of the omni arm's 68 starts on omni-v10, and 11 of its 44 on
omni-v11, began while the host was at least 70% busy. Native's starts never did. At the same host load on the same kind of
node, the omni arm's starts were as fast as native's or faster (−0.14 s and −0.98 s). These numbers are pooled over the runs'
repetitions, so they differ a little from the table's paired means. They are shown, never judged. The judged row stays the
three-run table's.

### 67.4 The mechanism on one machine

A kind cluster is one machine. All seven nodes (a control plane and six workers) are containers on one 4-core GitHub runner,
and they share its processor and its disk. Omni-Compass conveys idle processor to the serving pods: it raises their CPU
limits in place. That is the work behind the response-time GAIN, and it shows as CPU used, power given. On kind, that
processor is the same one on which every node unpacks an image. A pod placed on an empty node therefore unpacks its image on
a processor that the conveyed pods on other nodes are keeping busy. Unpacking is processor and disk work, so it took longer:
the node side on an empty node rose from 6.9 to 7.9 s with the host under half busy to 10.4 to 11.9 s with it at least 70%
busy. omni-v7's shared-host guard (`omni_controller/capacity.py`) already holds every new raise while the runner is 75% busy
or unread. It cannot move the unpacking off the processor the raises already granted are using.

### 67.5 What it predicts on a fleet of separate machines

This section is a prediction, not a measurement. On a fleet, each node is its own machine. A new pod's image is unpacked on
its own node's processor, and the processor conveyed to pods on other nodes does not touch it. A pod placed beside pods
already serving finds the image on its node and starts in about the time this rig measures for such a pod (1.3 to 1.7 s in
total). So the coupling in section 67.4 is a property of the single machine. It is a test machine's limit, never Omni's result,
and the row that showed it is reported as measured. The cloud sets (Azure now; Google and Amazon behind their $0 check) run
every node on its own machine, and they measure it.

### 67.6 The amendment (2026-10-18): the served image pulled onto every worker before each arm

On kind, before each arm and before the governor starts or the window opens, `scripts/kind_bench.sh` applies an image
pre-puller (`deploy/kind/prepull.yaml`). This is a DaemonSet with one pod on every worker, which pulls `registry.k8s.io/hpa-example`
as an operator's image pre-puller does on a production fleet. The bench waits until the pre-puller's pod is ready on every
worker, then deletes it. A pre-puller that does not finish on every worker fails the arm's checks, so the arm is marked
invalid and never runs on the other rig. Each arm's `preflight.txt` records `images=pre-pulled on every worker before the arm`
and the digest each worker pulled.

- **The same in both arms.** Every worker carries the image before either arm is told apart.
- **The operator's manifests are left as written.** `deploy/kind/demo.yaml` still names the image without a tag, so the
  kubelet still asks the registry for its digest at every start, in both arms. It then finds every layer on the node.
- **Not the engine.** No fingerprinted file changes: the pre-puller is the rig's, and it moved no engine's digest (`python3 tools/omni_version.py`).
- **Not the clouds.** On AKS, GKE and EKS every node is its own machine and unpacks on its own processor. Their sets keep
  `demo.yaml` and their rig as their A, B and C started.
- **Never two rigs in one table.** A kind workflow's run on omni-v11 counts toward its three only when the run's own commit
  carries the pre-puller (`RIG_FILE` in `scripts/dispatch_grid.py`, read from GitHub at that commit). That covers the core
  benchmark, the seven Kubernetes repetition sets, the large organisms, fixed capacity, KEDA's add-ons, CruiseKube,
  Goldilocks and the robustness pair. Their omni-v11 runs on the rig before run to their end, since nothing is cancelled, and stay as their own record. `tools/confirm_abc.py` reads the
  rig from every arm's preflight record and heads any table whose A, B and C ran on different rigs with that fact. The
  grid's squares with the real cluster inside count runs by protocol, carried in each run's name. This rig is protocol 4
  (`KUBE_PROTOCOL`), and no omni-v11 run with the cluster inside had started on protocol 3, so all of theirs run on it.

### 67.7 What the next runs are expected to show (written before any of them)

On the amended rig, a serving pod on an empty node should start in about the time one beside a serving pod takes, about 1.3
to 1.7 s in both arms. The host's busy share should then stop deciding the wait. Whatever the three runs read is the
reading. A LOSS is root-caused again and never cut.

### 67.8 Threats to validity, and what stays

- **Every worker carries the image**, including workers no serving pod would reach in a given repetition. That costs disk
  before the window and nothing inside it.
- **The registry is still asked for the digest** at every start, in both arms (pull policy Always, as the operator wrote
  it). The round trip is inside the 0.72 to 0.94 s node side measured on nodes already serving.
- **The host still couples the arms' other work.** Conveyed processor still shares the runner with the kubelets, the probes
  and the load generator. omni-v7's shared-host guard and the window's refusal rules stand as before.
- **The batch jobs' small image** (`busybox:1.36`, about 4 MB) is still pulled on first use inside the window, as before. It
  unpacks in well under a second.
- **The model gate carries the old rig.** The conveyance model's pod start time (`start_time` in `tools/model_gate.py`: 8 s up to
  half busy, rising to 12.4 s near the top) was fitted to the omni-v6 KEDA run's 151 starts. That curve is the empty-node
  unpacking of section 67.4 in model form, and it is why the gate reads the pod start wait under conveyance LOSS (+9.0% on
  omni-v10 and omni-v11, `docs/OMNI_V11.md`). The curve is refit from the first amended-rig KEDA runs' own files, never
  guessed. Until then the model's start-wait row reads this coupling, not the governor.

scripts/raw_archive.sh open /addons-run-39108180989/ /addons-run-39115242861/ /addons-run-39123583570/ \

## 68. The 95th and 99th Percentiles: Where a Tail Reads Higher, and Why



The founder asked on 19 October why the 95th and 99th percentiles show a loss on the live page. This page answers from the
receipts themselves. Every number is read from omni-v11's three-run tables (the engine that stood when this page was written) and from the raw
files of their runs. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these
results.

### 68.1 No tail reads LOSS

By the preregistered rule (a gauge reads LOSS only when it moves away from its aim in all three of our runs, every 95%
interval clear of zero), **no 95th- or 99th-percentile row reads LOSS in any omni-v11 table** (23 tables), and none read
LOSS in the omni-v10 tables before them. The one omni-v10 LOSS, the pod start wait under KEDA's HTTP add-on, was the test
machine (an empty node unpacking the image inside the window); since the kind rig pulls the served image onto every worker
before each arm, it reads STEADY on omni-v11 (`docs/POD_START_WAIT.md`, `results/live/V11_KEDA_REQUESTS.md`).

### 68.2 Real Kubernetes: Omni-Compass's tail was below native's in every repetition

The 90 paired repetitions of the three omni-v11 Kubernetes tests (Goldilocks, KEDA's HTTP add-on, KEDA on CPU and requests;
ten pairs in each of runs A, B and C), each scored from its own raw files by `tools/live_reps.py arm_gauges`:

| Test | Repetitions | Omni-Compass's 95th percentile above native's | 99th percentile above native's | The 95th percentile, three-run reading |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Goldilocks and the VPA | 30 | 0 | 0 | cut 61% to 64%, GAIN |
| KEDA's HTTP add-on | 30 | 0 | 0 | cut 72% to 74%, GAIN |
| KEDA on CPU and requests | 30 | 0 | 0 | cut 52% to 53%, GAIN |

### 68.3 Where a single run's tail rose: the data stores and the kill test

Six tail rows on omni-v11 have one or two runs whose interval lies wholly above zero. None holds in all three runs, so each
reads STEADY; a page that colours each run's cell on its own shows them red.

| Table, workload | Gauge | A | B | C | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kafka at the max, light | end-to-end latency, 99th percentile | +4.2% (+2.0 to +6.5) | −1.6% (−11.8 to +8.6) | −2.8% (−12.6 to +7.0) | one run up, two down: run-to-run variation |
| MySQL at the tune-down, read and write | latency, 95th percentile | +11.4% (+6.9 to +15.9) | −3.6% (−57.6 to +50.4) | +0.2% (−76.5 to +76.9) | one run up, the other two within wide noise |
| Redis at the tune-down, small values | latency, 99th percentile | +0.1% (+0.1 to +0.2) | +0.1% (−0.2 to +0.4) | +0.2% (−0.1 to +0.5) | about 6 µs on 5,600 µs, consistent in sign |
| Redis at the max, small values | latency, 99th percentile | +0.1% (−0.5 to +0.6) | +0.2% (+0.1 to +0.4) | +0.2% (+0.1 to +0.3) | the same |
| The governor killed outright mid-run (robustness) | response time, 99th percentile | +25.2% (+7.7 to +42.7) | −27.3% (−60.1 to +5.5) | −24.5% (−55.7 to +6.8) | one repetition of run A (below) |
| Redis at the max, the tuning workload | latency, 99th percentile | +0.3% (−0.0 to +0.5) | +0.2% (+0.1 to +0.2) | +0.0% (−0.2 to +0.3) | the same (the tuning workload, not counted) |

**The Kafka and MySQL rows are single-run excursions.** In each, one run rose and the others fell or sat inside a wide
interval; the three-run rule exists to keep such a run from being read as a result. On MySQL's read-and-write workload the
three runs' intervals are ±4.5, ±54 and ±77 points wide: with three pairs a run, the test cannot resolve a tail change of
under about 10% of native (`docs/POWER.md`).

**The kill test's row is one repetition.** In nine of run A's ten repetitions both arms' 99th percentile is the probe's
10-second timeout. In the fifth, the omni arm's slowest answers reached 9.2 s 140 to 190 s after the kill, at the load's peak,
with every setting already handed back to native's and both arms at the same ten replicas; the runner's processor was 100% busy
for 70 s, and the second governor had started 50 s before on the same four cores. That is the likely cause, not proven
(`docs/ROBUSTNESS_PREREGISTRATION.md`, "On omni-v11").

**The Redis rows are a real, tiny, consistent rise: about 6 µs at the 99th percentile.** Pooled over the 27 counted pairs
of each set, Omni-Compass's 99th percentile is +5.8 µs (standard deviation 8.9 µs) at the tune-down and +7.1 µs (8.9 µs) at
the max, while its mean latency falls about 32 µs (the larger ceiling turns misses into hits). The order of the arms does
not explain it: with Omni-Compass running second the rise is +4.9 µs, running first +8.5 µs. The cause is examined in
section 68.4.

### 68.4 The Redis tail: the harness's own layout, not Omni-Compass's effect on Redis

In the Redis harness (`tools/run_redis.py`) the brain runs as a thread inside the load generator's own Python process. Once a
second it reads the last second's requests (twice rebuilding a list of about 1,500 of them under the application's lock),
decides and writes its audit line. While it computes it holds Python's interpreter lock, so a request thread that wakes from
its store-trip sleep at that moment waits before its clock is read. Omni-Compass in a deployment is its own process and never
a thread inside the application it governs; only this harness puts the two together. The harnesses of the other data stores
do not: Kafka's producer and consumers, pgbench, sysbench and YCSB all run as processes of their own.

**The test** (`tools/redis_brain_probe.py`, the record in `results/REDIS_BRAIN_PROBE.json`, class S). It runs the harness's
own application at the GitHub rate (1,500 requests a second, 32 request threads), with and without the harness's own brain
loop in the same process, paired, the order alternating. Two outside parts are stand-ins, the same in both arms. The store
answers every request in a fixed 0.1 ms (a sleep, as a socket wait is), a hit with probability 0.6 and otherwise the declared
5 ms store trip. The plug writes nowhere, so the brain reads, decides and runs its trials while the cache never changes. The
only difference between the arms is the brain thread computing in the same process (1.4 ms of processor a second).

| With the brain in the process, against without (12 pairs of 20 s) | Change | 95% interval | Pairs with a rise |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| response time, 99th percentile | +101 µs | +50 to +151 µs | 10 of 12 |
| response time, 95th percentile | +6.8 µs | +1.2 to +12.4 µs | 9 of 12 |
| response time, median | +2.1 µs | +0.2 to +4.0 µs | 9 of 12 |
| response time, mean | +5.4 µs | +2.9 to +7.9 µs | 11 of 12 |

**What it shows.** The brain's presence in the load generator's process, with nothing else changed, lengthens the timed
requests, most in the tail. In this stand-in the effect is larger than on GitHub's machines (+101 µs at the 99th percentile
against about +6 µs), because the stand-in's store answers in a fixed time and its tail is narrow. Three findings agree with it:
- in the Redis set run with native as shipped, the brain is idle (the knob is at its limit on native, and it computes
  nothing), and the 99th percentile shows no rise of consistent sign (`V11_REDIS_SHIPPED.md`);
- the rise appears in both of the operator's sets, where the brain computes every second;
- the mean still falls in those sets, because the larger ceiling turns misses into hits.

The tail rise is the harness's layout, and it weighs against Omni-Compass, because only the omni arm carries the brain inside
its process. A direct test on a real Redis on this machine (three pairs) could not resolve it: the arms differed by hundreds of
microseconds from pair to pair, and it was replaced by the test above.

**The fix.** The harness runs the brain in a process of its own, as a deployment does. It changes how the omni arm is
measured, so it lands with the next engine version and its reruns, never inside the omni-v11 tables
(`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`).

### 68.5 Why the live page showed red

The live page (`docs/engine/OMNI_COMPASS_LIVE_ENGINE.html`, rebuilt by its own workflow) reads each benchmark's newest
table. Until the omni-v11 tables reached main it read omni-v10's, where the KEDA pod start wait read LOSS. It also shows
each run's own interval beside the three-run reading, so a single run's rise, like those in section 68.3, can show as that
run's own excursion even where the three-run reading is STEADY. With the omni-v11 tables on main (19 October), the page's
only LOSS is gone, and its next rebuild reads them.

## 69. How Small an Effect Each Test Can See



Generated by `python3 tools/power.py` from the newest three-run table of each benchmark that stores its rows (`results/live/V*_*.json`); `tools/power.py --check`, run by `verify.py`, fails a push where this page is not what the tables give.

A row reads **STEADY** when a run's 95% interval includes zero: the change is smaller than the test resolves, not zero. The columns say how small:

- **MDE, one run**: the smallest true change one run detects with 80% power (two-sided 5%).
- **MDE, all three runs**: the smallest true change that reads GAIN or LOSS in all three of our runs with 80% power (each run at 92.8%).
- **Repetitions for 5%**: the paired repetitions a run would need for the three-run MDE to reach 5% of native.

Each figure is in percent of native's mean in the least favourable of the three runs. Every number is computed from the table's own intervals with the Student t quantiles the tables use (`omnicompass/student_t.py`).

### 69.68 What the STEADY rows mean

157 rows read STEADY. In 2 of them the test could not resolve a change under 10% of native in all three runs, so STEADY there means "no change larger than the MDE shown", and nothing finer is claimed.

## 70. Every Change to Every Preregistration



Generated by `python3 tools/deviations.py` from the preregistrations in `docs/`; `tools/deviations.py --check`, run by `verify.py`, fails a push where this register is not what they give. Each amendment's reason, and what it changed, is written in the preregistration it amends; this register is the index to all of them, newest first. The timing is the amendment's own statement in its heading. Earlier windows, runs and tables keep the rule they ran under, and a three-run table never pools runs from either side of an amendment that changes what it reads.

94 amendments in 18 preregistrations: 76 before the runs it governs; 11 not stated in its heading; 7 after runs began.

## 71. Limitations and Threats to Validity



What the newest three-run tables (omni-v11's; omni-v23, the engine that stands since 31 October, runs every benchmark again)
can and cannot support, written the way a referee reads a
study: who ran it, what could bias a comparison, what a gauge really measures, how often the reading rule could be fooled,
and how far a result travels. Each limitation names what would remove it. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own
code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

### 71.1 Independence

- **Every run is ours.** The harnesses, the runs, the tables and this page are The Omni-Compass LLC's own; no outside party
  has run, reproduced or reviewed them. What reduces the dependence on us: every table is rebuilt from its raw receipts by a
  public command and compared byte for byte (`tools/reproduce.py`, `reproduce.yml`), every rule was written before its
  runs (`docs/DEVIATIONS.md` lists every later change with its timing), and every raw file carries its SHA-256.
- **What would remove it:** an outside party running the same workflows from a fork, or the paired protocol on its own
  system (`docs/PILOT_PROTOCOL.md`).

### 71.2 Internal validity: could something other than Omni-Compass explain a difference?

- **Pairing and order.** Each repetition runs native and Omni-Compass back to back on the same machine, alternating which
  goes first. With three pairs a run (the data stores) the order cannot balance (two to one). Where it was checked (the
  Redis tail, `docs/TAIL_LATENCY.md`) the difference held in both orders.
- **The machine moves between runs.** GitHub's free machines differ from run to run. On MySQL's update workload the
  throughput was +0.3% in every pair of run B and −0.4% in every pair of run C, so the row reads "the runs disagree": a
  machine-level effect larger than the change, under an offered rate that pins throughput near 98% of what is offered.
- **One machine under kind.** Every Kubernetes node in the kind tests is a container on one runner; the governor counts that
  machine's processor once (omni-v6) and the served image is pulled onto every worker before each arm (18 October). A
  multi-machine cluster (Azure) is the test of the cloud's own behaviour.
- **The measuring process.** In the Redis harness the brain runs as a thread inside the load generator's own Python
  process, and its once-a-second work shares Python's interpreter lock with the request threads. The 99th percentile there
  reads about 6 µs higher with Omni-Compass in two of three runs. A controlled test shows the cause: the brain's presence in
  the process, with nothing else changed, lengthens the timed requests (99th percentile +101 µs, 10 of 12 pairs; mean +5 µs,
  11 of 12) (`docs/TAIL_LATENCY.md`, section 4). The bias weighs against Omni-Compass, because only its arm carries the
  brain, and no deployment runs the brain inside the application. The next version's harness runs it in a process of its
  own. The other data stores' load generators already run as processes of their own.
- **Simulators that do not reproduce exactly.** CityLearn's comfort score moved by up to 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ between runs in both
  arms alike; PyBullet (the drone swarm) reproduces to about one part in a thousand across GitHub's machines. Rows that do
  not reproduce read "the runs differ", and the tables say when the paired change was exactly zero.

### 71.3 Construct validity: does each gauge measure what its name says?

- **Energy in the Kubernetes and swarm tables is a declared model**, not a meter (evidence class S inside a live test).
  No physical meter has measured Omni-Compass yet (class P: none), so less energy is **undetermined**.
- **Node-hours on kind are not a bill.** The cloud bill is measured only in the cloud (Azure, running).
- **The modelled muscles and organisms are our own models** (class S): 1,107 muscles, 527 GAIN, 0 LOSS
  (`results/realms_v5/REALMS_V5.md`) say what our models do, never what a real plant does.
- **A margin no gauge judges, and a fault it hid.** In the drone swarm the judged safety gauge is the near miss (two drones
  under half the 0.3 m keep-out, 0.15 m). The closest approach is shown, not judged. With Omni-Compass on top it fell from
  about 0.30 m to as low as 0.156 m (run C, the short cell). There was no near miss and no collision in any counted run, but
  the margin native keeps was spent to fly faster. On mission draws outside the preregistered seeds it read LOSS: on the mixed
  cell with draw 214, the omni-v11 wire let two drones come within 0.083 m, with 5 near-miss ticks and 3 collision ticks, where
  native flew the same draw with none (`results/model_gate/V12_SWARM_REFLEX.md`). A preregistered set of seeds could not show
  it, and only flying draws the wire was never tuned on did.
- **The cause is in the wire, not the brain.** The proximity reflex is written to return the planner's cruise at once. The
  code lowered the speed by 0.01 a tick instead, so a drone that saw a neighbour within 0.5 m flew fast for about a second more.
- **The fix**: the reflex at once, reaching out with the square of the speed, as the stopping distance does. In our own
  flights it held every drone at or outside the full keep-out (the least, 0.304 m), with no near miss and no collision, on all
  ten cells and draws tried, the four preregistered cells and six untouched draws. It kept 49% to 92% of the energy cut.
- **What came with it.** The fix landed in omni-v12 (`docs/OMNI_V12.md`), and the same version's preregistration amendment
  (`docs/SWARM_PREREGISTRATION.md`, amendment 2, written before its runs) makes a collision with Omni-Compass on top a judged
  LOSS row, voids a cell only when native itself collides, and adds three mission draws no wire was ever run on.

### 71.4 Statistical conclusion validity: how often could the reading rule be fooled?

- **The three-run rule is strict.** A row reads GAIN or LOSS only when three separate runs all move the same way with every
  95% interval clear of zero. With no true change, and runs independent, one run's interval is clear of zero on a given side
  with probability 0.025, so a false GAIN or LOSS in a row has probability 2 × 0.025³ ≈ 3.1 × 10⁻⁵. Over the 1,039 judged
  rows of the omni-v11 tables the expected number of false readings is at most 0.03. Of those rows, 613 are in tests that
  carry noise; the other 241 are in deterministic simulators, which reproduce to the digit. Over the 613 the expectation is
  0.02. Runs share the harness, so they are not fully independent of it; the number is a guide, not a guarantee.
- **STEADY is not zero.** A row reads STEADY when the test could not resolve a change; `docs/POWER.md` gives, for every judged
  row, the smallest change all three runs would detect. Many data-store rows (three pairs a run) cannot resolve a change
  under 10% of native; STEADY there means "no change larger than that", and nothing finer is claimed.
- **Rows where the runs disagree** (omni-v11): MySQL's update throughput (above), CityLearn's comfort score in two districts
  (CityLearn's own drift; the paired change exactly zero), and the drone swarm's closest approach, tracking error and
  cruise override (PyBullet's reproduction; the first is the margin of section 71.3, the other two are shown, not judged).
- **A fixed set of seeds is a sample, not a guarantee.** Every preregistered test runs on seeds written before its runs, so a
  reading holds for those draws. The swarm's collisions (section 71.3) appeared only on a draw outside them. The swarm's omni-v12
  runs add three draws never flown (amendment 2); the other tests still run on their fixed seeds alone.

### 71.5 External validity: how far does a result travel?

- **Loads.** Open-loop load generators on synthetic schedules, one public day of demand (Google 2011) on kind, and the data
  stores' published benchmark workloads (sysbench, YCSB, pgbench). No production traffic.
- **Size.** kind clusters of six workers on one machine; an Azure cluster of four workers. No large production fleet.
- **Undetermined:** the cloud bill (Azure running, Google and Amazon gated by their $0 checks), energy (no meter), the GPU
  (no run on the engine that stands), production readiness (no deployment). These are written as undetermined wherever
  they appear, never as results.

### 71.6 The engine changed often

Twelve versions in twelve days (omni-v5 to omni-v16, `docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`), each through omni-v15 a fault found in a real
run and fixed, and omni-v16 the decision pace made a clean setting on the founder's word.
No table mixes engines, and each benchmark runs again on every version; the cost is that each version's three-run tables
take a day or more to land, so the newest tables of some benchmarks are an older engine's until they do.

## 72. The Evidence Ledger



Every material statement in the technical package gets exactly one primary evidence class. A statement never
borrows a stronger class from the one printed beside it.

| Class | Meaning | Layer |
|---|---|---|
| **T** | formally proved theorem, under stated assumptions | L1 mathematical mechanism |
| **V** | finite computational verification: exact over a declared finite set, never a theorem beyond it | L1 |
| **S** | simulation / model result | L2 modelled systems |
| **L** | live observation of external software (a real Kubernetes API, a real process) | L3 external software |
| **P** | independent physical measurement (a meter Omni does not read or control) | L4 physical plant |
| **O** | open: not established | — |

No layer stands in for another: a theorem is not a physical validation, a Monte Carlo result is not a theorem, and a
model's energy is not a meter's.

Mechanism identity for every row: `results/MECHANISM_IDENTITY.json`. Canonical engine `symmetric_verified`, mechanism
id `29d9808dfb8f…`; the printed configuration `printed_eight_line`, id `cd333dc166fb…`, is a named alternative
(Option A of the directive: one canonical, one alternative embodiment; no equivalence is claimed).

|---|---|---|

## 74. Comparison with Existing Controllers



People who run these systems often see "autoscaling" everywhere and assume it all does the same thing. It does not.
This page sets out, from public descriptions, what each system controls, and where Omni-Compass sits among them.
The five systems named most often, nine open-source pieces read from their own repositories (license, kind, where
each can run, its register row) and the formal distinction between one governor and a collection of tools:
`docs/THE_SEAT.md`.

**How to read it.** Borg and Twine are private to Google and Meta; Turbonomic is closed commercial software. None of
them can be run here, so they are compared by what their makers have published (papers, documentation, product
pages), never by a run. A mark of "—" means the capability is not in the system's public description, not that it
is impossible for it. The only fair measured comparison is on the customer's own system: their stack as it runs today
against the same stack with Omni-Compass on top, in paired runs (`docs/INTEGRATION_MANUAL.md`, section 6).

---

### 74.1 What each system controls

| System (public description) | Pods / replicas | Machines | GPU power | CPU clock / power | Moves watts between CPU and GPU | Site power budget | One decision across all of these |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Kubernetes HPA | ✓ | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| Kubernetes VPA | ✓ (requests) | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter | — | ✓ | — | — | — | — | — |
| KEDA | ✓ (to zero) | — | — | — | — | — | — |
| Red Hat OpenShift / OKD | ✓ (the Kubernetes autoscalers) | ✓ (machine autoscaling) | — | — | — | — | — |
| IBM Turbonomic | ✓ (sizing, scaling) | ✓ (placement, sizing) | — | — | — | — | partial (resource actions across layers) |
| Google Borg | ✓ (job scheduling) | ✓ (cluster placement) | — | — | — | Google has published separate power-capping work | — |
| Meta Twine | ✓ | ✓ | — | — | — | Meta has published separate power management (Dynamo) | — |
| NVIDIA DCGM | — | — | ✓ (limits, monitoring) | — | — | — | — |
| Linux schedutil, RAPL | — | — | — | ✓ | — | — | — |
| AMD SmartShift, NVIDIA Dynamic Boost (laptops) | — | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (inside one laptop) | — | inside one device |
| Intel GEOPM (HPC) | — | — | partial | ✓ | partial (per job) | ✓ (per job / cluster) | partial |
| **Omni-Compass** | ✓ (on top of HPA; or deciding) | ✓ (park and wake) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (conveyance law; simulated) | ✓ (simulated) | ✓ |

### 74.2 How each one decides

| | Typical rule | Omni-Compass |
|---|---|---|
| Pods | add replicas when average CPU passes a target | the same autoscaler keeps working; Omni-Compass sets its target from the whole system's state and raises floors ahead of bursts |
| Machines | add when pods cannot be placed, remove when underused | park and wake machines by one law, and only when every sense is live, pods are not rising and nothing waits |
| GPU | vendor default: full power, or a fixed cap set by hand | a cap from the engine, bounded by a floor and released at once when the card is busy or response time slips |
| CPU | the kernel's governor picks a clock from recent load | a ceiling from the same engine, inside the nervous system's envelope |
| Power | a fixed plan leaving room for every device at peak; a breaker or capper reacts when the site goes over | one conserved budget: watts move from organs holding surplus to organs in need, never created, never over the budget |
| Safety | per tool | one OFF switch returns every organ to its recorded setting; watch mode first; service first |

### 74.3 What is different, in plain words

1. **One brain instead of many separate reflexes.** Today each tool watches its own gauge: the pod autoscaler watches
   CPU, the node autoscaler watches pending pods, the GPU runs at its default, the power plan is fixed on paper.
   Nobody decides for the whole. Omni-Compass reads the whole system into one state and tells each tool the envelope
   it may act in. The tools keep doing their own jobs.
2. **Power as a budget that moves.** Today a building keeps room for every device to hit its peak at once, so much of
   its power sits reserved and unused. Omni-Compass treats the building's watts as one conserved total and moves them
   to where the work is: from CPUs and quiet GPUs to busy GPUs, never over the limit (`docs/CONVEYANCE_LAW.md`).
3. **A proof, not a tuned dial.** The budget law is proved to conserve the budget and to converge, and those
   properties are checked on every build (`tests/test_conveyance.py`).
4. **Service guarded on every power move.** Power is only taken back while response time is inside the target, and
   given back at once when it is not.
5. **Reversible in one move.** Every setting is recorded before it is changed and restored by one switch.

### 74.4 What the numbers show today, and what kind they are

| Against | Result | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| Kubernetes as it runs by default (HPA + fixed nodes) | p95 response time −37% to −55%, replicas −12% to −25%, machines in service −17% to −21% | measured on real Kubernetes (kind), 10 paired runs each, `results/live/` |
| A GPU at its vendor default | +1.3% to +5.1% work per energy, p95 within +10% | modelled card (MLPerf-calibrated), `results/gpu/sim/after` |
| Today's power practice (every GPU at one fixed cap that leaves room for every CPU at peak) | +1.4% to +5.7% work served, backlog −16% to −28%, never over the site budget | modelled, `results/hardware/NODE_EXCHANGE_*.json` |
| A reactive site capper alone | 60-196 minutes over the site budget without Omni-Compass; 0 with it | modelled |

Turbonomic, Borg and Twine cannot be measured here. Against a customer who runs one of them, the comparison is made on
the customer's own system, with the same paired method.

### 74.5 Sources

- Kubernetes HPA, VPA, Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter, KEDA: the projects' own documentation.
- Red Hat OpenShift / OKD: Red Hat's documentation of its autoscaling and machine management.
- IBM Turbonomic: IBM's product documentation.
- Borg: Verma et al., "Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg", EuroSys 2015; Google's public Borg traces.
- Twine: Tang et al., "Twine: A Unified Cluster Management System for Shared Infrastructure", OSDI 2020.
- Meta Dynamo: Wu et al., "Dynamo: Facebook's Data Center-Wide Power Management System", ISCA 2016.
- NVIDIA DCGM and Dynamic Boost; AMD SmartShift; Intel GEOPM: the vendors' documentation.

Where a row above is wrong or out of date, correct it from the maker's own publication.

## 75. The State of Play



<!-- how to read this receipt (tools/readings.py) -->
**How to read this receipt.** Every judged row reads one of three words, decided by what its gauge is for and never by the plus or minus sign of its number. **GAIN**: the gauge moved toward its declared aim against native (more work done, a shorter wait, fewer misses or failures, or a resource cut). **STEADY**: native and Omni-Compass within 0.5% of each other (the mean of the three runs' changes under the 0.5% floor, or no change at all), or the knob is at its limit on native. **LOSS**: the gauge moved away from its aim (less work done, a longer wait, more misses or failures). A resource spent or held (energy, the power drawn and its peaks and swings, machines, memory, processor time, a bill, wear) that fell is a cut, a GAIN; one that rose is **power given**, what Omni-Compass put in to buy the work and the speed shown beside it, always shown and never called a loss; work bought with each unit of a resource (work per energy) that fell is power given too. So a minus can read GAIN (a response time cut) and a plus can read LOSS (failed requests up). A change of 0.5% or more, the mean of the three runs' changes, reads GAIN, LOSS or power given: **in all three of our runs** where A, B and C moved the same way with every interval clear of zero, otherwise **by the mean of our three runs**, with the count of runs beyond the noise beside it; **the runs disagree** names runs that moved 0.5% or more in opposite directions, a test unstable there; **shown, not judged** is a gauge declared shown only. The output follows the input: every reading is the result of the tune, the wiring and the load it names, and where a reading elsewhere differs the first presumption is the wiring (`DISCLOSURES.md`, section 4). The full key, letter by letter: `docs/HOW_TO_READ_THE_RESULTS.md`. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results. Preregistered means the rules were written down in our own repository before the runs; nothing was filed with any outside body.
<!-- end: how to read this receipt -->

Current facts only. Earlier states, failures and chronology are kept whole in `docs/HISTORY.md`. The release this page
describes is identified by `RELEASE_MANIFEST.json` (commit, fingerprints of the engine, the C++ twins, the GPU protocol,
the live evidence and the verification receipt), which `verify.py` checks against the files.

**Rerun everything:** `pip install -r requirements.txt && python verify.py` ends with `VERIFICATION: PASS`.

# Part Eight. Value, License and History

*What a receipt is worth, how the license is priced against it, how the code is sealed, and how Omni-Compass came to be.*


## 76. Where the Value Comes From


### 76.1 The problem we are attacking

Computing has run into a wall that is not made of silicon. Data centers cannot get the power they need, cannot get it
fast enough, and are running out of room to put more machines. AI made it harder: every new model needs more chips, and
every chip needs more electricity and more cooling. The answers on the table are expensive and slow: new chips that do
more work per watt (a new generation, new hardware to buy), new power plants and power contracts (billions, and years),
and point fixes at a single layer (an AI serving trick, a scheduler, a power cap on one chip).

We attack it from the other side. Every system already running wastes room it paid for:

- GPUs boost to the top of their clock range and are knocked back by their own power limiter many times a second;
- Kubernetes keeps replicas and machines sized for the worst minute of the day;
- cooling runs colder than the heat requires; batteries hold more reserve than the hour needs.

That room is paid for in energy, in machines and in floor space, and it produces nothing.

Why the room is there is worth a paragraph, because it decides what can be done about it. Each layer of a stack is sized
by someone who cannot see the others. The autoscaler's author does not know what the power cap will do; the cooling
engineer sizes for the hottest hour of the year; the database operator sets a buffer pool for the largest table and leaves
it there; each of them, sensibly, leaves a margin against the layer next door, and the margins add up. None of these
people is wrong. The waste is not a mistake anyone made; it is the price of layers that cannot talk to each other, and it
is why a fix at one layer, however good, moves the margin rather than removing it. The benchmarks in this manual are
each a measurement of one such margin on real software: the connections a pooler holds open that no client is using, the
memory a cache keeps for data it will not be asked for, the machines a cluster keeps in service for a minute that has
passed. Each is small on its own and each is paid for every hour of the year.

The attack, then, is not another autoscaler or another cache. It is a governor that reads every layer's own gauge, keeps
each layer in the middle of its own band, and gives the margin back where the layer's own controller shows it is not
needed, with the layer's own controller still underneath and the layer's own setting restored when the governor is gone.
That is a different kind of thing from a point fix, and it is why it stacks on top of every point fix a data center has
already made rather than competing with any of them.

### 76.2 What Omni-Compass is, in one paragraph

Omni-Compass is software that sits **on top of** the controllers a system already has (the GPU's firmware, the
Kubernetes autoscaler, the building's thermostats) and governs every layer under one law: a bounded push and pull that
keeps each service in the middle of its band instead of far below its limit. It never replaces the native controller,
never asks for more than the native settings allow, hands every knob back the moment it is switched off or loses a
sense, and refuses any step that measures a LOSS of more than 2% on anything. No new hardware. It stacks on top of every
other fix a data center makes.

### 76.3 The benefit: more work from what is already paid for

The room that was spent on nothing becomes one of two things, and a company chooses which:

- **More work for the same cost:** the same machines and the same watts carry more work; or
- **The same work for less:** fewer machines in service, fewer watts, a smaller bill.

They are the same gain read from two sides (3.4). The health side comes with it: faster answers, faster recovery from
failures, nothing waiting, every knob returned, no human babysitting the stack.

The results to date (Chapter 60) show both readings on real software, and show that which one a stack gets is decided by
the stack, not by Omni-Compass. On the real Kubernetes cluster the gain was taken as **more work, faster**: the cluster
carried more requests inside its response line on the same machines. On PostgreSQL behind its pooler, on MySQL's buffer pool
and on MongoDB's storage-engine cache the gain was taken as **the same work for less**: the same transactions answered inside
the same line with fewer connections open, a smaller pool or a smaller cache, each notch proved on the stack first and the
resource handed back at the end of every run. On Apache Kafka the earlier set had taken the gain as more work, faster, at the
cost of three to four times the consumers, and on Redis the compass had bought the hit rate with three to four times the
memory; under the brain's own verdict on the knob (10 October) neither spend was judged on the first set, because the trial
rule of the day ended a spend trial on the calm the spend itself produced, so both read exactly nothing until the amended
set lands (section 60.7). The combined index (section 60.11) is +4.8% over the six real categories on the sets of 10 October,
with no loss in all three of our runs in any category. An operator
should expect the same honesty from their own paired run: the receipts will say which side of the gain their stack took,
and whether the compass's own cost (its CPU, its reads) ate into it.

### 76.4 How to read the benefit: the arithmetic

Every comparison is paired: the same system, the same work, the same moments, native alone against native with
Omni-Compass on top. Let

- *W* be the work served (requests answered, tokens generated), held equal in both arms;
- *C* be a resource it used: machine-hours, CPU core-hours, or joules.

**Productivity** is work per resource, *P = W / C*. With the work held equal, the gain from Omni-Compass on top is

  *G = P[omni] / P[native] − 1 = C[native] / C[omni] − 1.*

A gain *G* means the same resources can carry *G* more work. Read from the other side, the same work needs only

  *C[omni] / C[native] = 1 / (1 + G)*

of the resources, a saving of *S = G / (1 + G)*. So **a third more work (G = 33%) is a quarter off the bill
(S = 25%)**; 20% more work is 16.7% off; 50% more work is a third off. Both columns are the same measurement.

Three rules for reading any receipt:

1. **The work must be equal.** Every receipt states that the load was fixed-rate (open loop): the same requests at the
   same moments in every arm. Without that, a lower resource count could just mean less work was done.
2. **Nothing may read LOSS.** Beside every gain the receipt prints response times, failures, waiting and the controller's
   own CPU, each with its 95% interval. Our one rule (`DISCLOSURES.md`, section 3): no LOSS of more than 2% on any measure, and
   only where energy or the bill is saved. A GAIN paid for with a LOSS of service is not a GAIN.
3. **Know the class and the comparator.** A machine-hour gain on kind (where idle machines stay powered and native has
   no node autoscaler) is not yet a bill; a modelled energy line is not a meter. Chapter 58 lists the classes; Chapter 60
   says, for every result, what it is measured against.

**Three worked examples, from the tables.** In the all-four Kubernetes test on v3, the same ten machines carried 35% to
49% more requests inside the response line: *G* is 0.35 to 0.49, so the same work would need 1/1.35 to 1/1.49 of the
machines, a saving *S* of 26% to 33%, had the fleet been free to shrink; on kind it was not, which is why the table
reports the work column and not a bill. In the database test, the pooler held 61% to 72% fewer connections open for the
same work: the resource there is connections, *C[omni] / C[native]* is 0.28 to 0.39, and the gain read as "more work for
the same connections" would be *G* = 1.6 to 2.6, which the table reports as the machines-equivalent column, "fewer
connections by". In the Kafka test the work inside the line rose 16% to 21% while the consumers running rose by a factor
of 2.6 to 4: there the gain in work was bought with resources, and the table reports both, the one as GAIN in all three of our runs
and the other as power given in all three of our runs, because that is what happened.
