### 88.4 Omni v8: the battery that carries its building through an outage stays native (the engine of 17 October)



Omni v8 stood on main on 17 October; later that day it was followed by Omni v9 (`docs/OMNI_V9.md`), omni-v8 with the
CityLearn battery wire reading the coming hour, which cuts the one row this page names (section 88.3.3; printed LOSS, power given by
the key, `docs/OMNI_V9.md`, section 1), and on 18 October by Omni v10 (`docs/OMNI_V10.md`), the engine that stands. This page
stays as omni-v8's record, read beside no other engine's.

Omni v8 was the engine that stood on main from 17 October (the founder's order: "there's a new version 8 ... push in all and
update all"). It is omni-v7 (`docs/OMNI_V7.md`) with one change to one wire, made because a three-run table of omni-v7 read LOSS
and the cause was found to be ours. Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V8.json` (digest `f93d233136a1f902`, 46 files); of those 46 files,
45 are omni-v7's bytes, and the one that differs is the CityLearn runner. Every benchmark runs again on it (`scripts/reruns.txt`;
the conductor's reruns, grid and Azure queues restarted on it the same day), and every omni-v7 table stands as omni-v7's result
until its three runs on v8 land; results from two versions are never pooled. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code.
No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

| # | Change | Where | What it tightens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A battery whose building simulates power outages stays native: Omni-Compass moves only the batteries with no second duty | `tools/run_citylearn.py` | do no harm where the battery's charge is also its building's reserve |

#### 88.4.1 What omni-v7 read, and why

The omni-v7 CityLearn table (`results/live/V7_CITYLEARN.md`; runs 38937540021, 38949618073, 38959444615) read GAIN in all three
of our runs on the electricity bought and the daily peak in all ten battery districts, and **LOSS in all three of our runs in the
seven 2023 districts** on the energy not served (+2.0% to +9.8%) and the time uncomfortable (+0.01% to +0.15%), beside the
ramping +4.5% to +6.2%, the highest peak +2.5% (three districts) and the monthly unevenness +0.07% (one), power held and so power
given by the key (the table printed those three LOSS too, until the CityLearn tool was corrected on 17 October).

The cause was found on CityLearn itself (version 3.0.2, the version the runs installed), run locally on the same district files
and reproducing the omni-v7 numbers of `citylearn_challenge_2023_phase_2_local_evaluation` to the last digit:

- The seven 2023 districts are the only districts CityLearn ships whose buildings simulate power outages (every building in each:
  3, 3, 3, 3, 6, 6 and 6; every other district none, read from each district's own `schema.json`). CityLearn counts the energy not
  served only in outage hours (`citylearn/cost_function.py`, `normalized_unserved_energy`), and the time uncomfortable rises when an
  islanded building cannot run its cooling.
- The battery wire read the district's draw alone. It did not see the outage hours, and it did not see that in these buildings
  the battery has a second duty: carrying the building through the outage. A command that moves the battery for the district's
  draw during an outage asks for energy the islanded building cannot have.
- Three narrower repairs were tried on the tuning district first and refused there: charging only (the energy not served
  unchanged at +5.96%, LOSS, the ramping +3.5%); handing the battery back to native only during outage hours (the energy not
  served −2.7% and the discomfort −0.13%, both GAIN, with the ramping +7.0% and the monthly unevenness +0.06% beside them); and
  moving no more energy than the draw's excess over its band (the daily peak +0.5% and the ramping +2.6%). With peaks, swings and
  unevenness then read as misses, each was refused. By the key (17 October) those rises are power given, so the second, native
  only in outage hours, reads GAIN on both misses; it is studied again for the next engine version.

#### 88.4.2 The change

The wire now leaves native every battery whose building simulates power outages (CityLearn's own `simulate_power_outage`, read
from the building), as a water tank was left native in round 2: a battery that is also its building's reserve is a muscle with a
second duty, which needs its own wire and its own reading (the outage risk) before Omni-Compass moves it. Every other battery is
moved exactly as before: the compass law, its gain, its response, its glide, its band and its hand-back are unchanged. An action
list the wire cannot place on its buildings moves nothing. The hour count of the file counts only hours where a command moved,
and each district's file says how many batteries were left native for outages (`batteries_left_native_for_outages`).

#### 88.4.3 What it does, read on CityLearn before any GitHub run

On the seven 2023 districts the omni arm is native's to the last digit (every battery left native; checked on
`citylearn_challenge_2023_phase_2_local_evaluation` and `citylearn_challenge_2023_phase_3_1`). On every district without outage
buildings the wire's commands are the same bytes as omni-v7's, so their results are omni-v7's (checked to the digit on
`citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_all_robustness`, every gauge of both arms identical to omni-v7's GitHub run 38937540021, no
battery left native). So v8 removes every LOSS of the 2023 districts and, with them, their small GAINs (the electricity bought
−0.1% to −0.3%, the daily peak −1.3% to −2.6%), which were bought with the LOSS beside them.

One row the table printed LOSS remains, and it is said here: in `citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_all_robustness` (no outage
buildings) the monthly unevenness rose 0.11% in all three of our runs (power given by the key: a ratio of the power held), beside the bill −8.6%, the electricity bought −14.7%, carbon −11.9%, the
daily peak −14.0% and the highest peak −2.7%, all GAIN. The score is a ratio (one minus each month's mean over its peak), and it
rose because the energy fell faster than each month's top hours, which sit at the batteries' limit. Its repair is looked into on
its own, in the model gate first; v8 does not change it.

#### 88.4.4 The model gate and the trial

The change touches no Kubernetes, card or cloud controller, so the model gate's models (`tools/model_gate.py`) read the same on both
checkouts by construction; the gate was run all the same, omni-v8 against omni-v7 on the same seeds, and is recorded in
`results/model_gate/V8_VS_V7.md`: seeds 1 to 8, a day each, every gauge of every model (the cluster at 60 s and at 15 s, conveyance
with the quota readable and unreadable, the verdict on noisy work) identical between omni-v8 and omni-v7, to the last digit and
in every count (steps allowed and refused, trials abandoned, machines parked, errors). The models' readings against native are
omni-v7's and stay disclosed in `docs/OMNI_V7.md`, section 6 (at a decision every 15 s the cloud setting makes pods wait longer
than native, which is why the decision period stays 60 s). These are our own models (class S), never a benchmark result.

The trial is the CityLearn benchmark itself, A, B and C on the v8 commit, read by `tools/citylearn_abc.py` into
results/live/V8_CITYLEARN.md when they land: it must read no LOSS in the 2023 districts and the same table as omni-v7 everywhere else. The
disclosure every amendment carries: every CityLearn district has now been seen, so no untouched district remains for this
amendment; it was fixed on one district (`citylearn_challenge_2023_phase_2_local_evaluation`) and is reported on all
(`docs/CITYLEARN_PREREGISTRATION.md`, amendment of 17 October).

#### 88.4.5 What runs again on it

Everything, A, B and C, from the moment it landed (`scripts/reruns.txt`, released by the conductor a few a tick: A of every
benchmark, then B, then C); the grid on its own manifest (`results/grid_v8/`); every Azure set from A again
(`scripts/azure_queue.txt`). The omni-v7 runs already started run to their end (nothing is cancelled) and stay as omni-v7's
record. Google Cloud and Amazon carry the same sets behind their switches, off until the founder turns them on; the GPU runs on
Lambda wait for his word and one exact commit. The organisms are the seven of 16 October, the spine first (`docs/THE_SPINE.md`).

### 88.5 Omni v9: the battery wire reads the coming hour (the engine that stood on 17 and 18 October)



Omni v9 stood on main from 17 to 18 October; on 18 October it was followed by Omni v10 (`docs/OMNI_V10.md`), the engine that
stands: omni-v9 with the battery glide at 0.0875 an hour, the speed that cuts the bill most with no LOSS (section 88.3.2 below gives
the ladder it was chosen from). This page stays as omni-v9's record, read beside no other engine's.

Omni v9 was the engine on main from 17 October (the founder's orders: "we're going into another version of
Engine ... Apply the fix, run it, and see in the model sim that it works"; "Omni-Compass should be tuned to exploit all that can be
and keep all healthy and never raise its bill ... the tuning stays where it doesn't ever hurt anyone"). It is omni-v8
(`docs/OMNI_V8.md`) with one wire repaired and one statistical table made exact. It was written for one omni-v8 row the table
printed as LOSS; on 17 October the founder found that word misapplied (section 88.3.1): the row was power given. The repair it led to
stands on its own, because it cuts the bill further in every district. Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V9.json` (digest `7379f3a79ff2c475`, 47 files); 44 are omni-v8's bytes, two
differ (the CityLearn runner and the realms harness) and one is new (`omnicompass/student_t.py`). It was proven in our own runs of
CityLearn and in the model gate before it was pushed. Every benchmark runs again on it, and every earlier table stands as its own
engine's result until its three runs on v9 land; results from two versions are never pooled. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass
LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

| # | Change | Where | What it tightens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The battery wire reads the coming hour's draw (the mean of the same hour over the past seven days, only hours already seen) and its adjustment glides at up to 0.0625 of the command's range an hour (0.05 before), the fastest glide that read no LOSS on any score in any district | `tools/run_citylearn.py` | the battery answers the hour it moves, not the hour gone |
| 2 | Every 95% interval uses the exact Student t quantile for its number of pairs | `omnicompass/student_t.py`, `realms/harness.py` and the table tools | no interval narrower than its sample allows, at any count |

#### 88.5.1 What omni-v8 read, and why

One row of the omni-v8 table was printed LOSS: in `citylearn_challenge_2022_phase_all_robustness` (17 buildings, a battery in
each, no outage buildings) the monthly load unevenness (`monthly_one_minus_load_factor_average`: one minus each month's mean draw
over its peak) rose 0.11% in all three of our runs, beside the bill −8.6%, the electricity bought −14.7%, the daily peak −14.0% and
the highest peak −2.7%, all GAIN (the omni-v7 table, whose commands omni-v8 repeats to the byte outside the 2023 districts). **By
the key that row is power given, not a LOSS**: the unevenness is the shape of the power the district holds from the grid, a
resource held, as a peak is; it is neither time waited nor work done nor a miss. The CityLearn table tool had filed the peaks, the
swings and the unevenness as misses; it was corrected on 17 October (`tools/citylearn_abc.py`, `tools/readings.py`: one key for
every gauge, as a cluster's peak power always was). Run locally, the same wire also raised, on districts the GitHub benchmark does
not run (CityLearn ships them only in its source repository), the tuning district's monthly unevenness +0.26%; in the 2022 phase 2
the highest peak +0.17%, the daily unevenness +1.03% and the monthly unevenness +0.68%; in the 2022 phase 3 the highest peak +0.45%
and the ramping +3.37%: power given, every one, and shown here with the rest.

The cause was found in an hour-by-hour trace of the omni-v8 wire on the robustness district (CityLearn 3.0.2, run locally):

- The compass read the district's draw of the hour just gone and moved the batteries for the hour coming, and its adjustment
  could change by only 0.05 of the command's range an hour. Averaged by hour of day over the year, the adjustment discharged
  hardest at 00:00 and charged hardest at 15:00, while the district's draw peaked at 19:00 and bottomed at 13:00: it ran about five
  hours behind the day, still adding charge at 17:00 and 18:00 as the evening peak climbed.
- So the batteries were empty when each month's top hour came: at the month's highest net draw the mean state of charge was 0.000
  to 0.037 in ten of the eleven months the trace covers.
- The score is a ratio. Lowering a month's mean (less energy bought) while its peak hour stays at the batteries' limit raises one
  minus mean over peak: the energy fell faster than the top hours.

Narrower repairs were tried on the robustness district first; each left the unevenness up, so none is in the engine:

| Candidate | What it changed | Monthly unevenness against native |
|---|---|---:|
| no discharge below the band's middle | Omni-Compass adds no discharge in a quiet hour | +0.11% (power given) |
| no new peak (the month's top so far, and the month's or the week's) | the charge it adds never lifts the district above its top so far | +0.11% (power given) |
| peak push | full discharge where the draw nears the month's top so far | +0.12% (power given) |
| a reserve of 30%, 50% or 70% of charge | its added discharge stops at the reserve | +0.42%, +0.25%, +0.25% (power given), and the highest peak's GAIN lost |
| the hour gone, glide 0.25 | faster only | −0.61% (GAIN), the ramping +13.2% (power given) |

#### 88.5.2 The change, and how far it is pushed

The reading is the draw of the hour the batteries are about to move: the mean of the same hour of the day over the past seven
days, h[t−24], h[t−48], …, h[t−168] (only hours already seen; before a day has been seen, the last hour's draw). Nothing else in
the wire changed: the compass law, its gain (0.5), its response (1 h), its band (the 10th to the 90th percentile of the past week's
draw), the hand-back at 90% of the year, the batteries left native in outage buildings (omni-v8) and the water tanks left native.

The glide was set where no score of any district rose: with the new reading, every glide from 0.05 to 0.10 an hour was run on the
districts where the edge lies, and the fastest at which nothing rose in either is 0.0625. Read by the key, no glide on the ladder
reads a LOSS anywhere: every rise below is power given, and the bill keeps falling up to 0.0875 to 0.10:

| District | Score | 0.05 | 0.0625 | 0.075 | 0.0875 | 0.10 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| phase 2 | daily unevenness | +0.25% power given | -0.09% GAIN | -0.67% GAIN | -0.94% GAIN | -0.91% GAIN |
| phase 2 | net-zero shortfall | -7.53% GAIN | -4.77% GAIN | -3.38% GAIN | -2.54% GAIN | -1.99% GAIN |
| phase 2 | the bill | -14.12% GAIN | -17.22% GAIN | -18.75% GAIN | -19.17% GAIN | -19.03% GAIN |
| phase 3 | the ramping | -5.05% GAIN | -1.91% GAIN | +2.32% power given | +6.18% power given | +9.59% power given |
| phase 3 | net-zero shortfall | -2.21% GAIN | -0.76% GAIN | -0.04% STEADY | +0.25% power given | +0.41% power given |
| phase 3 | the bill | -6.60% GAIN | -7.32% GAIN | -8.10% GAIN | -8.43% GAIN | -8.32% GAIN |

At 0.05 the 2022 phase 2's daily unevenness rises; from 0.075 the 2022 phase 3's ramping does, and from 0.0875 its net-zero
shortfall: power given, each. At 0.0625 every score of every district reads GAIN (section 88.3.3). The founder's rule for the tune (use
everything that can be used, keep everything healthy, never raise the bill) takes the glide past 0.0625, to the speed that cuts the
bill most with no LOSS: that is the next version's change, read on CityLearn first.

The second change is statistical and moves no command. The interval tables written in each tool stopped at a few sample sizes and
fell back to 1.96 (the normal quantile) for a number of pairs they did not list, too narrow an interval for a small sample. Every
tool now takes the exact quantile from one file, `omnicompass/student_t.py` (the regularized incomplete beta function, checked
against the published table to three decimals). Every value the old tables held is unchanged; no published table used a count the
old tables lacked, so no published reading moves.

### 88.6 Omni v10: the battery glide at the speed that cuts the bill most (the engine that stood on 18 October)



Omni v10 stood on main on 18 October; the same day it was followed by Omni v11 (`docs/OMNI_V11.md`), the engine that stands:
omni-v10 with the Kubernetes governor's hold on a reading with no machine in service. This page stays as omni-v10's record,
read beside no other engine's. The founder's orders behind it: "Omni-Compass should be tuned to exploit all
that can be and keep all healthy and never raise its bill ... whatever one can't be achieved doesn't get achieved. And the tuning
stays where it doesn't ever hurt anyone"; and, on 17 October, "a minus doesn't mean a loss and neither does a plus mean a gain if
you don't understand what it's against". It is omni-v9 (`docs/OMNI_V9.md`) with one setting changed: the most the CityLearn battery
wire's adjustment may change in an hour (the glide) goes from 0.0625 to 0.0875 of the command's range. The CityLearn runner's own
receipt now reads every score by the one key, as every table already did.

Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V10.json` (digest `4bf39b0d707784de`, 47 files). Forty-six files are omni-v9's bytes and one differs (the CityLearn
runner). The change was proven in our own runs of CityLearn and in the model gate before it was pushed. Every benchmark runs again on
it. Every earlier table stands as its own engine's result until its three runs on v10 land, and results from two versions are never
pooled. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

| # | Change | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The battery wire's glide: 0.0875 of the command's range an hour (omni-v9: 0.0625) | `tools/run_citylearn.py` | the batteries follow the coming hour faster, and the bill falls further in every district that has a price |
| 2 | The runner's receipt reads every score by the one key: a fall is a GAIN; a rise in energy not served or time uncomfortable is a LOSS; a rise in any other score is power given | `tools/run_citylearn.py` | one key for every output, as the three-run table (`tools/citylearn_abc.py`) already read |

#### 88.6.1 Why the glide moved

omni-v9 set the glide at the fastest speed at which no score in any district rose. That rule counted a rise in the ramping or in
the distance from net zero against the engine. The one key of 17 October (`tools/readings.py`) does not. The ramping, the peaks, the
unevenness and the net-zero distance describe the power the district holds from the grid: they are resources held. A rise in one of
them is power given, shown beside what it bought, never a LOSS. Only what the occupants miss is a LOSS: energy not served and time
uncomfortable.

Read by that key, the ladder omni-v9 ran shows that no glide reads a LOSS anywhere, and that the bill keeps falling up to 0.0875. At
0.10 it falls less in both districts that set the edge:

| District | Score | 0.05 | 0.0625 (omni-v9) | 0.075 | 0.0875 (omni-v10) | 0.10 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| phase 2 | the bill | -14.12% GAIN | -17.22% GAIN | -18.75% GAIN | -19.17% GAIN | -19.03% GAIN |
| phase 2 | daily unevenness | +0.25% power given | -0.09% GAIN | -0.67% GAIN | -0.94% GAIN | -0.91% GAIN |
| phase 2 | net-zero shortfall | -7.53% GAIN | -4.77% GAIN | -3.38% GAIN | -2.54% GAIN | -1.99% GAIN |
| phase 3 | the bill | -6.60% GAIN | -7.32% GAIN | -8.10% GAIN | -8.43% GAIN | -8.32% GAIN |
| phase 3 | the ramping | -5.05% GAIN | -1.91% GAIN | +2.32% power given | +6.18% power given | +9.59% power given |
| phase 3 | net-zero shortfall | -2.21% GAIN | -0.76% GAIN | -0.04% STEADY | +0.25% power given | +0.41% power given |

So 0.0875 is the glide that cuts the bill most with no LOSS: the founder's rule for the tune. Nothing else in the wire changed. The
compass law, its gain (0.5), its response (1 h), its reading (the coming hour, from the same hour of the past seven days), its band
(the 10th to the 90th percentile of the past week's draw), the hand-back at 90% of the year, the batteries left native in outage
buildings and the water tanks left native are all omni-v9's.

### 88.7 Omni v11: a reading with no machine in service is blind, never an overload (the engine that stood 18 to 19 October)



Omni v11 stood on main from 18 to 19 October; on the night of 19 October Omni v12 (`docs/OMNI_V12.md`) took its place, which
is omni-v11 with a refused raise held and the swarm's reflex acting at once. This page stays as omni-v11's
record, read beside no other engine's; its 23 three-run tables (`results/live/V11_*.md`) are its own. The founder's order behind
it: every fault found is fixed, none set aside. It is omni-v10 (`docs/OMNI_V10.md`) with one guard added to the Kubernetes governor. When the cluster's reading shows no
machine in service, the governor holds. It records why, decides nothing from that reading, writes nothing, and keeps the last
reading that had machines. Every setting, gain, preset and muscle is omni-v10's, and so is every rule but this guard.

Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V11.json` (digest `745aa53ec8eeb67b`, 47 files). Forty-six files are omni-v10's bytes; one differs, the
Kubernetes governor (`omni_controller/controller.py`). The change was proven in a unit test that reproduces the fault and in the
model gate before it was pushed. Every benchmark runs again on it. Every earlier table stands as its own engine's result until its
three runs on v11 land, and results from two versions are never pooled. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No
outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

| # | Change | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A decision whose reading shows no machine in service holds: it is recorded as held, with its reason, and nothing is decided from it or written | `omni_controller/controller.py`, the decision | the engine is never fed a load measured against no capacity; the decision never divides by zero |
| 2 | The fast floor check returns at once on the same reading | `omni_controller/controller.py`, the floor check | no machine is added from a blind reading |
| 3 | The last reading with machines stays the one the conveyance is bounded by | `omni_controller/controller.py` | a blind moment never lifts the bound on the CPU each pod may be given |

#### 88.7.1 The fault, found in a real run

In the omni-v10 CruiseKube test (run 39120444653, repetition 8, the arm with Omni-Compass on top), every worker of the kind
cluster left service for two minutes. All six workers sit as containers on one GitHub runner. Eight of the capture's readings
show no machine in service, while the service answered every one of its probes (no failed request in any minute of the window).
In that reading the machines' capacity was zero. omni-v10's governor fed the engine a load measured against that zero capacity,
read as the highest overload its scale allows (a load ratio of 2). It then divided by the capacity when it computed the machine
floor. Two of its fifteen decisions and one floor check ended in a division by zero. Each wrote nothing, as the audit shows,
and the cluster kept the settings it had. But the engine's own state had been given a false overload. The words of the rig
named neither: they said the governor was not running.

omni-v11 reads such a reading as blind. The engine is not stepped, the floor is not computed and no machine is added. The audit
says "held: the cluster's reading shows no machine in service; nothing decided, nothing written". When the machines return, the
next decision reads them and the governor takes up where it was. `tests/test_blind_reading.py` builds the same cluster:
two workers serving, then both out of service in the reading. On omni-v10 both of its tests end in the division by zero; on
omni-v11 both pass, with no write and no error.

The rig was repaired beside it (no engine file; `docs/K8S_COMPASS_PREREGISTRATION.md`, amendment of 18 October). A window whose
capture shows no machine in service is refused in either arm, because its machine count is wrong. A failed decision is named by
its error. The capture records each node's taints and conditions at the moment it sees no machine in service.

#### 88.7.2 The model gate

The candidate was run against omni-v10 on seeds 1 to 8 in our own models (`tools/model_gate.py`; `results/model_gate/V11_VS_V10.md`),
on every model: the cluster at a decision every 60 s and every 15 s, the new blink model, conveyance with the quota readable and
unreadable, and the verdict on noisy work. This is the first gate in which each arm is proven to import its own checkout's
engine. From omni-v9's gate on, the gate had put its own tree first, so both arms ran the candidate; omni-v9 and omni-v10
changed no file a model runs, so their readings hold by construction, and each page carries the correction.

| Model | Gauges identical to omni-v10 | Decisions that failed (omni-v10 / omni-v11) | Decisions held (omni-v10 / omni-v11) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| the cluster, a decision every 60 s | 6 of 6 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| the cluster, a decision every 15 s | 6 of 6 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| the blink: every machine out of service in the reading for 2 minutes every 6 hours | 6 of 6 | 64 / 0 | 0 / 64 |
| conveyance, the quota readable | 8 of 8 | (no decision of the governor) | |
| conveyance, the quota unreadable | 8 of 8 | (no decision of the governor) | |
| the verdict on noisy work | 5 of 5 | (no decision of the governor) | |

Every gauge and every count is identical. A decision that failed and one that held both write nothing, so nothing the models
measure moves; what moves is the record (a reason where there was an error) and the engine's own state, which a blind reading
no longer reaches. Against native, the two engines read the same, and four rows read LOSS in both: the pod start wait under
conveyance (+9.0% mean, +10.0% at the 95th percentile), the pending-pod minutes and the response time at a decision every 15 s
(+111.7%, +0.33%; no run decides that often), and the alert minutes in the blink model (+2.35%). They are not this change's; they
are the next version's work, in the gate first. The first is the test machine, not the governor: the model's pod start time was
fitted to the empty-node image unpacking of the single kind host (`docs/POD_START_WAIT.md`, section 8), and the kind rig now
pre-pulls the image. These are our own models (class S), never a benchmark result.

#### 88.7.3 What runs again on it

Everything runs again, A, B and C, from the moment v11 lands (`scripts/reruns.txt`, the omni-v11 campaign, released by the
conductor a few at a time each tick). The grid runs on its own manifest (`results/grid_v11/`), and every Azure set starts again
from A. The omni-v10 runs already started run to their end as omni-v10's record; nothing is cancelled, and no table pools the
two. Google Cloud and Amazon run the same four sets from A once their queues are switched back on (Google's key stored whole,
Amazon's account on its Paid plan). The GPU runs on Lambda wait for the founder's word and one exact commit.
### 88.8 Omni v12: a refused raise is held, and the swarm's reflex acts at once (the engine that stood 19 to 20 October)



Omni v12 stood on main from 19 to 20 October; on the evening of 20 October Omni v13 (`docs/OMNI_V13.md`) took its place, which
is omni-v12 with the conveyance's hand-back. This page stays as omni-v12's record, read beside no other engine's. The founder's
order behind it, of the night of 19 October: "Of course I want you to land version 12. I want you to keep fixing and building
and straightening and enhancing and benchmarking and defensibility, and every time you do that ... it becomes a new version." It is omni-v11 (`docs/OMNI_V11.md`) with two faults fixed, both found on
the omni-v11 runs on 19 October: one in the Kubernetes governor's conveyance, one in the swarm's wire. Every setting, gain,
preset and muscle is omni-v11's, and so is every rule but these two.

Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V12.json` (digest `d38b58fbe28939b8`, 47 files). Forty-six files are omni-v11's bytes; one differs,
the governor's muscles (`omni_controller/muscles.py`). The swarm's wire (`tools/run_swarm.py`) sits outside the fingerprint's
scope, as the data-store wires do (it is versioned by git and tested); its change is declared here as part of omni-v12, and a
swarm table counts only on a commit that carries it. Both changes were proven in their tests and in the model gate before they
landed (`results/model_gate/V12_VS_V11.md`, `results/model_gate/V12_SWARM_REFLEX.md`). Every benchmark runs again on omni-v12, A, B
and C, from the conductor's campaign of 20 October, 00:30 UTC. Every earlier table stands as its own engine's result until its
three runs on v12 land, and results from two versions are never pooled. The readings below are our own models (evidence class
S), never a benchmark result. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these
results.

| # | Change | Where | The fault it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A raise the cluster's admission refuses is not written again until the pod's limit changes, the raise shrinks, or a wait passes (5 minutes, doubled at each refusal up to an hour) | `omni_controller/muscles.py`, the conveyance | omni-v11 capacity test: admission refused every CPU-limit raise (`exceeded quota: omni-cap`) and the governor wrote it again at every fast check, about 9 refused writes a minute, 970 to 1,000 an hour (`results/STEERING.md`) |
| 2 | The swarm's proximity reflex hands back the planner's cruise in the tick it is triggered; its reach grows with the square of the speed (0.5 m at the planner's cruise, as before) | `tools/run_swarm.py`, `Drone.step` | the omni-v11 reflex let the override fall 0.01 a tick, so a drone kept flying fast about a second after it saw a neighbour; on one mission draw outside the counted cells two drones came within 0.083 m (`results/model_gate/V12_SWARM_REFLEX.md`) |

#### 88.8.1 The refused raise

On the kind rig the governor's role cannot read the namespace's quota. As written since omni-v7, an unreadable quota is "no
budget known", and the cluster's admission is the authority. In the omni-v11 capacity test admission refused each raise; the
refusal was read back and audited, so nothing wrong was ever set, and the table read STEADY. But the governor asked again at every
fast check: a controller that repeats a refused command every few seconds loads the API server and fills its own audit. In
omni-v12 the refusal is the authority's answer. The same raise is held until something changes: the pod's limit (another writer
moved it), a smaller raise (the budget moved), or the wait (5 minutes, then 10, 20, 40, 60, never longer). An accepted raise
clears the hold. The audit records each hold and its wait (`held_s`), and `omni_errors_total` and `omni_writes_total`
(`tools/omni_exporter.py`) show it to the operator.

The model gate's `convey_refused` model (the quota unreadable and every raise past the operator's limit refused, seeds 1 to 8):
omni-v12 wrote **49.75 commands a day against omni-v11's 1,985.5 (−97.5%, GAIN)**, and every other gauge was identical to
omni-v11's to the last digit: requests served, pod start wait, p95, alert minutes, host busy, CPU given and pod-seconds. On the
convey models with a readable quota and with an unreadable quota that admission accepts, omni-v12 and omni-v11 are identical on
every gauge. Tests: `tests/test_refused_raise.py`.

#### 88.8.2 The swarm's reflex

`results/model_gate/V12_SWARM_REFLEX.md` holds the whole reading on gym-pybullet-drones, an outside simulator, on the counted
cells and on mission draws the wire was never run on. With the fix, every drone stays at or outside the keep-out on every cell
and draw tried, and 49% to 92% of omni-v11's energy cut is kept. That is the price of the reflex acting at once: on the long
cell the energy cut falls from −19.8% to −14.5% against native, power given back to the margin between the drones.

#### 88.8.3 The model gate against omni-v11

`results/model_gate/V12_VS_V11.md` (seeds 1 to 8; the cluster models at 60 s and 15 s and with the blink, the three convey models and
the verdict model at 20 and 200 pieces of work a decision): omni-v12 reads **identical to omni-v11 on every gauge of every model but
one**, the convey model whose every raise is refused, where it writes 97.5% fewer commands (GAIN). No reading of omni-v12 against
omni-v11 is a LOSS. The standing engine's own readings against native in these models are omni-v11's and unchanged.

#### 88.8.4 Studied and left out: the verdict's upper end (branch `v12-verdict-study`)

The candidate as first built also carried a stricter verdict: a step kept only when the upper end of every 95% interval of its
change in cost is inside the 2% allowance, each phase measuring as many pieces of work as a free step needs to show that, and a
trial that could not be read in its time never started. It answers a real fault (omni-v11 keeps a step whose interval reaches
past the allowance on its estimate alone: on noisy work a step that truly costs 3% is kept about a quarter of the time). On
work fast enough to read a step it kept a free step 98% of the time against omni-v11's 66%, and a 3% step 0% against 26%. But in
the model cluster set from a real run's regime the governor reads about 80 requests a decision and the rule needs about 4,000 a
phase: 1,102 of its give-back trials never started, no step was allowed, and the governor read identical to native, omni-v11's
machine-hour and energy cuts gone (shown under each cluster table of `V12_VS_V11.md`). On the data stores (one cost sample a
second, 40 to 120 a phase; 432 to 23,430 needed, read from the omni-v11 audits) every knob would stay native. Refused as
written; the fault stays on the next version's list (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`) until a trial design that reads a 2% step in a
trial's time is shown in the model gate.

#### 88.8.5 What stays omni-v11's

Every other engine file, rule, gain, preset and muscle; the verdict (`omnicompass/verdict.py`) byte for byte; the control
panel, the gauges feed, the alert rules and the steering report, which sit outside the engine and read or drive it only through
the interfaces it already has (`docs/OBSERVABILITY.md`). The next version's list (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`) carries what is still
to fix: the power cap's band, the after-kill window widened to 300 s, the Redis harness's brain in its own process, the commands
without a shell, every governor wire in the fingerprint, the Kubernetes governor counting a worker an add-on marks while it
serves, and the verdict's reading of a step. The kind rig's governor role still cannot read the namespace's quotas: the
Operator's Manual, section 5.5, makes that grant optional, and the omni-v12 capacity rerun reads the hold in the real cluster.
### 88.9 Omni v13: no other muscle's room is conveyed (the engine that stood 20 to 21 October)



Omni v13 stood on main from 20 to 21 October; on 21 October Omni v14 (`docs/OMNI_V14.md`) took its place, which is omni-v13
with a knob for every muscle and the operator's commands run without a shell. This page stays as omni-v13's record, read beside no other engine's. The founder's order behind
it, of 19 October, night: every fault found is
fixed, and every fix is the next version, told, not asked. It is omni-v12 (`docs/OMNI_V12.md`) with one fault fixed, found on
the omni-v12 runs of KubeRay's rig on 20 October: the governor's conveyance, which hands a machine's idle processor to the
serving pods on it, kept handing it on a shared host after the host had none left, and the batch muscle beside the web paid.
Every setting, gain, preset and muscle is omni-v12's, and so is every rule but this one.

Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V13.json` (digest `0088837333c6f0fc`, 47 files). Forty-six files are omni-v12's bytes; one differs, the governor's muscles
(`omni_controller/muscles.py`). The change was proven in its tests (`tests/test_convey_handback.py`) and in the model gate before
it landed (`results/model_gate/V13_VS_V12.md`). Every benchmark runs again on omni-v13, A, B and C. Every earlier table stands as
its own engine's result until its three runs on v13 land, and results from two versions are never pooled. The readings from
the model gate below are our own models (evidence class S), never a benchmark result. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's
own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

| # | Change | Where | The fault it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | On a shared host (kind) at its top (busy at or over 75%), while another workload there has room of its own (a pod, not a serving one, whose limit is above its request), every limit given goes back to the operator's; it is conveyed again only under 70%, the band's 5% cushion below the top | `omni_controller/muscles.py`, the conveyance | KubeRay's rig, the organism alone (`results/live/V12_KUBERAY_4W_BARE.md`): the web pods' limits were raised to 3,700m in the queue's first half minute and kept through the saturated queue; the batch queue finished 0.6% to 0.8% later and the web's 99th percentile rose 4% to 13%, LOSS in all three runs |
| 2 | Every other pod on a machine is counted by what it may use: its own limit where it has one, its request where it has none | the same | omni-v12 counted requests alone, so a batch pod's room between its request (500m) and its limit (1 core) read as idle and was conveyed |

#### 88.9.1 What the KubeRay runs show

The table's two LOSS rows were first put down to the give-back, the governor parking machines during the queue (the batch
preregistration, amendment 10). The repetitions' own files say otherwise (`docs/BATCH_QUEUE_PREREGISTRATION.md`, amendment 11).
Twenty-nine paired repetitions of the organism alone, A, B and C:

- **The cost sits where the host was saturated.** In 16 repetitions the native queue ran past 760 s: the runner's processor was
  slower and the batch filled the kind cores (the host's busy share 0.78 through the queue, 95% of readings at or over 0.75).
  There, each batch pod hashed its work in 63.1 s with Omni-Compass on top against 59.2 s natively, **+7.6%**, and the queue
  finished 1.1% later. In the other 13, where the host kept room, the same pods read +0.3% and the queue +0.1%.
- **No machine was parked during a saturated queue.** Six workers were in service through the queue in both arms in all 16;
  the machines Omni-Compass gave back were given back after the queue. The give-back is not the cause.
- **The web's limits were raised at the queue's start and kept.** In 15 of the 16 the conveyance raised the web pods' limits
  to 3,700m at 33 s (one at 65 s), on a reading of the host's busy share averaged over the 15 s since the governor's previous
  reading, which caught the dip as the stream's first pods started. From then on the host was at its top, so omni-v7's guard
  held every further raise, but limits already given stayed, for 92% to 96% of the queue.
- **The web gained nothing while the queue ran.** Pooled over the 29 repetitions, the web's median while the queue ran was
  266 ms with Omni-Compass on top against 253 ms natively, its 99th percentile 3,429 ms against 3,226 ms, and the requests
  served the same (14,454 against 14,480). After the queue, with the host free, the conveyance did what it is for: the median
  fell from 114 ms to 69 ms and the 99th percentile from 194 ms to 113 ms.

So the lifted quota bought the web no processor on a host with none to spare (the kernel shares a saturated host by the
weights of the requests, and the web's share there sat under its operator's limit), and the batch pods lost work per processor
second while it was lifted. One saturated repetition had no raise during its queue and still read +4.0% on hashing: one
repetition is not a reading, and the omni-v13 runs read what remains of the governor's other costs on the shared cores.

#### 88.9.2 The rule

A limit above the operator's is idle processor conveyed. On a host at its top there is none, and what the serving pods take
there beyond their operator's limit can only come out of what another muscle may use. omni-v13 hands it back. The hold is on a
shared host only, where the nodes are containers on one machine and the machine's busy share is read directly; on separate
machines each node's own arithmetic bounds the conveyance, now with every other pod counted by its limit, so every muscle on
the machine can reach its own limit at the same moment as the serving pods reach theirs. A host where no other workload has
room of its own (a web-only rig: system pods with no CPU limit, or a limit equal to the request) keeps omni-v7's rule: raises
held at the top, limits given stay, because what the serving pods use there is the host's own idle and no other muscle's room.
A host whose busy share cannot be read is blind, never at its top (omni-v11): raises held, nothing handed back. The audit names
each hand-back (`"convey": "handed back"`) and each write gives the reason and the host's busy share.

#### 88.9.3 The model gate against omni-v12

`results/model_gate/V13_VS_V12.md` (seeds 1 to 8). A new model, `convey_batch`, sets the batch muscle of KubeRay's rig beside the
serving one on the batch rig's host: the kind nodes on 3 of 4 cores and the governor on the fourth, the stream of 24 jobs
(one every 30 s, ten pods each, five at a time, 500m requested and a 1-core limit), each pod's work set so the native queue
finishes where the saturated runners' did (834 s), the processor shared between cgroups by the weights of their requests, the
pods' measured start lag (2.66 s) and the governor's own windowed reading of the host. The batch pods' loss of work while a
serving pod's quota is lifted on a host at its top is the saturated repetitions' own (+7.6% hashing time, 0.071 of the work).

Against omni-v12, on the same seeds, **no reading is a LOSS in any model**:

- The three cluster models (a decision every 60 s, every 15 s, and with the machines blinking out of the reading) and the
  verdict model at 20 and 200 pieces of work a decision: identical to omni-v12 on every gauge, to the last digit. The cloud
  setting conveys nothing, and the verdict is omni-v11's byte for byte.
- The three web-only convey models (the quota readable and empty, unreadable, and refusing every raise): identical on every
  gauge. No other workload there has room of its own, so omni-v7's rule holds unchanged.
- `convey_batch`: against omni-v12, the batch queue finishes **1.48% sooner** and the job turnaround is **9.59% shorter**
  (GAIN), the web's 95th percentile **17.4% lower**, the requests served 0.43% more, the pod start wait 1.46% shorter, the
  commands written 15% fewer, the CPU given 1.2% less and the host's busy share 0.5% less (GAIN); the pod-seconds +0.84%,
  power given; the alert minutes identical.

Against native in `convey_batch`, omni-v12 read LOSS on six gauges: the queue +1.50%, the job turnaround +10.7%, the 95th
percentile +14.8%, the requests served −2.5%, the pod start wait +1.9% and the alert minutes +9.8%. omni-v13 reads the queue
identical to native's, the 95th percentile (−5.3%) and the start wait STEADY, and three LOSS rows. The job turnaround +0.05%
(0.04 to 0.17 s a job): the queue's first reading spans the seconds before the batch pods ran, so the web's limits are raised
once and handed back 15 s later; the rule that closes it is on the next version's list. The requests served −2.1% and the
alert minutes +9.8%: both engines read the same way with no batch at all on this 3-core host, while the real KubeRay runs
served 4% more after the queue, so the model's web model is out of its regime there (section 88.3.4). These are our own models,
class S.

#### 88.9.4 What stays omni-v12's

Every other engine file, rule, gain, preset and muscle; the verdict (`omnicompass/verdict.py`) byte for byte; the refused-raise
hold; the swarm's reflex. The next version's list (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`) carries what is still to fix, with one item added:
the model's web model on the batch rig's 3-core host, where both engines read fewer requests served than native (section 88.3.3)

### 88.10 Omni v14: a knob for every muscle, the operator's commands without a shell (the engine that stands since 21 October)



Omni v14 was the engine on main on 21 October, from 04:47 UTC until omni-v15 (`docs/OMNI_V15.md`) landed that evening. The founder's orders behind it: knobs on every monitor, "to turn off and
on such a mechanism, a muscle, or tweak and turn any muscle" (20 October, evening), and, the next night, "tune the engine". It is
omni-v13 (`docs/OMNI_V13.md`) with two changes, each written before it was built and read in the model gate against omni-v13 on the
same seeds before it landed: a knob that leaves any one muscle native, and the operator's own commands run without a shell. Every
setting, gain, preset and muscle is omni-v13's, and so is every other rule. A third change, to the conveyance's reading on a
shared host, was built, tried in the gate and refused there; it is not in omni-v14 (section 88.3.3).

Its fingerprint is `OMNI_V14.json` (digest `7afba44615fcff8f`, 47 files). Forty-five files are omni-v13's bytes; two differ, the Kubernetes
governor (`omni_controller/controller.py`) and its muscles (`omni_controller/muscles.py`). Every benchmark runs again on
omni-v14, A, B and C. Every earlier table stands as its own engine's result until its three runs on v14 land, and results from
two versions are never pooled. The readings from the model gate are our own models (evidence class S), never a benchmark result.
Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

| # | Change | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `--native MUSCLE[,...]` leaves each named muscle where native runs it: never written, the rest running as before; a name that is not a muscle is refused at the start | the governor and its muscles; the control panel's muscle button | the founder's order of 20 October: a knob for every muscle; and his rule that a muscle Omni-Compass would hurt stays native |
| 2 | The operator's own commands (the site power reading, a muscle's read command, a wall meter's `cmd:`) run without a shell unless they hold a pipe, a redirect or a variable | `run_operator_cmd` (`omni_controller/muscles.py`), `tools/wall_meter.py` | the static scan's three high findings (`docs/SECURITY_SCAN.md`); the governor's site power reading no longer reaches a shell at all |

#### 88.10.1 The knob

`--native MUSCLE[,MUSCLE...]` (or `OMNI_NATIVE`) names the muscles the governor leaves native. A muscle named there is never
written: it stays where native runs it, and every other muscle runs as before. The governor still reads the whole body and
decides with all of it in view; only the write of a muscle left native is withheld, and the audit says so (`"held"`, and
`"native_muscles"` at the start). A name that is not a muscle is refused at the start, never ignored, so a misspelling can
never leave a muscle driven that the operator meant to leave native. With no name given, nothing is left native and the
governor runs exactly as omni-v13 does.

| Muscle | What is left native |
|---|---|
| `machines` | the node pool's size (the operator's node-scale command) |
| `replicas` | the pod autoscaler's target, the pod reflex's replica floor and the replica cap |
| `cpu` | the serving pods' CPU limits (the conveyance and the pod power cap) |
| `clock` | the processors' frequency ceiling |
| `gpu` | the GPU's power limit |
| `rollout` | the rollout guard (pause and undo) |
| `batch` | the batch admission and pacing |
| `rightsize`, `coldstart`, `contain`, `cooling` | the pods' rightsizing, the cold-start reserve, the namespaces' containment, the cooling setpoint |

The control panel (`tools/omni_control.py`) carries it as one more button, `POST /v1/muscle {"muscle": NAME, "on": true|false}`,
role operator, every press audited with its holder and reason, and as a row of On and Native buttons on the console. Like a
dial press it passes through native: the governor's own kill file is set, its exit awaited (every setting it wrote restored
and read back), and it starts again with the new list. Nothing is changed under a running governor. The monitor wall on the live
engine page (`docs/engine/OMNI_COMPASS_LIVE_ENGINE.html`, `#s-wall`) points every row at these buttons; the wall itself never presses one. Tests:
`tests/test_native_muscles.py`.

#### 88.10.2 The operator's commands without a shell

A command the operator configured (`--power-cmd`, a muscle's read command in the wiring file, a wall meter's `cmd:`) is split
into its words as a shell would split them and run directly when it holds nothing only a shell reads: no pipe, list, redirect,
subshell, variable, substitution, glob, home directory, comment or `NAME=value` before the command. One that does runs through
the shell as before, so no operator's wiring changes. Tests: `tests/test_operator_cmd.py`. The static scan reads two high
findings where it read three (`docs/SECURITY_SCAN.md`): the governor's own call to a shell is gone, and the two that remain are
the fallback for a command that needs one.

#### 88.10.3 Refused by the gate: the conveyance's reading on a shared host

The fault it was meant to fix: on the model set from KubeRay's rig (`results/model_gate/V13_VS_V12.md`), omni-v13 raises the web
pods' CPU limits once early in the batch queue and hands them back 15 s later, and the batch's job turnaround reads +0.05%
against native, a LOSS by the key. The governor reads the host's busy share as the change in its processor counters since its
previous reading (every 15 s); the trace of that raise shows it lands on the reading the second job's pods are starting at,
before their load is in the reading.

Three rules were written and tried, each against omni-v13 on the same eight seeds:

- **No raise on any reading older than another workload's newest running pod.** Refused: the web's 95th percentile read 6.4%
  higher than omni-v13's, a LOSS.
- **No raise on the reading that opens another workload's run** (none of its pods with room running at the previous reading).
  It never fires in the model: identical to omni-v13 on every gauge, because the batch is already running when the second job
  arrives.
- **That rule, and the starting pods counted:** a pod of another workload still starting ran for none of the interval, so what
  it may use is added to the reading, and nothing is raised when the sum reaches the 70% cushion. It fires where the fault is.
  The batch turnaround returns to native's exactly, and the web's queue period is native's second by second. But the web's 95th
  percentile reads 6.4% higher than omni-v13's, a LOSS. Traced seed by seed: omni-v13's one raise costs the batch pods 15 s of
  work, which moves when every later batch pod finishes, and with it the seconds the web runs on its last pod; in six of eight
  seeds that lowered the web's 95th percentile against native. Without the raise the web's queue is native's, and the gain that
  rode on the batch's delay is gone.

By the gate's rule a LOSS row is not carried into a real run, so none of the three is in omni-v14. They are kept on the branch
`v14-convey-study` with their tests and the model's readings. The next version's list (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`) carries the
work that comes first: the model's web model set from a real run's own files (its record already says it is out of its regime on
the 3-core batch host), then the third rule read again. The gate found one fault in the model itself and it is fixed for both
engines: a batch pod was listed as Running from the moment it was made; a cluster lists it as Pending until its container runs
(the rig's own pod start, about 3 s).

#### 88.10.4 The model gate against omni-v13

`results/model_gate/V14_VS_V13.md`: the shipped controller on the model cluster in the cloud setting at 60 and 15 s and with every
worker out of service for two minutes, the conveyance on one kind host (readable quota, unreadable quota, a quota that refuses
every raise, and the batch muscle of KubeRay's rig beside the serving one), and the verdict on noisy work, eight seeds each, the
same seeds for both engines. Every one of the 57 gauges reads identical between omni-v14 and omni-v13, and the verdict allows the
same share of give-back steps at every cost: no LOSS. That is what both changes should read there: with no muscle named, the
knob leaves nothing native, and no model calls an operator's command. The knob's own behaviour is proven in its tests (a muscle
named is never written, an unknown name is refused, every other muscle runs as before), and the commands' in theirs.

#### 88.10.5 What stays omni-v13's

Every other engine file; every rule, gain and guard, the conveyance and its hand-back of omni-v13 among them; the verdict byte
for byte. The next version's list (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`) carries what is still to fix. The GPU governors
(`omni_controller/gpu_governor.py`, `gpu_compass.py`) keep their own two levers, the power limit and the clock, and take the
per-muscle knob with the version that next changes them.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The brain trims the power cap to demand only while the response line has been clean for the governor's own clear time; a breach, or a line not yet clean, releases the request to the start limit in the same decision | `omnicompass/adapter.py` (the `power` rule, `observe_vector`'s `clean`), its C++ twin `cpp/src/governor.cpp`; the card governor hands the brain its clear flag (`omni_controller/gpu_governor.py`) | on the omni-v11 long run the request switched between the start limit and the trim at 126 of 350 decisions and turned back at 123 of them, at the one threshold on the queue and the state (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`, "the next version's list") |

#### 88.11.1 The request through the clear time

**The fault.** The brain (`omnicompass/adapter.Governor`) asks for a power cap at every decision: when the queue is under its
guard (q < 0.05) and the state's U is at or over the gate (0.85 in the fleet law), the request is the trim to demand,
clamp(cap_now × load × (1 + margin), cap_min, 1); otherwise it is the start limit, 1. On the omni-v11 long run (run
39173420146, the robustness long scenario: three paired repetitions of two hours on real Kubernetes, the wandering load) the
governor's own audit shows the request switching between 1.0 and 0.695 (the fleet law's floor, which the trim reached at every
calm decision) at 126 of its 350 decisions, and turning back the other way at 123 of them (41 of 116, 36 of 118 and 49 of 116 in
the three repetitions; `results/STEERING.md` reads it as moves and reversals an hour). Each switch was the line breached (the
controller folds the response-time pressure into the queue reading) and the next decision calm again. On Kubernetes the power
wire is off, so nothing was written; but the card governor reads the same request for the GPU's power limit, and a request that
hammers at one threshold is not the compass law's way (a band with cushions, smooth, not hammering).

**The rule.** The Kubernetes governor already declares the reflex: while the response line is breached, and for its clear time
after (`--slo-clear-s`, 180 s), Omni-Compass may not pack replicas tighter than the HPA's target and may not cap power. It
handed that flag to its muscles and not to the brain, whose request kept trimming the moment one decision read calm. The card
governor applied the same gate outside the brain (`cap = requested if slo_clean else 1.0`, its `--slo-clear` 3 decisions).
omni-v15 puts it inside: the observation vector carries the line's clear flag (`slo_clean`; a caller that senses no line is
clean), and the trim is asked for only while it is set. A breach, or a line not yet clean for the clear time, releases the
request to the start limit in the same decision; the spread under backlog at the power envelope and the backlog bound are
untouched. No constant is added to the law: the clear time is each governor's own, as it already declared it.

**Read on the run's own decisions.** The three audits' decisions (their queue reading, state U, clear flag and the request
recorded) are kept as a fixture (`tests/fixtures/robust_long_39173420146_decisions.json`, the source files' SHA-256 inside).
The recorded request is omni-v14's rule on the recorded queue and state, decision for decision. On the same decisions, read
with the recorded clear flag, omni-v15's rule leaves 35 moves of 126, 32 reversals of 123, and 28% of the travel
(`tests/test_cap_band.py`). A fault's fix is read first where the fault was found.

**Refused by the gate.** A second form was written first: a dwell of three calm decisions and a glide of 0.05 a decision toward
the trim, the release at once. On the run's own decisions it reads 67 moves and 33 reversals; but in the model gate, where the model
cluster's calm stretches are long, the glide turned each trim into seven small moves (the request's moves in a day 149 against
omni-v14's 38 on one seed, the travel the same), and on the model card it wrote the limit 25 times against 16 for the same travel
and 0.17% more energy. More writes of smaller size is not the fix the fault asked for; by the gate's rule it is not carried.
The clear-time gate alone is in omni-v15.

**The card.** With the flag inside the brain the card governor's own gate becomes a second reading of the same rule: the model
card reads omni-v15 identical to omni-v14 on every gauge (section 88.3.4), as it should, and the GPU's run on Lambda starts from
`gpu-omni-v15`, one exact commit.

#### 88.11.2 Every wire in the fingerprint

`tools/omni_version.py` hashes every file whose bytes decide what Omni-Compass does. Up to omni-v14 the scope held the brain,
the live governors, the realms and three outside-simulator wires (`tools/run_kil.py`, `run_citylearn.py`, `run_pandapower.py`);
the data stores' wires (`run_redis.py`, `run_kafka.py`, `run_pgbench.py`, `run_sysbench.py`, `run_ycsb.py`) and `run_swarm.py`,
`run_mujoco.py` and `run_cpu_power.py` were versioned by git and tested but did not move the digest, and one of them carried a
fault fixed in omni-v12 without the digest moving (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`, "Gaps this page names"). From omni-v15 every one
of them is in the scope: a change to any rule changes the version. A version declared before them is read without those eight
wires and only those: a commit carrying omni-v14's 47 files byte for byte reads omni-v14 whatever those eight wires hold,
because its fingerprint never covered them, while any other file omni-v14's list does not name (a new rule, a new module)
still makes the tree a different engine (`tests/test_omni_version.py`); and the tool prints a version's own digest and file
count as its fingerprint records them.

#### 88.11.3 The kill test's reading: 300 s after the kill

Declared before omni-v15's runs, as `docs/ROBUSTNESS_PREREGISTRATION.md` ("On omni-v11") proposed: the kill scenario's paired
gauges, the time over the line and the failed requests after the kill, are read over the 300 s after the kill mark, where they
were read over 120 s (`tools/live_reps.py`, `ROBUST_AFTER_KILL_S`). The one tail rise of the omni-v11 kill test came 140 to
190 s after the kill, past the old window. The omni-v11 kill table stands as read then; omni-v15's kill runs are read over 300 s
from their first. The rig is unchanged (the probe runs through the whole 900 s window).

#### 88.11.4 The model gate against omni-v14

`results/model_gate/V15_VS_V14.md`: the shipped controller on the model cluster in the cloud setting at 60 and 15 s and with every
worker out of service for two minutes, the conveyance on one kind host (readable quota, unreadable quota, a quota that refuses
every raise, and the batch muscle of KubeRay's rig beside the serving one), the verdict on noisy work, and, new with this version,
the GPU governor on the modelled card (the card whose voltage falls with its clock and the card near its voltage floor), eight
seeds each, the same seeds for both engines. Every service gauge of every model reads identical between omni-v15 and omni-v14:
machine-hours, energy, pending-pod minutes, the HPA's shortfall, the 95th percentile and the alert minutes on the cluster models;
requests served, start waits, the 95th percentile, host busy, limits given, pod seconds and writes on the conveyance models; the
batch queue and turnaround; requests served, the 95th and 99th percentiles, energy, peak temperature and the limit's writes,
moves, reversals and travel on both card models (the card governor applied the same gate outside the brain, so the brain's gate
inside changes nothing there: 17 writes, 16 moves and 15 reversals a run on the card whose voltage falls with its clock, 35, 34
and 33 on the card near its floor, the same in both engines); and the verdict allows the same share of give-back steps at every
cost. The request's own wear is the one place the two engines differ, and it reads STEADY: on the model cluster, where the response
line is breached in about 27 of a day's 1,440 minutes and the calm stretches between are long, the request moved 67.3 times a day
against 64.9 (+3.7%, STEADY), turned back 66.1 times against 63.8 (+3.7%, STEADY) and travelled 20.4 against 19.6 (+3.9%, STEADY) at a
decision every 60 s; at a decision every 15 s 98.8 moves against 100.1 (−1.4%, STEADY), 96.1 reversals against 97.5 (−1.4%, STEADY),
29.3 travel against 29.7 (−1.4%, STEADY); with the blink, +3.0%, +2.9% and +3.0%, STEADY. The small rise at 60 s is the gate doing
what the governor declares: omni-v14 kept trimming while the line was breached by less than the queue guard's 5% (a pressure
between 0 and 0.05), and omni-v15 releases there too, so in a regime of rare, light breaches it releases a little more often. The
fault was found in the opposite regime, the long run's clustered breaches (126 switches in 350 decisions), where the same gate
leaves 35 (section 88.3.1); the cluster model's regime is the cloud setting's, set from a real run's own files, not the long run's, and
the next long run on omni-v15 reads the request's moves and reversals an hour in `results/STEERING.md`. No LOSS anywhere: the
change lands.

#### 88.11.5 What stays omni-v14's

Every other engine file, byte for byte; every gain, guard and preset; the conveyance and its hand-back; the verdict. The next
version's list (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`) carries what is still to fix, first among them the Redis harness's brain in its own
process (its model, `tools/redis_brain_probe.py`, is read before the harness changes, with the version that changes it) and the
model's web model set from KubeRay's after-queue files. The GPU governors keep their own two levers; the brain they call now
reads the line's clear flag from them.
### 88.12 Omni v16: every clock of the governor in seconds; the heartbeat at 15 s



Omni v16 (`OMNI_V16.json`, digest `5c5502f12b1c0ce4`, 55 files) stood on main on 22 October, from the morning until omni-v17
landed that evening (`docs/OMNI_V17.md`: the same engine with the heartbeat a dial, the main engine at 60 s, and the cruise
wait never under two readings at a slow beat). Two words of the founder's
made it. That night ("Go"), on the plan put to him: put every clock of the Kubernetes governor in seconds, read the decision
pace at 60, 15, 10 and 5 s in our own models, and run each pace three times on GitHub's own machines
(`docs/PACE_PREREGISTRATION.md`). Then, once the models had read: "15 sec all over heart beat fix update code". So the
governor's heartbeat, its full decision, comes every 15 s by default, native's own pod autoscaler's pace, where every engine
before it decided every 60 s; the fast checks stay every 5 s. It is omni-v15 (`docs/OMNI_V15.md`) with the clocks changed and
the heartbeat set, and nothing else: every gain, guard, preset and muscle is omni-v15's, and 50 of its 55 files are
omni-v15's bytes (the five changed: `omnicompass/adapter.py`, `omnicompass/edge.py`, `omni_controller/controller.py`,
`omni_controller/muscles.py`, `omni_controller/capacity.py`; the brain's C++ twin `cpp/src/governor.cpp` with it, sealed).
Read in the model gate against omni-v15 on the same seeds before it was pushed (`results/model_gate/V16_VS_V15.md`), and the
pace read alone on a plant that moves every 5 s (`results/model_gate/V16_PACE.md`). The readings from the model gate are our own
models (evidence class S), never a benchmark result. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has
reviewed or approved these results.

#### 88.12.1 Why

Every engine through omni-v15 took its full decision every 60 s. The number was written into the first harness on 26
September, with no reason recorded, and never measured against another; the engine was then tuned at 60 s and several of
its rules were written in decisions, which locked 60 s in. Native's pod autoscaler checks every 15 s, the metrics it reads
refresh every 15 s, the Cluster Autoscaler scans every 10 s, KEDA every 30 s. The founder asked for 15, 10 and 5 s on 14
October; six rules moved to seconds on 16 October (omni-v7) and the rest did not, so turning the period also changed what
the remaining rules meant. omni-v16 finishes the job: turning the period changes only how often the governor looks. The
cushion each muscle keeps is set by its own climb, wobble and reaction time in seconds, and is the same at any pace; the pace
sets only how soon trouble is seen (within 15 s at 15 s, within a minute at 60 s), and so the default moves to native's 15 s.

The founder asked, before the default was set, whether a longer period would make a larger cushion and a stronger engine.
It would not: a longer period leaves the governor blind for longer between looks (up to two minutes at 120 s, while native
checks every 15 s), and to stay as safe while blind longer it would have to hold more back, which is less work done. The
cushion has its own setting (each muscle's z of 3.09, 99.9% of steps inside it, and the dial's tune-down), and the period is
not it.

#### 88.12.2 What counted in decisions, and what it counts now

Every value below is the one omni-v15 used when a decision comes every 60 s (the reference step; `REF_PERIOD_S`).

| Clock | omni-v15 (per decision) | omni-v16 (per second) | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| the brain's blending of each reading | 0.339 of the state a decision | 1 − (1 − 0.339)^k a decision, k = period / 60 s: 0.339 a minute | `omnicompass/adapter.py` (`Governor.step`, `period_s`) |
| the brain's inner time | 0.1 of its macro interval a decision | 0.1 k a decision | the same |
| the brain's dwell and wait before giving a machine back | 1 and 5 decisions (the fleet law) | the same seconds: 60 and 300 s | the same |
| the brain's machines added or removed | up to 8 and 1 a decision | up to 8 and 1 over the last minute's decisions | the same; the C++ twin `cpp/src/governor.cpp` identically |
| the compass's damping (kd) | critical damping for the decision period | critical damping at the minute, so the law's push and pull per second are the same at any period | `omni_controller/controller.py` |
| the compass's velocity smoothing | 0.3 a decision | 0.3 a minute | the same |
| the edge's window, narrowing, the floor's forgetting, memory, wobble step | 20 decisions; 0.05, 0.9995 a decision; one decision's change | 20 minutes; 0.05, 0.9995 a minute; a minute's change | `omnicompass/edge.py` (`pace`) |
| what a breach teaches the edge | 0.1 a decision of breach | 0.1 a minute of breach | `omni_controller/controller.py` |
| machines added past the scheduling floor | one step a decision | one step a minute (the release has been one a minute since v7); the floor's machines at once | the same (`ADD_PERIOD_S`) |
| a command's time to land (proprioception) | the next decision | a minute, every decision reading it until it lands | the same (`LAND_S`) |
| the host's busy share (kind's shared runner) | since the last decision | over the last minute | `omni_controller/capacity.py` (`span`) |
| the heat law | 0.86 of the heat kept a decision | 0.86 a minute | `omni_controller/muscles.py` |
| held batch jobs admitted; jobs paused or resumed | one a decision | one a minute | the same |
| a quiet deployment scaled to zero | 3 idle decisions | 180 idle seconds (`--coldstart-idle-s`) | the same |
| the coast toward fewer pods | coast step × period / 60 a raise | the coast step a raise (a raise comes at most once a window) | `omni_controller/controller.py` |
| the conveyance | every third fast check, never at a decision (so never at a decision every 5 s) | every 15 s, whichever check falls due (`--convey-every-s`) | the same |
| the loop | each wait began when the step ended (a 60 s decision came every 62 to 67 s on kind) | keeps its own schedule; a missed slot is skipped, never run in a burst | the same (`main`) |

Six rules already counted seconds since omni-v7 and stay as they were: the line's clear time, cruise, the strict window,
the trial spacing, the wait after a refusal, and a trial's length; so does the release of one machine a minute.

#### 88.12.3 The heartbeat: a full decision every 15 s

The default `--interval` is 15 s and `--floor-interval` 5 s (`omni_controller/controller.py`; before, 60 s and 15 s, every rig
and install file setting the fast checks to 5 s). Every place that starts the governor carries it: the rigs
(`scripts/kind_bench.sh`, `kind_paired.sh`, `kind_robust.sh`, `kind_full.sh`, `kind_pilot.sh`), the install files
(`deploy/install/omni-compass.yaml`, `omni-compass-cloud.yaml`, `deploy/controller.yaml`), the cloud runs (which start it
through `kind_bench.sh`), the alert rules' staleness bound (`deploy/prometheus/omni-compass-rules.yaml`: three intervals, 45 s)
and the manuals. Each run writes its period beside its files (`omni_interval.txt`), and the receipts read each run at its own
(`tools/live_reps.py`; the robustness runs before it at 60 s). The page's controller trace and the modelled traces in the
manuals keep the 60 s step they were drawn at, and say so. The levers rig (`scripts/kind_levers.sh`) was left at three, two
and three decisions of 5 s when omni-v16 landed: under omni-v14 each of them was a minute of the brain's, under omni-v16 they
are 15 s, and the two levers that give back (rightsize, coldstart), which wait for the brain's calm (its contraction authority,
about a minute after it starts on an idle reading, `tests/test_pace_clocks.py`), failed three of the rig's 19 checks in the
first omni-v16 run (22 October, 13:50 UTC). The rig now runs at the default 15 s for the 3, 2 and 3 minutes its checks were
written for, with the idle time before cold start in seconds (120 s), and the levers check runs again, A, B and C
(`scripts/reruns.txt`).

#### 88.12.4 At 60 s it is omni-v15

On the model cluster at a decision every 60 s, omni-v16 makes exactly omni-v15's decisions: 4,578 audit records, none
different (seed 1; the gate's eight seeds read every gauge identical, on every model). The brain's C++ twin equals the Python
at 60, 15, 10 and 5 s (`tests/test_cpp_governor_parity.py`, 4,320 directives each, no difference), and every twin was
sealed again after its parity test passed (`results/SEAL.json`). Two changes can be seen at 60 s on a real cluster and
nowhere else: the conveyance comes every 15 s exactly (omni-v15: about 3.7 passes a minute), and the loop keeps its
schedule (omni-v15's decisions drifted by the steps' own time). The model gate's other columns, each engine against native,
read as they read for omni-v15 (the same rows, the same numbers at 60 s), because nothing but the clocks moved.

At 15 s, where omni-v15's rules counted in decisions ran four times as fast, every gauge reads STEADY against omni-v15, and the
machines parked over the eight days fall from 4,212 to 1,782 (omni-v15 at 60 s: 1,464): the pace no longer changes what a
rule means. As shipped (the model `cluster_shipped`: omni-v16 at its default of 15 s against omni-v15 at its 60 s, each started
without a period, as an install file starts it), every gauge reads STEADY: machine hours +2.4%, energy per core-hour −0.5%, the
pods waiting for a place −28.5%, the 95th percentile −0.3%, the alert minutes −0.9%. No LOSS against the engine it replaces.

The brain's lock (`results/LOCK_AMENDMENTS.json`) takes an amendment for `omnicompass/adapter.py`: the stack simulator steps
at 60 s, so the held-out seeds replay unchanged (`verify.py`).

#### 88.12.5 The pace in our models (`results/model_gate/V16_PACE.md`)

omni-v16 alone, eight seeds of a day each on a plant that moves every 5 s, at 60, 15, 10 and 5 s, each faster pace paired by
seed against 60 s and against native. In the cloud's setting (the tune-down, machines alone), against 60 s, every service
reading is STEADY at every pace (at 15 s: pending pod minutes −12.1%, the 95th percentile −0.0%, alert minutes +0.5%, machine
hours −0.4%) and energy per core-hour falls 2.6% at 15 s (GAIN); the power cap's request moves more (power given). In the
kind benchmark's setting (the compass law at the max, every autoscaler sensed), against 60 s, the alert minutes fall 14.7% at
15 s and 18.4% at 10 and 5 s (GAIN), the autoscaler's shortfall 6% at 10 and 5 s (GAIN), and every other reading is STEADY.
Omni's own processor: 1.6 to 1.7 s an hour at 60 s, 2.7 at 15 s, 3.4 at 10 s, 5.5 at 5 s (under a thousandth of one core
at 5 s); its reads: 1,650 an hour at 60 s, 2,190 at 15 s, 3,600 at 5 s. No LOSS against 60 s at any pace.

Against native, the rows read as the engine reads them at every pace, the old 60 s default included, and some read LOSS.
The pods waiting for a place: in the kind setting about four times native's at every pace (pending pod minutes an hour:
native 8.2; 32.0 at 60 s, 33.5 at 15 s, 28.8 and 28.6 at 10 and 5 s), LOSS at every pace; in the cloud's setting about twice
(20.9 at 60 s, 18.4 at 15 s), LOSS at 15 and 5 s and STEADY at 60 and 10 s only by the seeds' spread; on the model gate's 15 s
plant, +121.6% at 15 s (LOSS) and +209.8% at 60 s (STEADY by the spread). In the cloud's setting at 15 s two small rows read LOSS
as well: the 95th percentile, +0.47% on the 5 s plant and +0.36% on the gate's (at 60 s +0.49% and +0.63%, STEADY by the
spread), and the alert minutes, +2.31% on the 5 s plant (at 60 s +1.85%, STEADY). Against 60 s every one of them reads STEADY,
the 15 s point estimates the smaller, so they are the engine's and not the pace's: the faster pace narrows the seeds' spread
until the rows clear zero. They are on the next version's list to be root-caused (`docs/CHANGE_CONTROL.md`), beside the
blink model's alert minutes (+2.35% against native at 60 s, LOSS, the same in every gate since omni-v13).

#### 88.12.6 The real runs

`docs/PACE_PREREGISTRATION.md`: workflow `benchmark-reps`, five arms in every repetition (native; Omni-Compass on top at its
default heartbeat of 15 s; the same deciding every 60, 10 and 5 s), the reruns' steady scenario, three runs of 10
repetitions on GitHub's own machines at no cost, released by the conductor as the campaign's entry `kubernetes decision
pace`. They are the real-run reading of the heartbeat the founder set: a LOSS at 15 s there is root-caused and fixed in the
next version, as any other.
### 88.13 Omni v17: the heartbeat a dial; the main engine at 60 s



Omni v17 (`OMNI_V17.json`, digest `7c937d09e4031cc7`, 55 files) stood on main on 23 October, from the afternoon until omni-v18 landed that night (`docs/OMNI_V18.md`). The founder's order of the afternoon
before (22 October), once he had read the reads of the cluster a day in the pace study (about 86,000 at 5 s against 39,700 at 60 s): the
governor's heartbeat, its full decision, is a dial, "5, 15, 30, 60, 75, 90, 120 ... Heartbeat scaled in its monitors. And you're
going to set OmniCompass is main engine", because "who knows if maybe the purpose is somebody wants to set it at 5 seconds"; and
before it, "we are going to write the engine to have the 60 ... we have to actually have to be able to show the same 15 second
beats". So the main engine takes its full decision every 60 s; any beat can be set (`--interval`, 5 to 120 s and every value
between), the fast checks every 5 s at every beat; and every beat is shown beside native with what it buys and what it costs,
because an operator may want a fast beat for its reads and accept what it costs, or a slow one, and at each beat the other knobs
may want their own combination. It is omni-v16 (`docs/OMNI_V16.md`) with two changes, both in `omni_controller/controller.py`
(54 of its 55 files are omni-v16's bytes): the parser's default period moved from 15 to 60 s; and the cruise rule's wait never
fewer than two readings, a fault the dial's own ladder found at 90 and 120 s before the version landed (below, "The fault the ladder found"). Every clock
of the governor counts seconds since omni-v16, so the dial changes only how often it looks. Read in the model gate against
omni-v16 on the same seeds (`results/model_gate/V17_VS_V16.md`), and every beat read beside native and beside 60 s on a plant
that moves every 5 s (`results/model_gate/V17_LADDER.md`), before it was pushed. The readings from the model gate are our own
models (evidence class S), never a benchmark result. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has
reviewed or approved these results.

#### 88.13.1 Why a dial, and why 60 s for the main engine

Through omni-v15 the governor decided every 60 s, a number written into the first harness on 26 September and tuned around;
omni-v16 put every clock in seconds so that the period became a clean setting, and set it at 15 s, native's own pod
autoscaler's pace, on the founder's word that morning. The models then showed what each pace buys and costs: a faster beat
reads the cluster more often (about 39,700 reads a day at 60 s, 52,500 at 15 s, 86,400 at 5 s), spends more of the governor's
own processor (1.6 to 1.7 s an hour at 60 s, 2.7 at 15 s, 5.5 at 5 s, under a thousandth of one core at any beat), and in the
kind benchmark's setting sees trouble sooner (the minutes over the line 14.7% fewer at 15 s than at 60 s); against native the
same rows read at every pace. No one beat is right for every operator. The founder's order makes the beat the operator's
setting, as the tune-down is, and sets the main engine, the one the company ships and benchmarks first, at 60 s, the period
every engine through omni-v15 decided at; 15 s, native's own pace, is one setting of the dial, run and shown beside it.
