#### 88.13.3 The fault the ladder found: cruise on one reading at 90 and 120 s

The ladder's first reading of 90 and 120 s (kept on its page, "The first reading of every 90 and 120 s, before the fix") put the
kind benchmark's setting in another regime from 75 s down: against 60 s the machine-hours +17.1% and +21.4%, the minutes over
the line −71.6% at both, the pods waiting for a place −59.4% and −70.7%, the 95th percentile −15.4% and −21.3%, and the machines
parked over the eight days 82 and 46 against 329. A jump that sharp between two neighbouring beats is a rule's count crossing a
threshold, not a pace. The cause is the cruise rule (rule 7: work waiting for a place decision after decision puts every machine
in service until the line has been empty as long). Its wait is written in seconds, `--cruise-after-s 120`, and v7 converts every
such wait to decisions as n = max(1, round(seconds / period)): 2 at 60 and 75 s, but round(1.33) = 1 at 90 s and round(1.0) = 1
at 120 s. With one decision, a single reading with one pod waiting set every machine in service and a single empty reading let
them go: the rule no longer asked for work that waits "decision after decision", the words it is written by. The fix
(`omni_controller/controller.py`): the cruise wait is never fewer than two readings, `max(2, round(120 / period))`, when it
is derived from seconds; a count an operator sets by hand (`--cruise-after`) stands as set. At every beat up to 80 s the count
is what it was (24 at 5 s, 8 at 15 s, 4 at 30 s, 2 at 60 and 75 s), so nothing below 80 s moves; at 90 and 120 s it is 2
(`tests/test_pace_clocks.py`, which fails on the unfixed rule). Corrected, the kind benchmark's setting reads at 90 s, against 60 s, the machine-hours down 1.7%, STEADY, the minutes over the line down 4.7%, STEADY, the pods waiting down 12.1%, STEADY, the 95th percentile down 0.2%, STEADY; at 120 s the machine-hours down 2.1%, STEADY, the minutes over the line down 3.7%, STEADY, the pods waiting down 29.6%, GAIN; machines parked over the eight days 190 and 119 against 329 at 60 s. No other count of the
governor's falls to a single reading between 5 and 120 s: the breach's clear time (180 s) is 2 decisions at 120 s, the strict
window (300 s) 2, the trial's phase (1,200 s) 10; the brain's dwell is one step by design and its waits round to the nearest
step. In the cloud's setting (the machines alone, at the tune-down) every service, machine-hour and energy reading at 90 and
120 s is the same before and after the fix, seed by seed; what moves is the governor's own reads of the cluster, 1.9% and 1.2%
more (cruise pauses the five-second floor reads, and it now pauses less often), and the machines parked on three seed-beats
(128 against 126, 148 against 147, 83 against 80).

### 88.14 Omni v18: Omni direct in the engine; the three arms



Omni v18 (`OMNI_V18.json`, digest `1cb92edb64c4391d`, 62 files) stood on main from 23 October, night, to 25 October, when omni-v19 (`docs/OMNI_V19.md`) landed. The founder's orders of
the same evening: "Native is Kubernetes on the muscles. Omni on native is Omni on top of Kubernetes on top of the muscles. And
then Omni direct is simply Omni on top of the muscles, no Kubernetes ... they all need to be written in code and toned in ...
and push it all"; and, once it was pushed, "It should be not 17 anymore, it should be 18 ... Give me this new live engine wired
up now to where you're at".

omni-v18 is omni-v17 (`docs/OMNI_V17.md`) with Omni direct taken into the engine: the seven files of Omni-Compass's own
orchestrator that hold its rules are fingerprinted like every other wire, so no rule of Omni direct can change without the
version changing (the principle omni-v15 set for the eight wires it took in). 55 of its 62 files are omni-v17's bytes; the
seven new ones are `omni_orchestrator/__init__.py`, `agent.py` (the machine's hand), `brain.py` (the brain), `cgroup.py` (the
walls), `control.py` (the control plane), `front.py` (the front) and `scheduler.py` (the room rule). The showing's workload and
clients (`omni_orchestrator/workload.py`, `load.py`) are the harness and stay outside. A version declared before omni-v18 is read
without the seven (`tools/omni_version.py`, `ORCHESTRATOR_WIRES`), so every earlier commit keeps the version it ran on.

#### 88.14.1 The three arms

Every organism the orchestrator runs is shown three ways, all three in one showing and every pair read by the one key, paired
by step (`tools/orchestrator_show.py`, `.github/workflows/orchestrator.yml`, `docs/OMNI_ORCHESTRATOR.md`):

| arm | what moves the muscles | brain |
|---|---|---|
| native | Kubernetes' published autoscaling rule, written by us, every machine on, units spread | `yardstick` |
| Omni on native | that rule's units, never fewer; Omni's reflex and fail-up above it; Omni's conveyance, busy room rule, packing and machines on top; no fold, no verdict (the engine's strict form, as on the kind rigs) | `omni_native` |
| Omni direct | Omni alone on the muscles, no Kubernetes: everything Omni on native does, and the fold below the rule's count under the verdict | `omni` |

#### 88.14.2 What Omni direct carries

Every mechanism in Omni direct's brain is the engine's own, so the same gain goes to Omni on top of native:

- **conveyance** (omni-v7, omni-v13): each unit's processor wall set to the room its machine can spare under 75% busy, shared
  among the service's units there, never under the request, handed back between 70% and 75% and at the top beside another
  workload's room; journaled, written to the hand, read back from the kernel's `cpu.max`;
- **the reflex**: work waiting in line adds as many units as there are requests waiting, up to the step, in the same beat;
- **the twin**: Kubernetes' rule read on the same readings, each unit's use counted no higher than its request, as Kubernetes
  would see it; Omni never holds fewer units than the twin unless the verdict allowed the step;
- **the fold under the verdict** (`omnicompass/verdict.py`): a unit fewer than the twin tried on the service's own response
  times, under the same traffic (a trial whose arrivals move more than 15% is abandoned), kept only where it reads no LOSS
  within 2%; work waiting hands a step back at once (the immune reaction);
- **the hold on trials the traffic keeps abandoning** (new with omni-v18): a trial the traffic abandons holds the next off for
  6 beats, doubled at each abandonment in a row up to the verdict's recheck (24 beats), cleared by a trial judged to its end; a
  phase counts its step from the higher of the twin it found and the twin now. Found on the first three-arm showing, where every
  trial was abandoned yet each held a unit below the twin while it ran (Omni direct against Omni on native, work LOSS, down
  5.2%); fixed before the version landed (`docs/OMNI_ORCHESTRATOR.md`, section 2d);
- **the busy room rule** (omni-v7, `omni_controller/capacity.py`): no unit placed onto a machine at 75% of its measured busy
  share; the units packed onto the fewest machines, machines parked and woken;
- **the journal and the kill switch**: every change journaled before it is acted on and replayed when the control plane starts
  again; the kill switch holds the declared state and hands every conveyed wall back.

#### 88.14.3 What it read before it landed

Our own showing on one host, class L, one run of each arm (`docs/OMNI_ORCHESTRATOR.md`, sections 2c and 2d):

- **The three arms, quick form** (six steps of 15 s, after the fix): Omni on native against native, work GAIN, up 8.3%; Omni
  direct against native, work GAIN, up 9.1%; Omni direct against Omni on native, the 95th percentile GAIN, down 13.2%, and units
  GAIN, a cut, down 9.5%. No LOSS in any pair; nothing failed or wrong in any arm, the batch job or the drills.
- **Omni direct against native, full form** (18 steps of 25 s): work GAIN, up 4.7%; the 95th percentile GAIN, down 9.9%; units
  GAIN, a cut, down 10.3%; machines STEADY, down 1.7%; 0 failed and 0 wrong in 20,452 requests.

The model gate against omni-v17 (`results/model_gate/V18_VS_V17.md`): every model reads omni-v17's numbers, because none of omni-v17's
55 files moved; the gate's models do not run the orchestrator, whose own gate is the showing above.

And after it landed, the three runs on GitHub's machines (the full form, A, B and C from one commit) read Omni on native against native work GAIN in all three (up 5.2% to 7.4%) and the 95th percentile GAIN in all three (down 7.5% to 12.1%), Omni direct against native work GAIN in all three (up 5.7% to 9.4%) and the 95th percentile GAIN in all three (down 9.8% to 15.7%), machines STEADY, the units power given or STEADY, and Omni direct against Omni on native STEADY on every gauge; no LOSS in any pair in any run (`results/orchestrator/V18_THREE_ARMS_ABC.md`).

### 88.15 Omni v19: Omni-Compass by itself, a pod muscle of its own



Omni v19 (`OMNI_V19.json`, digest `36ee67284c035235`, 62 files) lands on 24 October, 16:54 UTC, under the founder's order of
23 October that every organism is shown three ways: native; Omni-Compass and native; and Omni-Compass by itself, "running direct
muscles" with native's own controller of that muscle switched off ("there's native, there's Omni and native, and then there's Omni
asked. It is omni-v18 (`docs/OMNI_V18.md`: Omni direct in the fingerprint) with one muscle added to the Kubernetes governor, in
`omni_controller/controller.py`, and the models' arm that runs it, in `realms/harness.py` and `realms/plants.py`; 59 of its 62
files are omni-v18's bytes. Nothing moves unless the operator names a workload to the muscle: with no workload named the engine is
omni-v18, decision for decision (the model gate below). Preregistered before any run (`docs/SOLO_PREREGISTRATION.md`). Read in the model
gate against omni-v18 on the same seeds (`results/model_gate/V19_VS_V18.md`), by itself against omni-v18 by itself arm by arm
(`results/model_gate/SOLO_V19_VS_V18.md`) and by itself beside native and beside Omni-Compass and native
(`results/model_gate/SOLO_V19.md`) before it was committed. The readings are our own models (evidence class S), never a benchmark
result. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed or approved these results.

#### 88.15.1 Why it is omni-v19: one name, two engines

This change was first built on the live engine's branch and landed there on 24 October, 01:30 UTC, under the name omni-v18
(digest `22486290b19349eb`, 55 files, on top of omni-v17), while main's omni-v18 (Omni direct in the fingerprint, digest
`1cb92edb64c4391d`, 62 files) had stood on main since 23 October, night. One version number names one engine, and no result is
read across engines, so the two are kept apart: the branch's omni-v18 never stood on main, and nothing it recorded is read as main's
omni-v18. Its change, the three files above and nothing else in the engine, is taken onto main's omni-v18 here, gated again against
main's omni-v18 on the same seeds, and lands as omni-v19. Every rule is the branch's; the code's own comments, which named the
branch's numbers (omni-v17, omni-v18), now name omni-v19, so the three files differ from the branch's bytes in those comments only.
Main's omni-v18 files and records stay as they were.

#### 88.15.2 The pod muscle of its own

On every engine before it, the Kubernetes governor moved a workload's pods only through the pod autoscaler's own object (its range
and its target): with the pod autoscaler switched off it had no pod muscle, so "by itself" held every workload at the operator's
count. omni-v19 gives it one (`--own-replicas namespace/name,...`, or `OMNI_OWN_REPLICAS`; `_own_pods`). For each workload the
operator names and no autoscaler governs, the governor sets the replica count itself, through the workload's own scale, by strict
C's rule: replicas = ⌈current × measured busy share / target⌉, up at once, down only to the highest recommendation of the last 300 s,
inside a tolerance of a tenth. The target is the one the compass moves for an autoscaler: the operator's own (the workload's
`omnicompass.io/target-utilization` annotation, else `--own-target`), down to 60% of it, the most pods the cover allows past the
wall. Never below the operator's own count at the max, never above the range's top (`omnicompass.io/replica-range`), never below
one pod; the count it shipped is recorded once on the workload and handed back by the reset. A workload an autoscaler governs keeps
its autoscaler: the muscle writes nothing there. `--native replicas` leaves it native and writes nothing; a security hold allows no
expansion. The muscle keeps the pace of the controller it stands in for: a reconciliation every 15 s on the fast checks
(`--own-every-s`, the pod autoscaler's sync), at the target the last decision set; the compass moves the target only in a decision,
at any beat of the dial.

In the models (`realms/harness.py`, `SOLO`; `realms/plants.py`, `native_off`), the arm by itself is the max with every pool whose
own count is the muscle's knob run with its autoscaler switched off, and its twin (the brain's sense of native) too. A power cap,
an admission limit and every other plant's knob are a setting native already holds still, or run through native's own loop as its
actuator: there by itself is the same arm as Omni-Compass and native.

#### 88.15.3 The fault found before it landed

On the branch, rebuilt on omni-v17, whose main engine decides every 60 s (as main's omni-v18 does), the first candidate moved its
pods only at a decision, once a minute. By itself in the model it then read the minutes over the response line LOSS against native
(34.8 minutes a day against native's 26.4), the 95th percentile still a GAIN. The pod autoscaler it stands in for syncs every 15 s. The muscle now
reconciles every 15 s between decisions; its window of fewer pods counts those reconciliations (the strict window's 300 s at any
beat). Two unit tests hold it (`tests/test_own_replicas.py`, 11 in all).

On Kubernetes, the kind rig's `ARM=solo` (`scripts/kind_bench.sh`): the pod autoscaler removed after the deploy, the operator's

(`fleet/capture/kube_capture.sh`). The three-run tables read it against native (`solo`) and against Omni-Compass and native
(`solo|compass`) (`tools/confirm_abc.py`, `tools/live_reps.py`). Its runs: `kubernetes by itself` in `scripts/reruns.txt`, the
steady load with the three arms in rotation (native, Omni-Compass and native, Omni-Compass by itself), A, B and C on GitHub's own
machines, written before the omni-v19 campaign opened. In our models, the organisms runner's third arm (`tools/run_realms_v5.py`):
every pool whose own autoscaler can be switched off, read against native and against Omni-Compass and native. Where native is a
setting, or its own loop is the actuator, the two Omni-Compass arms are one. No cloud runs by itself without the founder's word
(the order of 14 October: nothing in a cloud adds a machine).

#### 88.15.8 Beside it: Omni direct

Main's omni-v18 took Omni direct into the engine: Omni-Compass's own orchestrator (`omni_orchestrator/`, `docs/OMNI_ORCHESTRATOR.md`)

### 88.16 Omni v20: the data stores' wires fixed at their causes



Omni v20 stood on main on 25 October until omni-v21 landed that evening (`docs/OMNI_V21.md`).

Omni v20 (`OMNI_V20.json`, digest `1df07f8e36a97985`, 62 files) lands on 25 October, 13:24 UTC, under the founder's words of
25 October ("Fix, fix, fix ... The SYS bench, Kafka, whatever ... has got a problem, you got to fucking fix it ... it can be
fixed") and the standing order that every fault found is fixed and lands as the next version, told, not asked. It is omni-v19
(`docs/OMNI_V19.md`) with five of its wires changed: the data stores' runners `tools/run_sysbench.py`, `tools/run_kafka.py`,
`tools/run_ycsb.py`, `tools/run_redis.py` and `tools/run_pgbench.py`. 57 of its 62 files are omni-v19's bytes. The faults were
found by tracing why the Omni index read +4.32% before the 0.5% key of 24 October and +3.397% after it
(`docs/STORE_LOSS_ROOT_CAUSES_2026-10-25.md`): seven data-store rows, each with 0 or 1 of its three runs clear of the noise, that
the new key now counts. Three were faults in our own wiring, two were the test machine. The fixes were read in the store gate
(`tools/store_gate.py`, `results/model_gate/STORE_GATE.md`) before they were committed. The gate's readings are our own model
(evidence class S), never a benchmark result. Run and scored by The Omni-Compass LLC's own code. No outside party has reviewed
or approved these results.

#### 88.16.1 What changed

- **sysbench: the brain reads its own workload.** `status()` counted only `statement/sql/{select,update,insert,delete}`.
  sysbench sends prepared statements, which those counters never see, so the brain read 4.1 statements a second (the harness's
  own monitoring queries) while sysbench sent 999 to 4,198. The compass force and the verdict's work sample were the brain's own
  queries, and it resized the buffer pool blind, 10 to 23 times an arm. Now sysbench connects as its own account (`omni_load`,
  created by `--setup` with rights on `sbtest` only), and the brain reads that account's statements from the per-user summary
  table, prepared ones included (`statement/com/Execute`, `statement/sql/execute`, `execute_sql`, and the four plain ones).
  Every sysbench row, the GAIN rows included, stood on the blind reading and runs again on omni-v20.
- **Kafka: an extra consumer is handed back.** Above the operator's count, the hand-back needed a consumer whose 200 ms poll
  came back empty, which never happens with 8 round-robin partitions: a third consumer allowed after a load peak stayed 170 of 451
  seconds and bought nothing. Now, above the operator's count, calm gives one consumer back while the backlog is within one poll
  round (50 messages a consumer), 30 s after the last change, because every change pauses the whole group. "Idle" is a full
  second with nothing consumed, and a consumer starts busy; no trial starts on the seconds before the producer begins (the
  2→1→2 double rebalance at the start of every arm is gone).
- **YCSB: the cache grows back below native.** Below the operator's size, nothing grew the cache on misses; a give-back trial
  allowed before the working set widened left two arms 64 MB short with misses at 1% or more for 435 of 457 seconds. Now, below
  native, the cache takes 64 MB a second back while misses are 1% or more, up to native's size, and an open give-back trial is
  abandoned. "Full" is WiredTiger's own 80%, or evicting in the last second (it was 90%, a level WiredTiger never holds).
  `serverStatus` is read in full once, then only for the sections the brain reads. mongod's CPU and the harness's are recorded
  apart, steal apart, beside the host's.
- **Redis: the CPU apart.** redis-server's, the App's, the brain's and the sampler's CPU are recorded apart, steal apart, beside
  the host's. The knob's rule is unchanged.
- **pgbench: the same state every arm.** Each arm starts from `pgbench -i` and a CHECKPOINT; the give-back waits 30 s after an
  add-back (5 s before); one aggregate line a second is kept from the per-transaction log. The workflow logs vmstat, iostat and
  PostgreSQL's checkpoints, lock waits and autovacuum into the run's files, so the runner's write stalls (6.2 s of schedule lag
  in a native arm far under capacity on the omni-v16 runs) can be told from the engine.
- **The readers.** `tools/omni_index.py`, `tools/ycsb_abc.py` and `tools/redis_abc.py` prefer the stack's own CPU where a run
  recorded it; older tables read as before (the index stays +3.397% on them).

#### 88.16.2 The gate

The store gate replays every archived omni arm of the omni-v16 three-run tables, second by second, through omni-v19's wires and
omni-v20's, each with its own verdict fed the recorded cost samples and its own knob, and reads the pair by the gauge's aim. It
is open-loop: it shows what each wire decides on the same seconds, not how the store would have answered.

| Wire | Arms | What omni-v20 does against omni-v19 |
|---|---:|---|
| Kafka | 27 | rebalances in the first 15 s 2.0 → 0, GAIN +100%; writes GAIN +92.9%; seconds below native while short GAIN +100%; seconds above native while calm (light) 37.6 → 6.3, GAIN +83.1% inside the arms' noise; consumers held +0.6%, inside the noise |
| YCSB | 36 | seconds below native while short 38.9 → 2.2, GAIN +94.4%; cache held power given +5.2%; writes power given +76.6% |
| pgbench | 26 | writes GAIN +21.0%; seconds below native while clients waited GAIN +12.7%; pool size =0.4%, under the floor |
| Redis | 9,728 seconds | the two wires decide differently 0 times; the new CPU figures exist only in new runs |
| sysbench | | the decisions cannot be replayed: the archived files hold only the old reading's counter (4.1 to 4.2 a second against sysbench's 999 to 4,198); a short real run reads the new one |

No LOSS on any wire. The YCSB cache rise is a real change of behaviour: the new "full" opens the grow path on seconds that were
slow, missing and evicting, which omni-v19 refused as "slow with room to spare". It is power given, and the replay cannot show
what the extra memory buys; the real runs on omni-v20 read it. One pgbench arm (select, run C rep 3) is left out of the gate
because omni-v19's own replay matched only 32% of its record there; every other arm reproduces its record in 97% or more of the
seconds.

#### 88.16.3 What runs again

Every benchmark runs again on omni-v20 (`scripts/reruns.txt`, the conductor's campaign from 13:24 UTC on 25 October), the data
stores first in meaning: sysbench, Kafka, YCSB, Redis and pgbench. A fourth pgbench repetition, balancing the arm order against
the runner's drift, is written as a proposed amendment in `docs/POSTGRES_PREREGISTRATION.md`, not yet in force. Tests:
`tests/test_store_wires.py` (each check fails on omni-v19's runners and passes on omni-v20's) and `tests/test_store_gate.py`.

### 88.17 Omni v21: the immune system knows itself, knob by knob



Omni v21 (`OMNI_V21.json`, digest `b658f05d43c1e602`, 63 files) stood on main from the evening of 25 October to 30 October, when
omni-v22 (`docs/OMNI_V22.md`, the data stores' wires at the max) landed on it; its tables stand as its own record. It is omni-v20 with
the immune system's self-knowledge, the founder's order of 25 October:

> "OmniCompass's mechanism must know when something is redlining out of its band when OmniCompass is on it. And if OmniCompass
> couldn't fix it to stop it redlining, then OmniCompass's own mechanism must know that if native is better, then it switches
> itself to native. If native is not better, well, then it'll stay wherever and redline there, because redlining less with
> OmniCompass than something else is still a benefit ... against native ... This code and mechanism need to be built within the
> C++ harness, within the immune system ... The immune system has to be activated in nervous system to propagate."

#### 88.17.1 The rule, in plain words

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Redlining** | A knob Omni-Compass holds whose gauge is over its own line (the reading divided by the line is over 1) for three decisions in a row. |
| **Stuck** | Redlining, and Omni-Compass's own pushing has not brought it back: the knob is at its own limit, or the reading has not fallen by 5% of where the redline began. |
| **Native is stronger** | Native's twin, the same moment under native's own setting, reads lower than Omni-Compass by more than 5%. |
| **Hand back** | Stuck and native stronger: the knob goes to native and stays there 10 decisions, the hold doubling for each hand-back in a row (up to 160) and halving after a quiet hold. |
| **Stay** | Stuck and native not stronger: Omni-Compass keeps the knob and says so in its audit. It redlines less than native would, which is still a benefit against native. |
| **Return** | After the hold, Omni-Compass takes the knob back only when its own twin reads lower than native's by the same margin and nothing redlines with it. |
| **The nervous system carries it** | An organ every governed knob of which is handed to native has none of Omni-Compass's authority (`native_hold`) until it is returned. |

#### 88.17.2 Where it is written

| Place | What |
|---|---|
| `omnicompass/immune.py` | the rule, one knob at a time |
| `cpp/src/immune.cpp`, `cpp/include/omnicompass/immune.hpp` | its C++ twin, line for line, proven alike to the last bit on 200 seeded scripts (`tests/test_cpp_immune_parity.py`, sealed by `tools/seal.py`) |
| `omnicompass/nervous_system.py`, `cpp/src/nervous_system.cpp` | `native_hold`: the hand-back carried to the organ's authority, in both twins |
| `omni_controller/controller.py` | each service's autoscaler target: the response time over its line is the redline; native's twin is the same demand under the operator's target, the replicas native's own rule would ask and the M/M/1 wait they would give |

omni-v19's immune rules come with it onto omni-v20: the hand-back on a pod that waits, the immune memory, native's line, immune
maturity and the step back (`tests/test_immune_system.py`).

#### 88.17.3 What the model gate read

The model gate against omni-v20 (`results/model_gate/V21_VS_V20.md`, eight seeds, every model, our own models,
evidence class S): no LOSS against omni-v20 in any model.

| Model | Against omni-v20 |
|---|---|
| the cluster (the cloud's setting), at 60 s, at 15 s, with blinks, as shipped | pods waiting for a place down 12.9% to 13.3%, fewer waiting, GAIN; machine-hours up 0.9% to 1.3% and energy per core-hour up 0.8% to 1.0%, power given; the power cap's moves, reversals and travel down 1.3% to 1.4%, GAIN |
| the conveyance, its quota cases, the batch beside the service | every gauge the same as omni-v20, STEADY |
| the card, the card near its floor | every gauge the same as omni-v20, STEADY |
| the verdict | the same as omni-v20, STEADY |

Against native the gate reads the LOSS rows omni-v18, omni-v19 and omni-v20 carry, none caused by this version and each on the
next version's list: the pod start wait in the conveyance models (up 9.0% and 10.0%), the batch beside the service (requests
served down 2.1%, alert minutes up 9.8%), and the card's 95th and 99th percentiles (up 0.9% to 5.8%).

### 88.18 Omni v22: the data stores' wires at the max, through each store's own account of a miss



Omni v22 (`OMNI_V22.json`, digest `0e23a0bc561b900a`, 65 files) stood on main from 30 October to 31 October, evening, when
omni-v23 (`docs/OMNI_V23.md`) landed on it; its runs stand as its own record. It is omni-v21 with the five data stores' wires brought
to the max, the founder's order of 30 October:

> "Anything that has a problem is what your job is ... find out why they went one way or the other and tweak it and turn it and tune
> it to the best possible way for an Omni Compass engine to interact with this as a system governor, convergence control core plane
> that it is ... bring to a solid A mechanism."

The store wires were written on 9 and 10 October with the brain's verdict judging every move under the resource objective, before the
founder's order of 12 October that the max is the default brain, and were never brought to it. On omni-v21 they carried 33 of the 50
LOSS rows (`docs/LOSS_LEDGER.md`); their causes, read from the runs' own files, are on `docs/STORE_ROOT_CAUSES_2026-10-30.md`: the
wall abandoned every spend trial and the fail-up was clamped to the allowance those trials never earned, so in 4,426 of the 4,581
seconds Redis stood over its line the brain asked for memory and was refused, and Kafka's hand-back gave back a consumer the load
still needed.

#### 88.18.1 The rule, in plain words

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **The max on a store's knob** | The wire's own rule asks; what it asks goes through unclamped, up to the operator's cover, never below native. The resource it takes (memory, consumers, servers) is power given, shown beside what it bought. |
| **The store's own account of a miss** | MySQL: the performance schema's timer on the data files' reads against the workload's statement timer. MongoDB: WiredTiger's time reading pages from disk for the application's threads against the server's own read latency. Redis: the application's own split of each request into hits and misses. Over the last 10 s, the misses' share of the service's own time. |
| **The gate** | Memory is spent only where that share is at least the one key's floor, a half of one percent (`tools/readings.py`): under it the misses are nothing the record could read, so memory could buy nothing it could read, and the knob holds and says why. Where the account is not read this second, nothing is known and nothing is taken. |
| **The host's room** | A notch is taken only while the host keeps 5% of its memory available after it (`/proc/meminfo`, the compass's cushion). Unread, nothing is taken. |
| **The working set's floor** | A hand-back never goes below the most memory the store held in the last 60 s (with the fullness margin, rounded up to a notch), nor below native: a knob handed back into its working set evicts what the service still asks for and buys it back at the store's price. |
| **Kafka's twin and reflex** | Each partition's arrivals (the topic's log-end offsets, once a second) placed on the members by the range assignor; a member's rate learned from the seconds the queue grew; the count goes at once to the smallest one that carries the arrivals and the backlog at nine tenths of a member's rate, never clamped; handed back in one move only to a count that carries the last minute's peak at seven tenths, 30 s after the last change; never below the operator's count; the immune hand-back to native when Omni-Compass's count redlines, stuck, and native's twin reads lower. |
| **PostgreSQL's pool** | A server added while clients wait is never clamped; the pool is never taken below the pooler's own setting. |
| **The dial** | `OMNI_DIAL=save` keeps omni-v21's loop on every wire (the tune-down, where giving the resource back is the aim); every record carries its dial. |
| **The fingerprint** | `tools/store_brain.py` (what the three cache wires share) and `tools/knob_verdict.py` (the tune-down's verdict) join it: no rule of the store wires changes without the version changing. |
| **The hand-back lands** (the Kubernetes governor, the same version) | Every step of the governor's hand-back (the autoscalers' ranges and targets, the operator's own counts, every muscle's lever, the node pool) is tried 5 times against a transient failure of the cluster's API, 1 s apart doubling to 4 s, each on its own, and what did not land is raised and audited, never left silent. On 30 October (six-kube run 41044680505, repetition 346) one 500 from the API on the autoscaler list, at the reset, ended the whole hand-back on its first read: the conveyed CPU limits (1230m, 1850m) and the replica range (1 to 13) stayed behind and the arm was marked invalid. `omni_controller/controller.py` `_persist`, `omni_controller/muscles.py` `_guard_restore`, `RESTORE_TRIES`; `tests/test_restore_retry.py`. |

What was tried and withdrawn: a slope of latency on miss share inside the arms as the price of a miss. It read 0.5 to 1.3 ms a unit
of miss share on MySQL while the controlled comparison across pool sizes read none; the host's noise moves the misses and the latency
together, and a regression reads that as a price. The root-cause page's first reading of the MySQL and MongoDB runs, that a miss cost
the statement nothing, is withdrawn on the same page: the server's own meter, read on a machine of our own, puts the misses at 3% to
32% of what a statement waits for (a tuning-bench reading, class L on that host, no benchmark result).

#### 88.18.2 Where it is written

| Place | What |
|---|---|
| `tools/store_brain.py` | the working set's floor, the store's account of its misses, the gate, the host's room, the max's record |
| `tools/run_sysbench.py`, `tools/run_ycsb.py`, `tools/run_redis.py` | each cache wire's `Brain`: its own compass law and rule around the shared max; the server's account read each second; the attach check that stops a MongoDB run on a server without the account |
| `tools/run_kafka.py` | the group's twin, the reflex, the hold, the immune hand-back; the tune-down under the dial |
| `tools/run_pgbench.py` | the pool's `Brain`: never clamped upward, never below the pooler's own setting |
| `tools/knob_verdict.py` | the tune-down's verdict, now in the fingerprint; its summary reads the max's records |
| `omni_controller/controller.py`, `omni_controller/muscles.py` | the hand-back that lands: every step tried 5 times against the API's weather, each muscle on its own, what did not land raised |
| `tools/store_gate.py` | the store gate: every candidate replayed on omni-v21's archived seconds (class S) |
| `tools/kafka_model.py`, `tools/redis_model.py` | the two closed-loop models (class S), every input set from omni-v21's runs' own files |
| `docs/MYSQL_PREREGISTRATION.md` (amendment 6), `docs/YCSB_PREREGISTRATION.md` (6), `docs/POSTGRES_PREREGISTRATION.md` (4), `docs/REDIS_PREREGISTRATION.md` (5), `docs/KAFKA_PREREGISTRATION.md` (4) | declared before any run on them |

| **Same-tower OFF / observe / ON receipt:** observe identical to OFF; ON ahead of the graded-reflex comparison build on healthy time, recovery, energy, violations and peak power (peak below OFF) | simulation, held-out | `results/tower_off_on/`, `results/external_review/CHATGPT2_REVIEW.md` |
| **Live levers under the nervous system:** 19 of 19 checks on real Kubernetes; reset restores everything | live, kind | `results/live/LIVE_LEVERS_2_NERVOUS.txt` |
| **Shadow pilot kit:** a read-only identity made 0 writes across 40 decisions | live, kind | `results/live/LIVE_SHADOW_1.txt` |
| **Safety shield:** 2,000,000 adversarial cases, 0 violations (the test found 2 real bugs, both fixed); C++ twin matches | test | `tests/test_shield_properties.py` |
| **C++ engine:** 100,000,000 decisions, no failures, about 2.3 µs per decision | test | `results/SOAK.json` |

### 89.3 What still loses, measured

- **C, typical response time, web and four-cluster:** about 20% slower than every platform. Omni fills pods to 80%,
  where the others stop at 70%, and trades response time for energy.
- **C, machine starts and stops:** loses to plain Kubernetes and OpenShift, which hold machines steady and pay for it
  in machine-hours.
- **C, GPU and batch:** energy 1-2% lower and power and heat margins 1-4% lower than the tight packers (AKS/Karpenter,
  CAST AI, Spot).
- **Live, set 3, with a working probe:**
  - Omni kept all 6 machines. Latency near the 500 ms SLO blocks machine release.
  - There is no significant difference from native on anything else, except that C has more waiting pods.
  - The earlier live machine savings (sets 1-2) are withdrawn, because the broken probe had blinded the latency sense
    (`results/live/LIVE_REPS_PROBE_DEFECT.md`).
  - Set 4's decision trail showed why. Latency spikes from pod saturation at load steps kept the service from being
    clean, and the engine's calm stayed under the machine threshold (0.65 against 0.7). Both are addressed by the
    attribution gate and the two-way wiring above; the live test is pending (`results/live/LIVE_REPS_4_DIAGNOSIS.md`).
- **A bound, not a loss:** no controller, even one with perfect foresight, can match both the tightest packer's
  machine-hours and the calmest autoscaler's churn at once (`tuning/bound.py`).

### 89.4 Two-way nervous system (new, live test pending)

Manuscript Appendix J names delay and dropout handling and feedback interpretation as the nervous system's job. The
live controller now wires both directions (`docs/TWO_WAY_NERVOUS_SYSTEM.md`).

- **Blind senses are detected against the wall clock.** A hung probe was the root cause of the live set 1-2 error.
  - A blind sense feeds the engine's `stale` channel.
  - It blocks every give-back.
- **Commands are read back.** Drift feeds the engine's `drift_ratio`. No new machine release goes out before the
  last one has landed.
- **The machine organ has its own engine view and a release gate.** Pods move first, and the headroom proof uses the
  engine's rho.

**Tests:** 75,000 blind states, 200,000 gate states, 300,000 nervous-system states.

**Live sets 5 and 6 could not run.** From 03:51 UTC GitHub refused every job, including `verify`: runner ID 0, no
steps, failed within about 2 seconds. That is GitHub declining to start runners, which on a private repository is
most often exhausted Actions minutes or a spending limit. It is not a code failure. `python verify.py` passes
locally at this commit.

# Back Matter


## Glossary


| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Antagonist pair | the up side and the down side of a muscle's control, each with its own gain |
| Authority | how far the nervous system lets an organ move this decision |
| Band | a reading's or a knob's safe range |
| Compass | the band seen as a position from 0 (calm) to 1 (the line), with its bottom in the middle |
| STEADY | Equalized, Verified baseline, Equilibrium, Neutral: the mean change under 0.5% (under the floor), or nothing moved (the same), or a knob at its limit on native; the key, front matter |
| GAIN | Growth, Advantage, Improvement, Net-positive: a gauge moved the way its declared aim asks, against native; a resource cut is a GAIN; the key, front matter |
| GAIN in all three of our runs | the mean change 0.5% or more, every run (A, B, C) moved the same way with its 95% interval clear of zero, and that way a GAIN for the gauge's aim |
| GAIN by the mean of our three runs | the mean change 0.5% or more toward the gauge's aim, not every run clear of zero; the count of runs beyond the noise stands beside it (Chapter 59) |
| LOSS | Leakage, Off-track, Setback, Subpar: a gauge moved against its declared aim (less work, a longer wait, more misses); it should never appear, and where it does it is shown, its cause found and fixed; the key, front matter |
| Power given | a resource spent or held that rose: what Omni put in to buy the work and speed beside it; shown, never called a loss |
| Cover | a knob's hard range; every write is clipped to it |
| Cushion | the 5% at each edge of the compass, 10% in all |
| DEX-YLL-1 | the company's number, 1-888-DEX-YLL-1, read in order as the engine runs: DEX, Data Exchange (the input, the two-way plug); YLL, Yield Limit Line (the boundary: every muscle up to its own yield limit, never past it); 1, one closed loop (the output; in code 1 is true, in science 1 is unity) |
| Fail up | the return to full capacity the moment service crosses the wall or a sense goes blind |
| Governor | the process that reads, decides and writes; Omni-Compass |
| Muscle | any machine, service or controller Omni-Compass reads and sets |
| Native | the system as it runs without Omni-Compass: every muscle under its own native controller, as its vendor ships it (the native baseline) |
| Omni-Compass on native | the second arm: the native system with Omni-Compass on top of it ("omni") |
| Omni-Compass direct | the third arm, Omni-Compass by itself: each knob's native controller switched off and Omni-Compass the only controller moving it (section 1.1) |
| Factory profile | the complete, versioned set of Omni-Compass default settings shipped together (section 76.8; `docs/FACTORY_PROFILE.md`) |
| Candidate, active and custom profile | a proposed combination under evaluation; the settings actually governing the current run; an identifiable configuration that differs from the released factory profile (section 76.8) |
| The best validated factory profile for the declared operating conditions | the profile the eight steps of section 76.8 establish; the meaning "optimal" has here, and the only one |
| Restore factory profile; Return to native | the two restoring controls: reapply the released configuration; hand governance back and restore the recorded native settings (the reset) |
| The ten organisms; the twenty scenarios | the seven of the catalog, the orchestra, the live benchmark engine's organism and the whole organism, each read native and on native (sections 34.7 and 60.10) |
| The cloud is a wire | a cloud is the wire between the software end and the bare metal; Omni-Compass can live in all three places (section 60.6) |
| Beyond the noise | a run whose 95% interval excludes zero; a three-run reading carries the count of its runs beyond the noise (Chapter 59) |
| Off the clock | a repetition in which either arm ended more than 5% of its window late; marked, the pairing stands |
| Organism | a set of muscles run together on one clock |
| Omni index | the one combined number: the geometric mean of every real category's work, speed, machines and energy ratios, each read by the three-run rule |
| Omni v1, v2, v3 | the frozen engines, fingerprinted file by file; a result belongs to the engine its commit carries |
| Plug | the two-way connection to one muscle: read, write, read back, restore |
| Pool (Azure) | one machine family under Azure's autoscaler with its own ceiling; several pools make the fleet |
| Profile (service or batch) | a named set of the compass's settings for one kind of work, service (the default) or batch: a setting inside a configuration profile |
| Race | full speed at once while work waits, so a burst is never served slowly |
| Yield limit line | a muscle's own limit, read live: Omni-Compass takes it right up to the line and never past it, as an engineer loads a material up to its yield limit, the most it carries and still springs back unharmed |
| Speed floor | the clock a card reaches on its own while busy, learned from its own meter; the governor never sets the ceiling under it |
| Receipt | the paired record of native against Omni-Compass for one run |
| Snapshot | a knob's value read once before the first write; the restore point |
| The runs disagree | runs clear of the noise point different ways; the test is unstable on that measure and is looked into |
| Wire check | the test that proves every wire follows, reads back and returns before anything runs |
| Work per energy | work done divided by energy used; the primary outcome |
| Work inside the line | the requests, transactions or messages a second answered within the response line; the product number on every real stack |
| One pedal | push for more, lift off for less, idle (the pedal lifted all the way), reset (everything back to native): how the governor moves capacity under autopilot |
| Cruise | every machine in service while work waits for a place, held without second-guessing until the line has been empty for two decisions |
| Idle at once | the work done and demand at zero: the pedal lifted all the way in one move, every safety check still holding |
| Kill switch | security only: one switch in a human hand that turns every governor on the machine off at once; never the reset |
| Lease | the record every governor renews each decision; a lease older than its limit, or a dead process, makes the watchdog hand back for it |
| Watchdog | the service beside the governors that hands back for any governor that died or hung without doing it itself |
| Verdict | the paired trial on the muscle itself that allows a slow knob to move only where the cost is within 2%; "left native" where no step passes |
| Slack gate | v3's rule: a motion axis busy more than half the time at full speed keeps its speed native |
| Tuning case | the one workload, cell or swarm the rules were fitted on; shown in every table and never counted |
| Untouched case | a workload, cell or swarm the rules were applied to unchanged; the judged rows |
| Knee | nine tenths of a system's measured capacity, where its queue begins to grow; the broker's native was set there by design |
| Amendment | a change to a preregistration after it was written, with its time and reason; one made after a result was seen says so |
| Dwell | the seconds after a knob moves during which the law will not move it back |
| Notch | the smallest step a knob moves in one decision (one consumer, 8 MB of cache, one tap) |
| Evidence class P, L, S | a physical meter; live software with no meter; a model of ours |
| Handed back | the knob read back at the operator's value at the end of an arm; every table says whether every arm was |
| Off the clock | see above; a repetition whose arm ended more than 5% of its window late |
| Own cost | the governor's CPU (its process and every command it ran) as a share of one core over the window, from its audit; a few thousandths of a core at every size |
| Smoke run | one repetition that exercises a harness end to end before any counted run; never counted, always recorded |
| L + S | an organism run with a real cluster inside: the cluster is L, the organism around it S |
| Working set | the records a workload actually touches over a window; a cache benchmark measures nothing unless the working set reaches the cache |
| Key space | the records a benchmark may ask for at one notch; in the MongoDB test the knob's load, stepped one notch at a time |
| Uniform draw | every record in the key space equally likely, so the working set is the key space; YCSB's shipped zipfian draw concentrates on a few thousand hot records whatever the key space |
| Ordered keys | records named in load order, so a run that asks for record n finds record n; a run with hashed keys against an ordered load asks for records that do not exist |
| Full-cache gate | the MongoDB and Redis rule: slow reads grow the cache only while the cache is full (nine tenths used), because a miss in a cache with room to spare is not the cache's to mend |
| Buffer pool | InnoDB's cache of table and index pages, the one memory setting every MySQL operator sizes; resized online by the server in whole chunks |
| Chunk | the unit in which MySQL resizes its buffer pool (128 MB as shipped); the knob's notch on that stack |
| Page cache | the operating system's own cache of file contents; where the data fits in it, a storage-engine miss is a read from memory and a decompression, not a disk read, and the gain available to the cache knob is smaller |

## Appendix C. The Equations in Full


    (1) dE/dt     = −α[E] E + β[int] + β[ext] + v[eff]
    (2) dU/dt     = μ U (1 − U²) − (dE/dt)/E[max] − λ[U] U + u,
                    |u| ≤ U_AUTHORITY = 25
    (3) dI[U]/dt  = (1 − U) − σ₁ E − δ S − λ[I] I[U]
    (4) v[eff]    = cos(ω[B] t / 2) · c · tanh(λ₀ + λ₁ (U − 0.5) + λ₂ S)
    (5) Φ(S)      = αₛ S² / 2 + βₛ S³ / 4 − δ S
    (6) dS/dt     = −dΦ/dS = δ − αₛ S − (3/4) βₛ S²
    (7) dB/dt     = Ḃ ;  dḂ/dt = γ[c] δ S − (ω[B] / Q[B]) Ḃ − ω[B]² B
    (8) R[B]      = finite-difference audit of (7) at every step;
                    never fed back into the state

    Control (one micro step, zero-order hold across all four RK4 stages):
        u = clip(−f[U](x, t) + K[P] (σ − U), −U_AUTHORITY, +U_AUTHORITY)
        K[P] = 12,  σ ∈ {−1, +1}

    The compass (every muscle):
        p = position of the service reading in its band
            (0 calm, 1 the line)
        F = A tanh((K[P] (p − center) + K[D] v) / A)
        K[D] ≥ critical damping
        p ≥ 0.95  ⇒  full up force; down side held
        knob ← clip(knob + g[side] F span, cover)

    The GPU governor (two wires, omni_controller/gpu_compass.py;
    one law, amendments 8 to 10):
        p = (mean response of the last 5 s − S) / (SLO − S),  S = SLO / 10
        p95 ≥ SLO, a failure, blind  ⇒  fail up
        fail up / race (utilization ≥ 0.95)
            ⇒  ceiling = top clock, lid = start limit
               (the card's own settings)
        steady under the limit (saturated, drawing ≥ 0.97 of the limit)
            ⇒  ceiling = the card's own busy clock, lid = start limit
               (the same watts, no knock-backs)
        otherwise:
            step = round(g[side] F f[top] / 15 MHz) · 15 MHz
            ceiling ← clip(ceiling + step, c[floor], f[top])
            c[floor] = max(f[busy,own] × floor, f[top] − k* 15 MHz)
                       (never under the card's own busy clock, never past
                        the verdict's deepest step k*)
            lid = clip(ceil(1.10 P[busy,own]), envelope floor,
                       start limit)
        g[up] 0.10, g[down] 0.0125, center 0.4, floor 1.00

    The verdict (omnicompass/verdict.py; every slow knob, the GPU ceiling
    and the Kubernetes machine count):
        reference r = the costs of n requests at the deepest allowed step
                      (a card: at native), measured fresh
                      (Kubernetes n = 200; a card n = 30)
        trial t     = the costs of n more at one step past it, under the
                      same traffic
        d = mean ln c[t] − mean ln c[r] ± 1.96 √(s²[r]/n[r] + s²[t]/n[t])
                      (Welch); stepwise a second interval against the
                      costs first measured at native; τ = ln(1 + a), a = 0.02
        LOSS   iff an interval lies wholly above 0  ⇒  refused
        wide   iff a half-width > τ and n[t] < 3n   ⇒  measure on
        allow  iff median t ≤ min(r, c[native]) (1 + a)  and  d ≤ τ
               (else refused, past the allowance)
        a trial begins only while calm, P after the last began
        (Kubernetes 600 s; a card 8 decisions); a phase past its limit
        (Kubernetes 1,200 s; a card 30) or out of calm is abandoned
        a refused step is not tried again for R (Kubernetes
        R = 7,200 s; a card 900 decisions = 30 min); the knob never goes past
        the deepest allowed step, so steps cannot add up beyond the
        allowance; on the max the machine count gives nothing back

    Kubernetes, the compass on the HPA target
    (omni_controller/controller.py; sets 30 and 31):
        target x ∈ [0.6 x[op], x[op]] (times the conveyed gain);
        the up force lowers x (more pods)
        p ≥ 0.95 from load (line breached, every sense live, nothing
        pending)  ⇒  x = 0.6 x[op] at once
        p ≥ 0.95 from a blind sense or pods waiting for a lost machine
            ⇒  x = x[op] (native's own)
        fault over (p < center, line clean, nothing pending)
            ⇒  x = x[op] at once, never held
        machines: one more at once past the wall; one back only when the
        verdict and the release gate agree
        g[up] 0.10, g[down] 0.02, release force < −0.2

    The productivity arithmetic (every receipt; manual section 76.4):
        work W equal in both arms;  G = C[native] / C[omni] − 1;
        the same work needs 1/(1 + G) of the resources;
        saving S = G / (1 + G):  G = 1/3  ⇔  S = 1/4

**The symbols, and their names in the code.** The equations are written in the symbols above; the source
(`omnicompass/core.py`, `omnicompass/adapter.py`, printed in Appendix H) spells each one out, and an engineer reading the two
side by side needs the correspondence once. The values are those the live controllers run (`STACK_PARAMS` in
`omnicompass/adapter.py`); the pressures and the drive are computed from the nine observations every decision and have no
fixed value.

| Symbol | In the code | What it is | Value in the live controllers |
|---|---|---|---|
| α[E] | `alpha_E` | the deviation's drain rate | 3.487 |
| β[int], β[ext] | `beta_int`, `beta_ext` | the internal and the external pressure on the deviation | computed each decision |
| v[eff], c | `v_eff`, `c` | the bounded drive and its bound | c = 1.0 |
| λ₀, λ₁, λ₂ | `lambda_0`, `lambda_1`, `lambda_2` | the drive's offset and its weights on the alignment and the stress | −0.40, 1.55, 1.15 |
| μ | `mu` | the depth of the alignment's double well | 3.782 |
| E[max] | `E_max` | the deviation scale in the alignment's equation | 2.0 |
| λ[U] | `lambda_U` | the alignment's own damping | 0.0 |
| σ₁ | `sigma_1` | the deviation's weight in the memory | 0.38 |
| δ | `delta` | the stress's drive (the engine's own default is 0.5) | 0.705 |
| λ[I] | `lambda_I` | the memory's leak | 0.719 |
| αₛ, βₛ | `alpha_s`, `beta_s` | the coefficients of the cubic potential Φ(S) | 0.12, 0.10 |
| γ[c] | `gamma_c` | the stress's drive on the bath | 1.0 |
| ω[B], Q[B] | `omega_B`, `Q_B` | the bath's natural frequency and quality | 1.0, 2.5 |
| Ḃ | `B_dot` | the bath's rate, the engine's only second-order element | state |
| R[B] | `R_B` | the finite-difference audit of the bath, never fed back | recorded |
| K[P] | `KP` | the control law's gain | 12 |
| u, U_AUTHORITY | `u`, `U_AUTHORITY` | the command and its authority | ±25 |
| σ | the target pole | +1 (healthy) or −1 (failed), the nearer basin by default | ±1 |
| f[U] | computed inside `control_command` | the drift of U with the command at zero | computed each micro step |

Parameter ranges, defaults and the proof of convergence: `omnicompass/core.py`, `docs/TRACKING_THEOREM.md`,
`docs/CANONICAL_ENGINE.md`.


## Appendix D. Metrics


Every gauge, where it comes from, and whether it is measured or modelled: `docs/METRICS_CATALOG.md`. The gauges that
appear in the three-run tables of this manual, with their source and their direction, are these:

| Gauge | Source | Measured or modelled | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| work inside the response line (requests, transactions or messages a second answered within the line) | the probe's own records, pgbench's log, the consumers' records, the application's records | measured | the aim is higher; the product number |
| response time, mean, median, 95th and 99th percentile | the same | measured | the aim is lower |
| time over the response line (share of samples) | the same, against the preregistered line | measured | the aim is lower |
| failed requests, lost messages | the same | measured | any increase is marked |
| alert minutes: whole minutes whose 95th percentile, failed requests counted over, was over the line | the probe's own records, minute by minute | measured | the aim is lower: the minutes an on-call page would be open |
| settings commands the governor wrote on its own | the governor's audit | measured | shown, not judged (no person touched either arm) |
| the governor's additions decided while the service was still inside its line (% of its additions) | the governor's audit | measured | shown, not judged |
| worker machines in service, mean; node-hours | the cluster's own node records every 15 s | measured (machine-hours on kind; Azure's own count on AKS) | the aim is lower |
| compute bill at list price | Azure's own machine count × list price per family | measured (a real bill) | the aim is lower |
| energy (Wh), the standby model | a declared formula over the machines in service (kind) | **modelled**, said so on every line | the aim is lower |
| host CPU busy; host CPU-seconds; CPU-seconds per 1,000 units inside the line | `/proc/stat` of the real machine under the test | measured | the aim is lower |
| Omni's own CPU (cores), mean | the governor's audit (its process and every command it ran) | measured | shown, not judged in the Kubernetes tables; a loss in all three of our runs where it is one |
| connections held open, consumers running, memory ceiling held | the pooler's, the group's, the cache's own reports | measured | the aim is lower (the resource held) |
| cache hit rate; consumer lag | Redis's INFO; the consumers' records | measured | the aim is higher; the aim is lower |
| HPA replicas, pods started, pod start wait | the API server's own records | measured | shown, not judged except pod start wait |
| organism work, energy, time over its line | the organism's plant models | **modelled** | by direction; S class |
| energy a mission, missions a charge (drones) | the simulator's motor constants through a declared model | **modelled** | lower; higher |
| cache size held, mean; bytes in the cache, mean; pages read into the cache (MongoDB) | the server's own `serverStatus` (WiredTiger cache) | measured | the aim is lower (the resource held); shown, not judged (pages read) |
| seconds from the kill to every setting back at the operator's (robustness) | the harness polling the cluster once a second from the kill | measured | the aim is lower; past 60 s marked; never, INVALID |
| the governor's resident memory, last ten minutes over the first ten (robustness, long run) | the process table, sampled every 15 s by the harness | measured | a growth over a quarter is marked |
| decisions made of expected; failed decisions (robustness, long run) | the governor's audit | measured | under 95% INVALID; any failed decision shown with its reason |
| mission time, position error, collisions (drones) | the simulator's own state at every step | measured in the simulator (S class) | lower; under the safe error; any collision voids the cell |
| handed back (every arm) | the knob read back at the end of the arm | measured | yes in every arm, or the run is invalid |
| off the clock | the organism's own clock against its window | measured | shown; marks the cell |

**Three rules for reading any gauge in this appendix.** A measured gauge is one the system under test, or the host's own
kernel, reported about itself; a modelled gauge is one computed from a declared formula over measured inputs, and every
table says which it is on the line itself, never only here. A resource gauge (machines, connections, consumers, memory,
cache) is always judged as aiming lower, even where the governor's purpose was to add the resource to buy service, so that
a gain bought with a resource is paid for in the same table and in the index. And a gauge marked "shown, not judged"
never enters a reading or the index; it is there so that a reader can see what the governor did (how often it moved, how
many pages it read, how many pods it started), not to be counted for or against it.


## Appendix E. Troubleshooting


| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Wire check `FAIL 3 up wire (lock)` | the driver or VM refuses clock locking | use bare metal or full passthrough; or run the one-wire governor |
| Wire check `FAIL 3 up wire (follows down)` | the card ignores the ceiling | update the driver; check for another management agent holding clocks |
| Wire check `FAIL 4 down wire` | the power limit is refused or capped by the board | check `nvidia-smi -q -d POWER`; run as root |
| `another copy of this test is already running` | a second copy was started | wait for the first or reboot; start once |
| `something else is using the GPU` | another process holds the card | stop it; the benchmark must run alone |
| Governor exit 5 | another writer changed a knob | find the other controller; Omni-Compass left its value alone |
| Governor exit 3 | a restore did not read back | restore by hand (`nvidia-smi -rgc`, `-pl <start>`); investigate before rerunning |
| `decision failed (n in a row)` | the cluster API is unreachable | turn it OFF; native runs on |
| Energy saved but p95 slower than native | the card served bursts below its own clock, or the lid sat under its own draw | read section 42.5; in the audit compare `telemetry.clock_mhz` while busy with `native_busy_clock_mhz`, and `want_w` with `native_busy_draw_w` |
| Fail-up in most decisions | `--slo-ms` set too low for the workload, or a stale feed read as blind | set `--slo-ms` from the workload's own target; check the feed's age |
| No saving at all, service unchanged | the card is saturated almost all the time (it races), or the service sits above the compass's center | expected on a card with no slack; the saving comes from the quiet stretches |
| Kubernetes: no machine ever given back | the release gate refuses (its reason is in the audit), or the service is above the compass's center | read `node_gate.reason` in the audit; check `--slo-ms` and the latency feed |
| Kubernetes: a repetition marked OFF THE CLOCK | the machine could not step the organism inside its window | a longer window for that size on that machine; never a faster reading of the same run |
| Broker: consumers climb to the cover and stay | messages wait at every step (the producer is past the group's capacity) | the benchmark's capacity step sets the peak at nine tenths of the operator's group; check the measured capacity in the run's log |
| Cache: the ceiling grows while little memory is used | cold misses read as pressure | the full-cache gate is the rule (used ≥ 90% of the ceiling); check `used_mb` beside `maxmemory_mb` in the run's log |
| Cache: the ceiling never grows | the working set fits the operator's ceiling | expected: a cache that fits has nothing for the ceiling to mend, and the row reads inside the noise |
| Storage-engine cache: the cache never fills, whatever the key space, and omni reads as a free memory saving | the benchmark's requests concentrate on a few hot records (YCSB's shipped zipfian draw), or the run asks for records the load did not write (hashed keys over an ordered load), so the reads are served from the index | a result that flatters the governor is the first thing to suspect: check "in cache" against the cache size in the per-notch lines; draw requests uniformly over the key space and name the same key order in load and run; a knob with nothing to do is not a saving |
| Storage-engine cache: the compass only ever reads calm | the line is set far above the stack's own latencies (a 2 ms line over 0.15 to 0.45 ms reads) | set the line on the tuning workload's own figures so that a hit is calm and a full-cache miss is slow, and write the figures in the preregistration before any counted run |
| Swarm: a cell reads "void" | two drones came within two collision radii in either arm | a task or simulator setting (keep-out, altitude stagger, depot spacing); fixed before any counted run and said in the preregistration |
| Three-run table heads itself with a warning | a run's commit is not the engine it claims, or the three are not separate runs | run `tools/omni_version.py --commit <sha>` on each; make the table only from runs on one frozen engine |
| Archive bot skips a run | the run was not finished when the bot passed, or the pass had taken its share of bytes | nothing to do: the next hourly pass copies it |

`docs/MYSQL_PREREGISTRATION.md` (the rules written before each run), `docs/OMNI_V1.md` to `OMNI_V3.md` (every result by engine), `docs/REGISTER.md` (every benchmark
and its file), `docs/PROOF_PROGRAM.md` (the program to full size with its costs), `docs/DOSSIER.md` (every result in one
place), `results/OMNI_INDEX.md` (the one number), `docs/WIRING_VERDICTS.md` (which knobs earn a wire in, and every loss
with its cause), `docs/STATE_OF_PLAY.md` (where everything stands), `docs/HANDOFF.md` (every command in one page).

**The map, claim by claim.** Each claim this manual makes is listed here with the class of evidence behind it and the
document that carries it, so that a reader can go from any sentence of the executive summary to the file that would have
to be wrong for the sentence to be wrong.

| Claim | Class | Where the evidence is | What would falsify it |

**What a referee asks of each document.** Of a preregistration: is it dated before the first counted run, does it name the
tuning case and the untouched cases, is every amendment dated and does any amendment made after a result was seen say so?
Of a three-run table: are the three run ids separate runs, does the head name the engine at each commit, is every gauge
of the preregistration present including the ones that went against the governor, and is the reading one of the three the
rule allows? Of the index: is every real category in it, is every tuning row out of it, and does a loss in all three of our runs enter
as a loss? Of the raw folder: does the SHA-256 manifest in it match the files, does the governor's audit show every
decision with its reading and its write, and does the hand-back record read the operator's value? Every one of those
questions has a yes in this program or a disclosure naming the exception; the disclosures are in section 60.14.

**How to audit one result from this manual to its raw files.** Take any row of Chapter 60. Its source column names a
three-run table in `results/live/`; the table's head names the three GitHub run ids, the commit each ran on and the engine
`tools/omni_version.py` reads at that commit. Each run id names a folder `results/live/raw/run-<id>/` (the branch `raw`,
opened by `scripts/raw_archive.sh open /run-<id>/`) holding every
repetition's files (the capture, the response times, the governor's audit and log, the per-request records, one SHA-256
manifest per repetition). The table tool named in the table's text (`tools/confirm_abc.py` or its siblings) rebuilds the
table from those folders; `tools/omni_index.py` rebuilds the index from the tables; `tools/dossier.py` rebuilds the
dossier. The preregistration named in the table's text holds the rules, written before the first counted run, with every
amendment dated. Nothing in that chain is by hand.

**What one repetition leaves behind.** Take the first repetition of the first kill-scenario run, archived at
`results/live/raw/run-37716845219/paired-1/`. It holds two folders, one per arm, and the omni arm's folder holds
twenty-nine files, every one of which a reader can open: `preflight.txt` (the UTC time, the arm, the git commit the arm
ran at, the versions of Docker, kind, kubectl, the API server and Python, the metrics-server version with its SHA-256,
the worker count and the probe's address); `rbac_omni.txt` (twenty lines of `kubectl auth can-i`, each verb the governor
needs reading yes and each it must not have reading no); `window_start.txt` and `window_end.txt` (the window's clock);
`load_schedule.log` (every load step and when it was applied); `latency.csv` (the probe's response times, one row a
second); `capture.csv` (the cluster's state every fifteen seconds: replicas, workers, pods pending, the HPA's target);
`host_cpu.csv` (the runner's own `/proc/stat`); `pod_watch.json` and `pods_end.json`, `nodes_end.txt`, `hpa_end.json`
(the API server's own records at the end); `audit.jsonl` (one line per decision: the compass's position, heading and
letter, the engine's state, every write with its value sent and its value read back); `controller.log` and
`controller2.log` (the first governor's log, and the second one's after the kill); `audit_kill.jsonl` (the watchdog's
restore writes, each with its command and its reason, such as "reset: remove record"); `watchdog.log` (one record: which
governor, its process id, whether it was hung or dead, every command run and each exit code); `robust.log` (the kill at
the 360th second with the settings as they stood, "target=50 range=1,10 limits=1850m 3700m workers=5/6", and the
hand-back "every setting at the operator's after 8 s, target=50 limits=500m workers=6/6 left=none"); `rss.csv` (the
governor's resident memory every fifteen seconds); `omni_writes.txt` (how many writes the governor made in the window:
42); `kill_switch.txt` (the reset check: target restored, workers in service, no record left); `omni2.pid` (the second
governor's process id) and `kill` (the marker the harness wrote at the kill); `robust.out` (the same robustness log as the
job printed it); `end_reads.err`, `pod_watch.err` and `capture.csv.errors` (empty, as they should be);
`metrics-server-components.yaml` (the pinned manifest as applied); and `SHA256SUMS.txt`, one line per file. A reader who doubts a number in the kill table can find the second it was taken.


## Appendix G. The Muscles: What Each Is For, and How It Is Wired



A **muscle** is one setting on one machine that already has its own control: a replica target, a node pool's size, a GPU's clock ceiling, a chiller's setpoint, a battery's reserve, a joint's effort. Omni-Compass does not replace that control. It reads the machine's meters and, at its default, the max, moves the setting the machine already accepts toward the machine's own limit for the most work, never past it and never below native, through a plug that reads the setting once before the first write, reads back every write, steps aside if another controller moves it, and walks it back to native at the end. A knob native already runs at the top of its range is at its limit on native and is left there.

This chapter lists all 1107 muscles of the v5 catalog (`realms/catalog_v5.csv`); each run records its engine separately. For each one it says what kind of machine it is, which of the four kinds of knob it is, what Omni-Compass reads and does with it, how such a muscle is reached in a real stack, and which organisms it belongs to. The plants behind the benchmark numbers are models of these machines (evidence class **S**); a muscle in this list is wired on a real system only through the levels and the checks of the manual (chapters 4 and 6). See `DISCLOSURES.md`.

### G.1 How to read an entry

**The four kinds of knob.**

- **capacity**: how much of the machine is in service (replicas, instances, units, speed). At the max Omni-Compass pushes it to the machine's own limit for the most work, never past it and never below native.
- **admission**: what is let in (queues, rate limits, admission control). Native already lets everything in: the knob is at its limit on native, and Omni-Compass reads it and leaves it native.
- **power**: the power share or limit the machine may draw. Native already runs it at full: at its limit on native, read and left native.
- **setpoint**: the target the machine's own loop holds (a temperature, a reserve, a process value). At the max a room is cooled ahead of the heat and a battery's charge is held for its line, inside the safe band, never behind native on its line.

**The five kinds of plant.** Every muscle is modelled on one of five plants, each with its own service reading and lever:

| Plant | What it is | What Omni-Compass reads | What Omni-Compass moves |
|---|---|---|---|
| `compute_pool` | a pool of servers, pods, GPUs, links or disks serving a stream of requests or jobs | how far its queue and its load sit toward the service line (queue or lateness, and load above half) | the capacity it may use: its replica or instance count (through its autoscaler's target or floor), its power share, or one unit given back through the release gate |
| `thermal_zone` | a data hall or building zone cooled by chillers, air handlers or fans | its temperature against its limit | its supply setpoint (colder is more cooling), its power share, or one cooling unit given back when the room has margin |
| `energy_storage` | a battery, UPS or microgrid store with a load and a grid connection | its draw on the grid connection and its reserve | its reserve setpoint (how much charge it holds back); its power limit is left native |
| `motion_axis` | a motor-driven axis: a robot joint, a flight-control surface, a reaction wheel, a traction motor | its tracking error and its load | its speed and effort share, or its power share |
| `process_loop` | a regulated process: a temperature, pressure, flow, level, voltage or composition held at a setpoint | how far the process sits from its band | its setpoint within its safe band, its actuator range, or its power share |

**Every muscle its own card.** The brain is one, its settings each muscle's own. A muscle's card holds the settings the max uses for that muscle (a machine pool: how full it runs on its forecast before it calls for more, and how many decisions of history it reads; a battery: how many wobbles of margin it keeps under its line, and, wired by its power, how long it reads its line before it holds and how much of it it keeps clear). The cards were found by an automatic search over every muscle on the development seeds, today's global setting always one of the choices, and kept only where the card beat the global setting beyond the noise on two separate sets of seeds and on no seed under any load fell behind native: never over its line more often, never less work, never its line cleared later (`tools/tune_cards.py`, `realms/muscle_cards_v5.csv`, `results/cards_v5/`). Inside a body, a battery wired by its power keeps the body's own margins on its line. 364 muscles carry a card of their own; every other muscle runs the global setting (machines started at 95% full, the last 20 decisions read, 3.09 wobbles of margin on a battery's line, 5% of it kept clear). Each muscle's card is in the last column of its family's table.


**The organisms.** The 1107 muscles build seven organisms: the spine (267 muscles, every muscle that sits in all four realms: the base every stack runs on, as an operating system is the base of every program), each of the four realms (every muscle whose realm list includes it, the spine among them), the four stacked with every duplicate kept (1,908), and the whole tower with every muscle once (1107). Each is run native and with Omni-Compass on top of native (`docs/THE_SPINE.md`, `docs/REALMS.md`).

| Organism | Muscles |
|---|---:|

Wires marked *modelled only* exist as plants in the benchmark and are not built for live use.

**How to wire any muscle on your own stack (the plug, chapter 4).** Every muscle below is wired the same way: Omni-Compass never replaces the native controller; it reads the controller's own meters (the wire out) and writes the one setting the controller already accepts (the wire in), through a plug that (1) reads the setting once before the first write and records it, (2) reads back every write and stops writing if another writer moved the setting, (3) renews a lease every decision so a dead governor's settings walk back to native by themselves, and (4) restores the recorded setting at the end. Each family's entry says which native controller owns its muscles, where the reading is tapped, where the setting is written, how it is restored, and whether that wire has run live in this repository or only on a model (`docs/wiring_recipes.csv`). The muscle's name is the setting's own name on that controller. Where the entry says *modelled only*, the plant exists in the benchmark and the wire is written against the controller's documented interface, not yet run on the machine.

### G.2 The spine: 267 muscles in all four realms, an organism of its own

The machines every realm stands on: servers, machines, GPUs and CPUs, network, storage, observability, security, cooling and electrical distribution. The spine is the seventh organism (`spine`, the base every stack runs on, run native and with Omni-Compass on top like the other six; `docs/THE_SPINE.md`), and each spine muscle is also part of every realm's organism, counted once in the tower and four times in the stack.

#### G.2.1 Cloud VM & Capacity (21 muscles)

Each is a pool of servers, pods, GPUs, links or disks serving a stream of requests or jobs; its class is `node` (a fleet of machines or VMs that boot in minutes), reached through the node pool's size command (Karpenter, Cluster Autoscaler, MachineSet, cloud ASG). Omni-Compass reads how far its queue and its load sit toward the service line (queue or lateness, and load above half). It belongs to every organism.

**Wire it on your stack.**

- **Native controller:** the cloud's autoscaling group or scale set: AWS Auto Scaling, Azure VMSS, GCP MIG.
- **Wire out (read):** group size, instance states, the target-tracking metric (the cloud's API and monitoring).
- **Wire in (write):** desired capacity, min and max, the target-tracking policy's target, through the cloud CLI or SDK.
- **Restore:** the group's desired, min, max and policy recorded once; restored from it.
- **Run live?** live on AKS through the node pool (family 5); the cloud SDK path itself is written, not yet run live.

#### G.2.2 Container Resources (25 muscles)

Each is a pool of servers, pods, GPUs, links or disks serving a stream of requests or jobs; its class is `server` (an application service on servers or pods), reached through the Kubernetes API (HPA target and floor, pod resize). **Wire it on your stack.**

- **Native controller:** the pod's own resource requests and limits (the Deployment template) and, where it runs, the VPA, Goldilocks or CruiseKube recommender.

- **Restore:** the operator's limit recorded in an annotation before the first write; every pod returned to it.
- **Run live?** live: omni_controller/muscles.py convey() (conveyance); KEDA and Goldilocks tables.

#### G.2.3 Host CPU & Memory (26 muscles)

Each is a pool of servers, pods, GPUs, links or disks serving a stream of requests or jobs; its class is `cpu_host` (a CPU host whose clock and power can be set), reached through Linux cpufreq and RAPL. Omni-Compass reads how far its queue and its load sit toward the service line (queue or lateness, and load above half). It belongs to every organism.

**Wire it on your stack.**

- **Native controller:** the Linux kernel's own governors: cpufreq (schedutil or the processor driver), RAPL, cpuidle, the memory manager.
- **Wire out (read):** /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq (frequencies and governor), /sys/class/powercap intel-rapl energy counters, /proc/stat busy share, /proc/pressure.
- **Wire in (write):** scaling_max_freq per policy and the RAPL package power limit through sysfs (root); on Kubernetes through the Kubernetes Power Manager's PowerProfile or EAR's policy.
- **Restore:** the governor's files snapshotted once and restored byte for byte (tools/run_cpu_power.py --restore).
- **Run live?** written and tested on the modelled machine (tools/run_cpu_power.py, cpu-power.yml); GitHub's machines are virtual and cannot write the governor: the live run needs a real Linux machine.

#### G.2.4 Kubernetes Placement & Scheduling (21 muscles)

Each is a pool of servers, pods, GPUs, links or disks serving a stream of requests or jobs; its class is `server` (an application service on servers or pods), reached through the Kubernetes API (HPA target and floor, pod resize). Omni-Compass reads how far its queue and its load sit toward the service line (queue or lateness, and load above half). It belongs to every organism.

**Wire it on your stack.**

- **Native controller:** kube-scheduler and its profiles, the descheduler, PriorityClasses, scheduling gates.

- **Run live?** modelled; the API path is the same kubectl patch the live controller uses for the HPA.

#### G.2.5 Kubernetes Workload Scaling (32 muscles)

Each is a pool of servers, pods, GPUs, links or disks serving a stream of requests or jobs; its class is `server` (an application service on servers or pods), reached through the Kubernetes API (HPA target and floor, pod resize). Omni-Compass reads how far its queue and its load sit toward the service line (queue or lateness, and load above half). It belongs to every organism.

**Wire it on your stack.**

- **Native controller:** the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, KEDA ScaledObject or VPA that owns the workload's scale.
- **Wire out (read):** the HPA's current and desired replicas, the Deployment's ready replicas (Kubernetes API, metrics-server), the service's response time from the probe.
- **Wire in (write):** the HPA's target (spec.metrics averageUtilization) and floor (minReplicas) by kubectl patch; KEDA through its ScaledObject, so the add-on keeps its own loop.
- **Restore:** the operator's target and range recorded in an annotation before the first write, restored from it, annotation removed.
- **Run live?** live: scripts/kind_bench.sh and omni_controller (HPA target, KEDA, Goldilocks, CruiseKube), three-run tables in results/live.
